title: Charts as Epistemic Actions for Experience-Driven Agentic Data Analysis
abstract: Data agents built on ReAct-style loops now execute complex analytical workflows over structured data, yet their intermediate reasoning still runs almost entirely through text. Human analysts instead move between numbers, tables, and charts, reading visual evidence to expose trends and anomalies that text summaries drop. We ask whether charts can serve as internal epistemic actions inside a data agent's reasoning loop, and how to teach an agent to use them. We first build \probe{}, a suite of 200 controlled tasks under four matched interface conditions, and find a persistent gap between what agents can read and what they choose to use. Agents score as well from self-generated charts as from numeric output, yet plotting access alone does not translate into consistent use. Task slices show that charts lead on temporal, pattern, and anomaly reasoning, while text leads on precise reading and conditional verification. We then propose \method{}, which distils two families of experience from conditioned trajectory rollouts. One family records how to select and verify analytical operations, and the other records when to invoke text, charts, or both. A trajectory judge scores outcomes and labels intermediate steps, and a validation gate admits only experience that improves held-out performance. On three held-out benchmarks with four LLM backbones, \method{} raises analytical accuracy and visual evidence quality over matched baselines, and backbones that never drew charts begin using them, all without touching model parameters.

headings: Charts as Epistemic Actions for Experience-Driven Agentic Data Analysis
3 Learning to Use Charts through Experience
3.3 Consulting Experience inside the Analysis Loop
body_start:
Abstract

Data agents built on ReAct-style loops now execute complex analytical workflows over structured data, yet their intermediate reasoning still runs almost entirely through text. Human analysts instead move between numbers, tables, and charts, reading visual evidence to expose trends and anomalies that text summaries drop. We ask whether charts can serve as internal epistemic actions inside a data agent’s reasoning loop, and how to teach an agent to use them. We first build ProbeBench, a suite of 200 controlled tasks under four matched interface conditions, and find a persistent gap between what agents can read and what they choose to use. Agents score as well from self-generated charts as from numeric output, yet plotting access alone does not translate into consistent use. Task slices show that charts lead on temporal, pattern, and anomaly reasoning, while text leads on precise reading and conditional verification. We then propose ChartMind, which distils two families of experience from conditioned trajectory rollouts. One family records how to select and verify analytical operations, and the other records when to invoke text, charts, or both. A trajectory judge scores outcomes and labels intermediate steps, and a validation gate admits only experience that improves held-out performance. On three held-out benchmarks with four LLM backbones, ChartMind raises analytical accuracy and visual evidence quality over matched baselines, and backbones that never drew charts begin using them, all without touching model parameters.

## 1 Introduction

Data agents translate an analytical goal into a sequence of grounded actions and derive insights step by step. Recent progress in ReAct-style reasoning and acting loops (Yao et al., 2023) has enabled these agents to plan, execute, inspect, and revise increasingly complex workflows over structured data. Analytical report generation, long-horizon exploration, and exact-answer analysis all now sit within their reach (Lei et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Jing et al., 2025). Such agents execute text-based analytical actions competently.

Human analysts, in contrast, do not think only in text. They move continually between numerical summaries, tables, and charts, using visual evidence to expose trends, distributions, and anomalies that a scrolling table hides. A well-chosen chart at the right moment can reshape the next step of analysis. Charts thus act as epistemic actions in the analyst’s loop rather than as post-hoc report artefacts. We therefore ask whether an agent should also treat charts as intermediate evidence and learn when to invoke them.

Existing methods address only part of this decision. Chart-generation methods optimise visualisations requested by a user or an agent (Dibia, 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Namgoong et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025), while ChartMimic benchmarks chart-to-code generation (Yang et al., 2025). Chart-understanding methods assume that a chart is already available and focus on extracting information from it (Masry et al., 2023; Han et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023a; Liu et al., 2023b; Zhang et al., 2024; Kaur et al., 2026; Das et al., 2026), while ChartBench benchmarks complex chart reasoning (Xu et al., 2023). Recent work compares different input representations (Zhou et al., 2025; Ho et al., 2026), routes table–query pairs across textual, visual, and fused paths (Xing et al., 2026), or builds visual evidence on demand during report writing (Lin et al., 2026). We study how a data agent selects textual and chart evidence at intermediate analytical states.

To turn this open question into a concrete study, we build ProbeBench, a probe suite of 200 tasks synthesised from InsightBench (Sahu et al., 2025) with four matched interface conditions and a common ReAct backbone. Three findings emerge. First, charts alone already sustain end-to-end analysis. Second, plotting access alone does not translate into consistent use. Third, charts and text behave as complementary evidence across task slices, with charts stronger on temporal, pattern, and anomaly reasoning and text stronger on precise reading and conditional verification. These findings motivate a method that turns representation choice into a learned behaviour of the agent.

We propose ChartMind, an experience-driven method that teaches a data agent to use charts inside the analytical loop. For each ProbeBench, ChartMind generates diverse trajectories under different representation conditions and uses $f_{\mathrm{score}}$ and $f_{\mathrm{attr}}$ to score outcomes and label intermediate decisions. A builder agent distils the labelled trajectories into two experience families. Analysis experience $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ana}}$ records how to select and verify analytical operations, and representation experience $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{repr}}$ records when and how to invoke text, charts, or a mixture. Candidate packages are accepted only when a validation gate confirms that held-out performance strictly improves. On downstream tasks the data agent reads a frozen package as external memory, so representation choice becomes part of the analytical policy without changing model parameters.

Our main contributions are as follows.

• 

Probe study of chart use. We construct ProbeBench with four matched interfaces and four backbones. The suite exposes a capability–use gap in current data agents and quantifies where charts and text serve as complementary evidence.

• 

Experience-driven method for chart use. We propose ChartMind. Given conditioned trajectory rollouts, it distils analysis and representation experience under outcome scoring and step-level attribution, and only experience updates that pass a validation gate enter the frozen package. ChartMind is the first framework that treats charts as internal epistemic actions of a data agent through learned experience.

• 

Consistent gains on held-out benchmarks. On DAComp-DA, DDR-Bench, and DSBench with four LLM backbones, ChartMind raises analytical accuracy and visual evidence quality over matched baselines. Backbones with weak representation-selection habits begin using charts, and ablations confirm the contributions of rollout diversity, validation gating, and both experience types.

## 2 Charts in the Analytical Loop

This section asks whether charts carry genuine analytical value for data agents and how their utility differs from text. We design ProbeBench, a controlled probe suite, and evaluate representative agents under four matched interfaces, then report the suite’s construction, evaluation protocol, and three empirical findings.

## 2.1 Probe Design

Task construction. To isolate the effect of intermediate representations on agent reasoning, we build ProbeBench from InsightBench (Sahu et al., 2025), which provides enterprise tables, open-ended questions, executable analyses, and target insights. Each valid insight defines a task, yielding 200 tasks in total. A task contains a raw CSV, dataset description, analytical question, reference analysis, and target insight. The agent sees the table, question, description, schema, and first three rows, then selects and executes operations to answer in natural language; the target insight is hidden for evaluation.

Analytical dimensions. For post-hoc slicing without label leakage, we annotate two dimensions. Question type covers numeric lookup, composition, ranking, group comparison, temporal change, relationship, anomaly, diagnosis, and prediction. Cognitive load covers information location, scan-and-select, comparison, pattern recognition, relational interpretation, multidimensional integration, and conditional reasoning. An LLM proposes the labels and a human verifies them; they never enter the agent context.

Agent interfaces. To hold everything but the analytical interface constant, all four settings share a vanilla ReAct agent with one general-purpose Bash tool. Each call starts a fresh process, files persist in a shared working directory, and the CSV is exposed read-only. We fix the model, initial context, interaction limit, and tool budget across conditions. No-tool removes execution tools. Text-only exposes stdout and stderr but forbids plotting. Chart-only exposes generated images and stderr while hiding stdout. Free-style returns stdout, stderr, and images and allows both text and charts.

Evaluation. To obtain comparable scores across settings, a shared LLM judge grades each answer against the target insight on a normalised $[0,100]$ scale. Slice analyses use task-paired differences with clustered bootstrap intervals (Brown, 1995) and randomisation tests. Figure 1 and Table 1 summarise the two views used in the following analysis.

## 2.2 Empirical Findings

Finding 1. Charts alone already sustain end-to-end analysis. To check whether charts carry enough evidence for analytical questions, we compare the four interfaces under the same backbone. Figure 1 shows that removing execution tools collapses the agent to a low score, while the Text-only and Chart-only interfaces achieve similar performance. Chart-only slightly outperforms Text-only, so the agent can read charts it just drew and produce answers comparable in quality to those obtained from numeric tables. Charts already satisfy the sufficiency condition for intermediate evidence, so the remaining question is whether agents actually use them.

Finding 2. Representation choice is model-dependent, not capability-driven. To probe whether the sufficiency of charts translates into use, we let each backbone freely choose between text and charts under the same Free-style interface. Table 1 shows large behavioural divergence. Claude Sonnet 5 combines text and charts on nearly half of the tasks and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on more than a quarter, while GPT-5.6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Sol essentially fall back to text. The frequency of chart use does not track score. This shows that identical tool access yields inconsistent representation habits and confirms a capability–use gap. A method that closes this gap should shape when and how charts enter the loop, and cannot stop at exposing plotting tools.

Finding 3. Charts and text play complementary roles across analytical tasks. To locate where each representation helps, we slice results by question type and cognitive load. Figure 2 shows a clear pattern. Charts pull ahead on slices that demand visual pattern recognition, including temporal change, pattern recognition, and anomaly detection. Text pulls ahead on slices that demand precise reading, including numeric lookup, information location, and conditional verification. Free-style does not automatically inherit the stronger of the two on visual-pattern slices, so agents fail to switch to charts even where charts help most. Effective chart use therefore requires state-aware representation selection, and uniform access to both formats alone is not enough.

Summary of ProbeBench. ProbeBench shows that current data agents understand charts far better than they use them, and that charts and text play complementary roles under different task conditions. This gap and this complementarity together motivate a mechanism that learns state-dependent representation choice as part of the analytical policy, which we develop in Section 3.

Figure 2: Slice analysis of the four ProbeBench interfaces. Top: slices by question type. Bottom: slices by primary cognitive load. Markers show slice mean scores. The right column reports the Chart-only minus Text-only gap.

## 3 Learning to Use Charts through Experience

Section 2 leaves a concrete target. Charts already carry sufficient evidence, yet agents do not invoke them where they help, so representation choice has to become a decision the agent makes from the current analysis state. Reaching that target requires three things. The agent needs a place to hold representation knowledge, a way to acquire that knowledge from its own behaviour, and a way to consult it while analysing. ChartMind addresses these three needs in order. Section 3.1 stores experience as editable documents that keep analytical and representational knowledge side by side. Section 3.2 distils those documents from conditioned rollouts under outcome and step-level supervision, with a validation gate on every update. Section 3.3 lets the data agent consult the frozen documents inside its own analysis loop. Figure 3 shows the pipeline. Base model parameters stay unchanged throughout.

## 3.1 Storing Experience as Editable Documents

Representation choice depends on the analysis state, so the knowledge that governs it has to stay inspectable and revisable after training ends. We therefore keep experience outside the model as a document store that the agent reads during analysis and a builder revises during distillation. This choice also lets us audit what the agent learned and freeze it before any external evaluation.

Two-layer storage. To make experience readable, editable, and callable on demand, we organise it as a two-layer package. The storage layer is a filesystem tree in which an entry document indexes independent experience documents. Each document carries metadata fields name, description, and category together with its content, which supports direct reading, targeted editing, and versioning. The tool layer exposes Read, Create, Edit, and Bash for managing the package. The builder agent uses all four, while the data agent accesses experience only through a read-only retrieval interface, implemented as kb_read in downstream experiments. The data agent first fetches document metadata and then reads relevant content on demand, so context load stays low and grows with task complexity.

Analysis and representation experience. To separate what to compute from how to represent it, we index two experience families under different categories. Analysis experience $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ana}}$ holds reusable rules for selecting, organising, and verifying analytical operations. Representation experience $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{repr}}$ holds rules for when intermediate evidence should be represented as text, charts, or a mixture, and for how to consume the resulting evidence in later steps. The two families share the same storage and tool interface, and they are always updated and validated as one package. We write the $v$ -th accepted version as $\mathcal{E}^{(v)}=\bigl(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ana}}^{(v)},\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{repr}}^{(v)}\bigr)$ .

## 3.2 Distilling Experience from Conditioned Rollouts

A single rollout per task reveals only the habit the backbone already has, and Section 2.2 shows that this habit is text-heavy for most backbones. Distillation from such data would reproduce the gap we want to close. We therefore force each task to be solved several times under different representation conditions, so the corpus contains chart-led trajectories even for backbones that would never produce them on their own, and outcome differences become attributable to representation choice.

Conditioned rollout bundle. To realise this, we generate multiple trajectories per task while holding the base agent, tools, and interaction budget fixed. Let $p_{i}=(D_{i},q_{i},z_{i},y_{i}^{\star})$ denote the $i$ -th ProbeBench, where the four elements are the data, question, task context, and reference answer. A trajectory generated under representation condition $\rho\in\{\mathrm{U},\mathrm{T},\mathrm{C}_{1},\mathrm{C}_{2},\mathrm{C}_{3}\}$ is denoted by $\tau_{i}^{\rho}$ , and each task yields a bundle

 $\mathcal{B}_{i}=\bigl\{\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{U}},\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{T}},\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{C}_{1}},\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{C}_{2}},\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{C}_{3}}\bigr\},$ 

(1)

where $\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{U}}$ is an unconstrained rollout, $\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}$ is a text-preferred rollout, and $\{\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{C}_{k}}\}_{k=1}^{3}$ are three chart-preferred rollouts. To keep the chart-preferred rollouts from collapsing onto a single visual habit, we enforce type exclusion across them. The second rollout cannot reuse any chart type used by the first, and the third cannot reuse any type used by the first two. This diversifies visual analyses without presuming that any chart type is intrinsically superior.

Figure 3: Overall pipeline of ChartMind. Conditioned rollouts diversify representation preferences over each ProbeBench. A trajectory judge produces outcome scores and step-level attributions. A builder agent distils analysis and representation experience under a validation gate.

Outcome and step signals. Bundle-level outcomes alone would tell the builder which trajectory performed best but not which decisions contributed to its performance, so we attach two labels to every trajectory. The outcome scoring function $f_{\mathrm{score}}(\tau_{i}^{\rho}\mid q_{i},y_{i}^{\star})\!\in\![0,1]$ evaluates the final answer against the reference. Together the two functions tell the builder which behaviours to retain and which to avoid.

title: Which Differences Matter? Controlled Tests of Rule Transfer, Joint Reliability, and Information Use in Decision Models
abstract: Decision models map stated rules and observed states to discrete answers. Aggregate accuracy leaves unresolved which rule and information changes guide those answers. We connect controlled input changes to transfer, joint reliability, and directed information use through executable arithmetic rules. Semantic rule separation and crossed rule and state tests make transfer and joint success separately measurable. We compare equivalent wordings, calibrate joint correctness through marginal-preserving reassociation, and alter tables to define alternative answer targets. Adaptation gains increase with nearest-source answer agreement; fully conflicting quartets yield small pooled gains and different gain signs across source splits. Equivalent rewrites have opposing task-level effects, linking transfer gains to rule presentation. Joint-score departures depend on which rule and state associations the reference preserves. A decision service changes answers more across equivalent wordings than across identical-text repeats and usually follows the answer targets implied by altered table values or mappings.

body_start:
Abstract

Decision models map stated rules and observed states to discrete answers. Aggregate accuracy leaves unresolved which rule and information changes guide those answers. We connect controlled input changes to transfer, joint reliability, and directed information use through executable arithmetic rules. Semantic rule separation and crossed rule and state tests make transfer and joint success separately measurable. We compare equivalent wordings, calibrate joint correctness through marginal-preserving reassociation, and alter tables to define alternative answer targets. Adaptation gains increase with nearest-source answer agreement; fully conflicting quartets yield small pooled gains and different gain signs across source splits. Equivalent rewrites have opposing task-level effects, linking transfer gains to rule presentation. Joint-score departures depend on which rule and state associations the reference preserves. A decision service changes answers more across equivalent wordings than across identical-text repeats and usually follows the answer targets implied by altered table values or mappings. Code and data will be made available.

Figure 1: Overview of the three behavioral diagnostics: rule transfer and wording, joint reliability, and external information use. Scores and interventions illustrate the design.

## 1 Introduction

“A difference which makes a difference”

— Gregory Bateson, Form, Substance and Difference (1970)

Decision models turn stated rules and observed states into labels, ratings, or selected records. Accuracy measures agreement with the prescribed answer, but equal scores can conceal different responses to the inputs. In an archived routing example, two models answer half the questions correctly. One ignores both rule and state changes; the other responds to states alone. Valid option selection can also coexist with answer-symbol binding errors (Balepur et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2024). Understanding success therefore requires testing which input changes guide each rule-based decision.

Research Question

How can we determine which rule and information changes guide a decision model's answers?

A gain on unfamiliar rules can still depend on familiar wording. Low all-four correctness can follow from individual errors, so its magnitude alone does not establish unusual joint behavior. Better performance with an external table also leaves open whether its values and mappings direct the answers. Behavioral tests and contrast sets motivate controlled input changes (Ribeiro et al., 2020; Gardner et al., 2020); rule-following benchmarks examine inference, counterfactual rules, and regulations (Parmar et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025). We connect these controls to the specific ambiguities in interpreting decision accuracy.

Executable arithmetic rules make intended answers and controlled changes checkable. We separate rules by finite-domain behavior to evaluate transfer to semantic components excluded from training. Equivalent rewrites hold those behaviors fixed while changing presentation. Crossing rules and states tests responses to each factor. Marginal-preserving reassociation calibrates all-four correctness against the observed individual predictions. More restrictive references retain rule or state associations to identify what drives departures from that calibration. Finally, changing table values or mappings defines alternative answer targets. Transitions toward those targets reveal directed information use beyond an arbitrary answer change. Figure 1 links input changes to behavioral diagnostics.

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) improves accuracy on reserved rules, with larger gains at higher nearest-source answer agreement. Fully conflicting quartets have low joint success and opposite gain signs across source splits. Equivalent wording increases the adaptation advantage on binary decisions and reduces it on the other tasks. Joint-score departures further depend on the rule and state associations retained by the calibration reference. The decision service Jev changes answers more across equivalent wordings than across identical-text repeats. It benefits from complete value tables and follows the alternative targets implied by altered values and mappings. These diagnostics distinguish conflict-conditioned transfer, joint reliability, and directed information use in model decisions.

• 

We establish an oracle-checked evaluation that uses semantic rule separation and paired input changes to distinguish transfer, wording sensitivity, and responses to rules and states.

• 

We show that transfer gains depend on source-answer agreement and the source split under complete conflict. Joint-score departures depend on the associations retained by different marginal-preserving calibration references.

• 

We identify directed use of external values through paired answer transitions under value and mapping interventions, complementing the evidence from aggregate accuracy gains.

## 2 Related Work

## Behavioral evaluation and explicit rules.

Behavioral evaluation tests whether predictions respond correctly to controlled input changes. CheckList and contrast sets target capabilities through local perturbations (Ribeiro et al., 2020; Gardner et al., 2020). Metric rankings also depend on the evaluation context (Deviyani and Diaz, 2025). RuleTaker and ProofWriter evaluate inference from stated facts and rules (Clark et al., 2020; Tafjord et al., 2021). LogicBench spans logical systems; RuleArena separates rule selection from application in regulations (Parmar et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025). RuleBench and IRFT extend inferential rule-following evaluation and training (Sun et al., 2025). These designs motivate testing which inputs guide decisions. Our executable grammar combines finite-domain semantic separation with crossed rule and state changes, linking success to responses along each input axis. Appendix Table 28 compares these paired evaluation designs.

## Generalization, wording, and answer interfaces.

Generalization benchmarks vary combinations, presentations, and answer interfaces. CFQ and COGS test composition; Ordered CommonGen tests requested concept order (Keysers et al., 2020; Kim and Linzen, 2020; Sakai et al., 2025). Prompt-format and answer-symbol binding studies document interface effects (Voronov et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2024). LoRA supports adaptation tests (Hu et al., 2022). Cacheable-model studies test rule following with independently encoded inputs (Rajput et al., 2026). Choice2Seq measures correctness retained from complete-answer selection to sequential construction on matched problems (Lai et al., 2026). These studies motivate paired evaluations of generalization and presentation sensitivity. Our semantic rule separation and equivalent rewrites measure how adaptation to unfamiliar rule behavior changes across presentations of identical questions with fixed model weights and intended answers.

## Information use and internal mechanisms.

Information-use studies examine how context and representations influence decisions. Performance depends on where relevant context appears (Liu et al., 2024). Probing separates recoverable information from information used to answer (Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Belinkov, 2022). Causal abstraction and interchange-intervention training connect representations to high-level variables (Geiger et al., 2021; Geiger et al., 2022). Logit inspection and attention modification examine factual recall under contextual counterfactuals (Ortu et al., 2024). Accuracy gains from supplied values leave their influence on individual answers unresolved. We alter table values and mappings to define alternative targets. Paired transitions toward those targets test directed information use. Source-selected donor replacements separately test whether recovered rule-value information influences the final selected answer.

Takeaway

Choose input interventions that distinguish the behavioral properties behind a score. Separate evidence of transfer, responsiveness, and information use when designing each evaluation.

## 3 Controlled Rule–State Evaluation

## 3.1 States, Rules, and Decisions

A decision instance is $(s,r,t,O)$ : a state $s$ , an explicitly specified rule $r$ , a task family $t$ , and an ordered option set $O$ of size $K$ . A programmatic oracle returns the semantic answer $y=g_{t}(r,s)$ and its index in $O$ . A model predicts an option index. The semantic answers align option permutations.

Each record has three integer fields $(x,y,z)\in\{-12,\ldots,12\}^{3}$ . Rules follow

 $f_{r}(x,y,z)=o_{0}\bigl(o_{1}(x,y),o_{2}(y,z)\bigr),$ 

(1)

where each operator belongs to $\{+,-,\times,\min,\max\}$ . Eligible rules depend on all three fields and retain the same three-operator, depth-two structure. Binary decisions test whether $f_{r}>0$ . Ordinal ratings count how many prescribed thresholds the score strictly exceeds, so equality remains in the lower category. Minimum routing selects the record with the lowest rule value. Maximum selection selects the record with the highest value. Record identifiers resolve ties. The option counts are 2 for binary decisions, 3/5/7 for ratings, and 2/4/8 for routing and selection.

## 3.2 Semantic Separation and State Sampling

Syntactically different expressions can implement the same decision. We compare numeric, sign, rating, and ranking signatures over the finite record domain, including field permutations. Matching any signature creates an edge between rules. Connected components conservatively keep linked rules in one pool, even when the link is transitive rather than a direct match. The separation covers executable behavior on all records in the enumerated domain.

Replication excludes historically exposed components, then assigns disjoint source and development pools by root-operator quotas and rule characteristics. Reserved components support evaluation of fixed models. Natural sampling draws complete states before labeling. Previously used complete states are excluded across roles, while individual records may recur in different multi-record states. Appendix Algorithm 1 summarizes the construction. Appendix A.4 specifies the exact eligibility checks, allocation quotas, and constraints used to construct the paired diagnostic evaluation inputs.

## 3.3 Natural Accuracy and Joint Correctness

Natural accuracy is averaged first within each rule, then equally over rule identities, option counts within each task family, and the four task families. This prevents families with more option-count settings from dominating the pooled macro result.

limitations:
The findings concern the tested rule families and evaluation conditions. 
The core grammar uses fixed-depth arithmetic rules on three bounded integer fields. Semantic separation is established within this finite domain. Boolean and finite-state extensions test additional rule formats rather than broad natural-language policy coverage. Fully conflicting cohorts contain 39 and 32 quartet memberships with different task coverage. Their opposing gains describe source-dependent transfer within the observed task coverage under complete conflict.

LoRA–readout comparisons estimate outcomes of the selected training procedures, because independent source-audit competence remains unmatched. The larger-model comparison also changes system identity, so the observed effects cannot be attributed to parameter count alone.

QAcc describes joint success on the constructed rule–state quartets. Calibration departures concern the associations removed by each reassociation reference. Small or constant-prediction strata restrict the available reassociations. Multi-record second states use swapped winning-record fields, so the state-vector reference does not establish reliability under independently sampled pairs of input states.

Wording results compare the original rendering with two equivalent templates. Jev’s adjacent repeats estimate variability within the observed service window, rather than performance across service versions or observation periods. Table interventions establish directed use of supplied information in answers; they do not identify an internal decision mechanism. Model comparisons concern these controlled diagnostics, rather than comparative detection rates across existing behavioral tests.
conclusion: We asked which input differences guide decision models’ answers. Controlled tests distinguish conflict-conditioned transfer, all-four reliability, and directed information use. Adaptation gains increase with nearest-source answer agreement, while complete conflict yields opposite gain signs across source splits and low pooled QAcc. Equivalent wording changes task-level gains, and calibration conclusions depend on the associations retained by the reference. Paired value and mapping interventions identify directed use of supplied information. Evaluation and method design should distinguish source-consistent success from correct decisions under conflict and preserve correct answers across equivalent wording. Report joint success with explicitly specified prediction-reassociation calibration conditions. Method comparisons should report attained source competence alongside target scores. Joint reliability remains a design objective even when individual decision accuracy improves under unfamiliar rules or supplied information.

title: HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning
abstract: Harness optimization, which improves an agent's prompts, tools, and workflows, is an increasingly effective way to enhance agents built on frozen or closed-source LLMs. Leading approaches such as the Darwin--Godel Machine and the Huxley--Godel Machine (HGM) rely on recursive self-improvement and were developed mainly for coding, where the competence needed to improve the agent coincides with the competence being improved. Planning tasks, in which an agent must produce a sequence of tool calls that jointly satisfies interacting constraints, break this alignment. There, open-ended self-modification repeatedly explores ineffective changes and consumes substantial evaluation budgets. We introduce HGM-Dual, a diagnostic-guided framework for budget-efficient harness evolution for planning agents. First, HGM-Dual represents agent evolution as lineage-aware context. This context records what each ancestor changed, which behaviors improved or regressed, and which modifications were ineffective, giving the editor explicit edit-outcome attribution instead of an unstructured archive of past agents. Second, HGM-Dual introduces error-conditioned dual-path child generation. For each selected parent, it generates a general child that preserves open-ended exploration and specialized children that target the harness components most likely responsible for the parent's highest-ranked constraint violations. HGM-Dual outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 14.45% relative improvement in case accuracy while matching HGM variants' final performance with 2x-4x fewer evaluation budget.

headings: HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning
body_start:
Abstract

Harness optimization, which improves an agent’s prompts, tools, and
workflows, is an increasingly effective way to enhance agents built on frozen or closed-source LLMs. Leading approaches such as the Darwin–Gödel Machine and the Huxley–Gödel Machine (HGM) rely on recursive self-improvement and were developed mainly for coding, where the competence needed to improve the agent coincides with the competence being improved. Planning tasks, in which
an agent must produce a sequence of tool calls that jointly satisfies interacting constraints, break this alignment. There, open-ended self-modification repeatedly explores ineffective changes and consumes substantial evaluation budgets. We introduce HGM-Dual, a diagnostic-guided framework for budget-efficient harness evolution for planning agents. First, HGM-Dual represents agent evolution as lineage-aware context. This context records what each ancestor changed, which behaviors improved or regressed, and which modifications were ineffective, giving the editor explicit edit–outcome attribution instead of an unstructured archive of past agents. Second, HGM-Dual introduces error-conditioned dual-path child generation. For each selected parent, it generates a general child that preserves open-ended exploration and specialized children that target the harness components most likely responsible for the parent’s highest-ranked constraint violations. HGM-Dual outperforms the strongest baseline by up to $14.45\%$ relative improvement in case accuracy while matching HGM variants’ final performance with $2\times$ – $4\times$ fewer evaluation budget.

## 1 Introduction

Agent harness optimization Khattab et al. (2024); Yuksekgonul et al. (2024) improves large language model (LLM) agents without updating model parameters by optimizing the prompts, tools, and workflows that govern agent behavior. Recent self-improving systems Novikov et al. (2025) automate this process through evolutionary search. The Darwin–Gödel Machine (DGM) Zhang et al. (2026b) maintains an archive of agents and generates new candidates by modifying selected parents, while the Huxley–Gödel Machine (HGM) Wang et al. (2026) selects candidates based on clade-metaproductivity, their potential to produce strong descendants.

This paradigm is well suited to coding agents because the ability being improved, understanding and modifying code, also enables self-modification. Planning tasks, however, require sequences of actions that satisfy interacting constraints Zhang et al. (2026d); Xie et al. (2024), creating a mismatch that poses two challenges for existing recursive self-improvement methods.

First, effective improvement requires a structured context of the search
history. Planning benchmarks expose a relatively small and recurring set of
constraint failures, so different agents in the search tree often encounter
similar problems. If an editor observes only its current parent’s evaluation logs, it cannot determine whether a similar fix has already
been attempted elsewhere, whether it improved or degraded performance, or
which previous modifications led to the current behavior. As a result,
different branches may repeatedly rediscover the same ineffective changes.
In HGM’s shopping search, 41.8% of edits repeat an edit pattern already
present in the tree (Figure 1, left), with each repeated
attempt consuming another full planning evaluation. What is needed is not
simply access to more previous agents, but explicit edit–outcome
context: a concise record of what was changed, what behavior changed as a
result, and which changes succeeded, regressed, or proved ineffective.

Figure 1: Edit behavior in HGM. Among child nodes,
41.8% repeat previous edits, 19.4% target an error
category absent from the parent’s observed failures,
and 64.2% retain the parent’s dominant error category.
See Appendix A.1 for details.

Second, improvement must be targeted at the specific constraints the
agent violates. Planning success depends on the correctness of many
interdependent decisions: a single infeasible transfer, invalid coupon, or
unmet product requirement can invalidate an otherwise valid itinerary or
cart. Consequently, a broad modification that improves behavior in general may
still leave the failing case unresolved unless it corrects the particular
constraint violation responsible for failure. Without explicit guidance,
open-ended editing may instead modify an unrelated harness component or make
a diffuse change that does not address the observed error. In HGM’s shopping
search, 19.4% of edits target a constraint category that the parent never
failed (Figure 1, middle), and in 64.2% of edits the
child retains its parent’s dominant failure category
(Figure 1, right). These results suggest that efficient
self-improvement for planning requires both learning from prior edit outcomes
and directing new edits toward the specific constraint failures observed in
the current agent.

We introduce the Huxley–Gödel Machine Dual (HGM-Dual), a
diagnostic-guided framework for budget-efficient agent harness evolution. First, it represents
agentic evolution as structured contextual information. This agent-evolution context records what was changed, which
behaviors improved or regressed, and which attempted modifications were
ineffective. The editor therefore receives explicit edit–outcome attribution
instead of treating previous agent snapshots as an unstructured archive. This
context discourages repeated failures and allows subsequent edits to build
systematically on evidence collected throughout the search.

Second, HGM-Dual introduces error-conditioned dual-path child generation. For each selected parent, the framework generates complementary children: a general child, which preserves the broad and open-ended exploration of existing evolutionary methods, and specialized children, which target the harness component most likely responsible for the parent’s observed errors. The general path retains the ability to discover unexpected improvements, while the specialized path provides diagnostic-guided local refinement. Together, the dual paths balance exploration with targeted exploitation and direct the evaluation budget toward more informative regions of the harness search space.

Experiments on travel and shopping planning tasks show that HGM-Dual outperforms the strongest baseline by up to $14.45\%$ relative improvement in case accuracy while matching HGM variants’ final performance with $2\times$ – $4\times$ fewer evaluation budget. These results demonstrate that structured evolutionary context and diagnostic guidance can make harness self-improvement both more effective and substantially more resource-efficient.

## 2 Related Works

Harness Optimization through Self-Improvement.
Recent methods improve frozen LLMs by automatically modifying their agentic harnesses, including prompts, tools, skills, and workflows Khattab et al. (2024); Opsahl-Ong et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2026); Karten et al. (2026); Lou et al. (2026); Zhang et al. (2026a). ADAS Hu et al. (2025), DGM Zhang et al. (2026b), HGM Wang et al. (2026), GEPA Agrawal et al. (2026), and HyperAgents Zhang et al. (2026c) search over agent implementations through iterative or evolutionary self-modification. Meta-Harness Lee et al. (2026) gives an agentic proposer access to the code, scores, and execution traces of prior candidates, while SkillOpt Yang et al. (2026) optimizes a natural-language skill through bounded edits and validation. Collectively, these methods demonstrate that harness optimization can substantially improve agent performance without updating model parameters.

Nevertheless, two challenges remain. First, prior edit experience is either local or excessive: DGM Zhang et al. (2026b) and HGM Wang et al. (2026) primarily generate modifications from the selected parent’s code and evaluation logs, without providing enough context on the effectiveness of all edits attempted. On the other hand, archive-based methods Hu et al. (2025); Lee et al. (2026); Lin et al. (2026); Jiang et al. (2026) may flood the evolution context with numerous previous candidates and raw execution traces. This can obscure useful edit-outcome relationships and lead to repeated ineffective modifications across the search tree. Second, although prior methods guide candidate selection or validation Yang et al. (2026); Wang et al. (2026); Zhang et al. (2026b); Zhang et al. (2026c), edit generation itself remains largely open-ended and may not target the harness component responsible for observed failures. Such weakly targeted exploration can require substantial evaluation resources. HGM-Dual addresses these limitations by maintaining a concise, structured agent-evolution context and by generating both a general child for broad exploration and an error-conditioned specialized child for targeted refinement.

## 3 HGM-Dual

## 3.1 Problem Setup

Agent Harness Optimization.
We consider a frozen language model whose behavior is controlled by an agent harness

 $\mathcal{H}=(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{W}),$ 

(1)

where $\mathcal{P}$ specifies the prompt and instructions provided to the model, $\mathcal{T}$ denotes the set of available tools, and $\mathcal{W}$ defines the agentic workflow that governs how the model and tools interact to solve a task. The parameters of the underlying language model remain fixed throughout optimization; only the components of $\mathcal{H}$ are modified.

Given a task $x$ sampled from a task distribution $\mathcal{D}$ , executing the frozen language model under harness $\mathcal{H}$ produces an output $\mathcal{H}(x)$ . We evaluate this output using a task-specific scoring function $J(x,\mathcal{H}(x))$ , which measures the quality of the harness execution on task $x$ . Agent harness optimization seeks a harness that maximizes expected performance over the task distribution:

 $\mathcal{H}^{*}=\arg\max_{\mathcal{H}}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[J\!\left(x,\mathcal{H}(x)\right)\right].$ 

(2)

## 3.2 Overview

Figure 2: HGM search: select a parent, generate an
open-ended edit, evaluate the child, and add it
to the archive.

## HGM.

HGM optimizes an agent harness through
evolutionary self-modification. Starting from an initial harness
 $\mathcal{H}_{0}$ , HGM maintains an archive $\mathcal{A}$ of previously
evaluated harnesses organized as an evolutionary tree
(Figure 2). Each node corresponds to a harness, and
each edge corresponds to a modification that produces a child from its
parent. At each iteration, HGM selects a parent harness
 $\mathcal{H}_{i}\in\mathcal{A}$ using its clade-metaproductivity
criterion, which is designed to favor candidates with the potential to
produce strong descendants. An editor then examines the selected
harness and its evaluation feedback, proposes an open-ended
modification, evaluates the resulting child, and adds it to the
archive. The editor primarily conditions on the selected harness and its current evaluation context
 $\varepsilon_{i}$ :

 $\mathcal{H}^{\prime}=\operatorname{Edit}\left(\mathcal{H}_{i},\varepsilon_{i}\right).$ 

(3)

Thus, the archive records an evolutionary history, but that history is
not explicitly represented as structured edit-outcome evidence for
the editor. Moreover, because the edit is
open-ended, it is not explicitly constrained to address the failures
observed in the selected parent.

Figure 3: Overview of HGM-Dual and one expansion round. Given a selected parent $\mathcal{H}_{i}$ , HGM-Dual constructs
an evolution context $\mathcal{Z}_{i}$ by summarizing edits and outcomes
along its ancestral path $\mathrm{Anc}(\mathcal{H}_{i})$ . The evolution
context is provided to both editing paths: a general editor proposes
an open-ended improvement, while specialized editors target the
highest-ranked errors in the parent’s error profile $\varepsilon_{i}$ .
The resulting children are evaluated under the same protocol, and only
the strongest child is added to the archive.

## HGM-Dual.

HGM-Dual retains HGM’s evolutionary search procedure but changes how each selected parent is expanded (we refer readers to Section A.4 for full integration). As illustrated in
Figure 3, it introduces two mechanisms.
First, rather than conditioning an edit only on the selected harness
 $\mathcal{H}_{i}$ and its evaluation context $\varepsilon_{i}$ ,
HGM-Dual additionally provides an evolution context $\mathcal{Z}_{i}$ 
that summarizes the edits and outcomes along its ancestral lineage:

 $\mathcal{H}^{\prime}=\operatorname{Edit}\left(\mathcal{H}_{i},\varepsilon_{i},\mathcal{Z}_{i}\right).$ 

(4)

Second, HGM-Dual augments HGM’s open-ended child generation with
error-conditioned editing. Each expansion generates both general and error-conditioned children. Thus, HGM-Dual retains HGM’s evolutionary backbone while making edit generation both history-aware and error-aware. We summarize the HGM-Dual expansion process in Algorithm 1 and describe
them in Sections 3.3
and 3.4, respectively.

## 3.3 Agent Evolution as Interpretable Context

An editor observing only the current harness and its evaluation feedback cannot reliably attribute performance changes to prior edits or identify previously failed modifications. Providing the full archive and raw traces would address this limitation but is costly and difficult to interpret. HGM-Dual therefore compresses the relevant evolutionary history into a structured context.

For each non-root harness $\mathcal{H}_{i}$ with parent $\mathcal{H}_{p_{i}}$ , we define an evolution record

 $\zeta_{i}=\left(d_{i},\,u_{i},\,\Delta\widehat{J}_{i},\,\Delta\mathbf{f}_{i},\,b_{i}\right),$ 

(5)

where $d_{i}$ summarizes the edit, $u_{i}$ records functionality added, removed, or invoked,

 $\Delta\widehat{J}_{i}=\widehat{J}(\mathcal{H}_{i})-\widehat{J}(\mathcal{H}_{p_{i}}),$ 

(6)

measures its performance impact, and

 $\Delta\mathbf{f}_{i}=\mathbf{f}_{i}-\mathbf{f}_{p_{i}}$ 

(7)

captures changes in constraint-level errors. Finally, $b_{i}$ summarizes the observed behavioral consequences. Thus, $\zeta_{i}$ links each modification to its functional, performance, and behavioral effects.

Let $\operatorname{Anc}(\mathcal{H}_{i})=(\mathcal{H}_{0},\ldots,\mathcal{H}_{p_{i}},\mathcal{H}_{i})$ denote the ordered ancestral path to $\mathcal{H}_{i}$ . We define its lineage context as

 $\mathcal{Z}_{i}=\operatorname{Summarize}\left(\left\{\zeta_{j}:\mathcal{H}_{j}\in\operatorname{Anc}(\mathcal{H}_{i})\right\}\right).$ 

(8)

This bounded summary preserves which functionality was introduced and used, which edits produced improvements or regressions, and how behavior evolved along the lineage, while consolidating redundant records.

When expanding $\mathcal{H}_{i}$ , the editor receives its source, current evaluation context $\varepsilon_{i}$ , and lineage context $\mathcal{Z}_{i}$ . This compact memory helps avoid repeating failed changes, retain complementary improvements, and identify interactions between edits that are not apparent from the current score alone.

## 3.4 Error-Conditioned Dual-Path Child Generation

The space of possible modifications to $\mathcal{P}$ , $\mathcal{T}$ , and $\mathcal{W}$ is large, and unrestricted generation frequently produces plausible but irrelevant edits. HGM-Dual therefore uses two complementary editing paths: a general path for broad exploration and an error-conditioned path for targeting verified weaknesses. To avoid specializing to noisy failure signals, the error-conditioned path is enabled only when a one-time pre-search test shows sufficient task-level agreement ( $\kappa\geq 0.4$ ) and dominant-category stability ( $\rho_{B}\geq 0.7$ ); otherwise, expansion uses only the general path.

For a select
conclusion: We introduced HGM-Dual, a diagnostic-guided framework for efficient agent harness optimization. By incorporating structured agent-evolution context, HGM-Dual enables the editor to learn from prior edit outcomes and avoid redundant or ineffective modifications. Its error-conditioned dual-path generation further combines open-ended exploration with targeted refinement of error-relevant harness components. Experiments on travel and shopping planning tasks demonstrate that these complementary mechanisms outperform strong self-improving baselines while substantially reducing the required evaluation budget. Our ablations further show that evolution context provides consistent performance gains, whereas dual-path generation accelerates improvement under constrained budgets. Together, these results demonstrate that explicitly modeling evolutionary history and balancing general with error-targeted search can make agent harness evolution more effective and resource-efficient. Future work may extend the evolution context beyond individual lineages to share useful edit-outcome evidence across the entire search tree. Future work could jointly learn an evolving context and dual-path manager to adapt evidence selection, editing strategies, and resource allocation throughout the search. Finally, evaluating HGM-Dual across broader task domains and online environments would help characterize the transferability and long-term robustness of the evolved harnesses.

title: Robust Soft Skill Adaptation via Behavioral Localization in Tool-Using Agents
abstract: Text skills can extend the capabilities of tool-using agents, but long skill descriptions increase computational costs. Soft prompts provide a compact alternative, yet learning from entire successful trajectories may also introduce unnecessary behavioral changes. We find that the useful effect of a text skill is highly concentrated in a small subset of trajectory positions. Based on this observation, we propose Behavioral Localization, which compares the frozen agent with and without the text skill to identify positions where the skill both increases the likelihood of successful tokens and meaningfully changes the next token distribution. We use these localized positions to supervise a short soft prompt. Experiments on SpreadsheetBench with a frozen Qwen3.6-35B-A3B agent show that the top 10\% of trajectory positions capture 96.12\% of the total positive skill gain. In the shared prompt setting, selective supervision improves success from 30.36\% with full trajectory to 36.79\%. Under task-specific conditions, using the top 10\% localized positions achieves 57.38\%, outperforming both the full text skill and the on-policy OPCD baseline. These results show that a small set of behaviorally relevant trajectory positions can provide effective supervision of soft skills.

headings: Robust Soft Skill Adaptation via Behavioral Localization in Tool-Using Agents
body_start:
Abstract

Text skills can extend the capabilities of tool-using agents, but long skill descriptions increase computational costs. Soft prompts provide a compact alternative, yet learning from entire successful trajectories may also introduce unnecessary behavioral changes. We find that the useful effect of a text skill is highly concentrated in a small subset of trajectory positions. Based on this observation, we propose Behavioral Localization, which compares the frozen agent with and without the text skill to identify positions where the skill both increases the likelihood of successful tokens and meaningfully changes the next token distribution. We use these localized positions to supervise a short soft prompt. Experiments on SpreadsheetBench with a frozen Qwen3.6-35B-A3B agent show that the top 10% of trajectory positions capture 96.12% of the total positive skill gain. In the shared prompt setting, selective supervision improves success from 30.36% with full trajectory to 36.79%. Under task-specific conditions, using the top 10% localized positions achieves 57.38%, outperforming both the full text skill and the on-policy OPCD baseline. These results show that a small set of behaviorally relevant trajectory positions can provide effective supervision of soft skills.

## 1 Introduction

As agents are increasingly deployed across diverse domains, tasks often differ substantially in their knowledge requirements, operational procedures, and behavioral patterns. These task-specific differences are difficult to address efficiently through repeated retraining or modification of the underlying agent Liu et al. (2024). A flexible solution is to provide agents with task-specific guidance that helps them develop more effective task behaviors Li et al. (2026).

A direct approach to task adaptation is known as an agent skill, where natural language prompts are used to specify task goals, operational rules, and expected behaviors, allowing the model to perform new tasks without updating its parameters Anthropic (2025). However, this approach often relies on lengthy and carefully designed prompts, and its effectiveness can be sensitive to wording and example selection. As tasks become more complex, the prompts typically grow longer, increasing both context usage and inference cost Mu et al. (2023).

To obtain more compact and learnable skill representations, prior work has explored directly optimizing prompts in continuous representation spaces. Compared with natural language instructions, soft prompts typically require less storage and can support task adaptation by updating a small set of trainable prompt embeddings Tao et al. (2026); Lester et al. (2021). However, these continuous vectors lack clear counterparts in natural language Deng et al. (2022). As a result, while learning a target skill, a soft prompt can also introduce unexpected behavioral changes Ma et al. (2022). For agents, because generation is sequential, even small shifts in early predictions can propagate and amplify over subsequent steps, leading to incorrect tool selection, malformed outputs, or task execution failures Bengio et al. (2015); Li et al. (2023). Thus, acquiring new capabilities may come at the cost of degrading abilities that the base model already possesses Zhu et al. (2022).

We find that the behavioral effect of a skill is highly concentrated in a small number of critical decision points, while much of the remaining trajectory is already correctly handled by the base agent. This suggests that robust soft skill adaptation should focus on which behaviors truly need to be learned. Based on this observation, we propose Behavioral Localization, which identifies the trajectory positions where a text skill meaningfully changes the predictions of base agent and selectively uses these positions to train a compact soft skill. At the same time, we constrain selected preservation positions toward the base distribution to reduce unnecessary behavioral drift.

Our contributions are shown below.

First, through token-level distributional analysis, we find that skill induced behavioral changes are highly sparse.

Second, we show that training a soft prompt using only selected positions by Behavioral Localization in the trajectory as supervision outperforms training on the full trajectory.

## 2 Related Work

Prompt learning provides a foundation for representing task-specific capabilities in continuous spaces. Prompt Tuning, Prefix-Tuning, and P-Tuning show that a frozen base model can be adapted by optimizing only a small set of continuous prompt embeddings Lester et al. (2021); Li and Liang (2021); Liu et al. (2022). Later work explores how these representations can be reused. For example, SPoT transfers learned soft prompts from source tasks to similar target tasks Vu et al. (2022). XPrompt finds that some prompt tokens can hurt downstream performance and removes these negative parts Ma et al. (2022). These studies mainly focus on how soft prompts are parameterized and reused. Another line of work compresses long natural language contexts into compact latent representations. Gisting compresses long prompts into a small number of reusable gist tokens Mu et al. (2023). ICAE encodes long contexts into a few memory slots that can directly condition a language model Ge et al. (2024). These methods mainly aim to preserve the semantics of the original text after compression.

Agent skills differ from general text compression because their main purpose is to guide an agent’s behavior. Therefore, a compressed representation should preserve the behavioral effect introduced by the skill. Recent work has begun to reuse successful agent trajectories to compress textual skills offline. SoftSkill compresses a natural-language skill into a short continuous prefix while keeping the base model frozen Tao et al. (2026). It trains the prefix by predicting the next tokens in successful trajectories. LatentSkill instead converts textual skills into task-specific LoRA adapters, moving reusable skill knowledge from the context space into the model’s weight space Yu et al. (2026). These studies show that textual agent skills can be encoded as compact latent representations. However, they mainly focus on how a skill should be represented or stored. In contrast, we study which behavioral changes introduced by a skill should be used to learn such a representation.

## 3 Behavioral Locator

## 3.1 Problem formulation

Let $p_{\theta}$ be a frozen agent and let $S$ denote a text skill shared by a family of tasks. Our training set consists of task description $x^{i}$ and it’s trajectory $\tau^{i}=(y^{i}_{1},\ldots,y^{i}_{T})$ . $\tau^{i}$ is a verified successful trajectory called the teacher trajectory. $\tau^{i}_{t}$ denotes the sequence before position $t$ .
If we seek a soft prompt $P^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}$ that can replace $S$ at inference time. The parameters of the base model $\theta$ remain frozen, only $P$ is optimized.

We aim to identify a sparse set of trajectory positions

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{C}\subseteq{1,\ldots,T},\qquad|\mathcal{C}|\ll T,$ 

(1)

We use $\mathcal{C}$ to supervise a short soft prompt. The goal is to focus on skill useful behavior while avoiding harmful updates induced by other trajectory positions.

## 3.2 Method

We compute the next token probability distributions along the teacher trajectory under three different conditions.

 $\displaystyle=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid S,x,\tau^{i}_{t})$ 

(2)

 $\displaystyle p_{t}^{\mathrm{n}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\tau^{i}_{t})$ 

 $\displaystyle p_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid P,x,\tau^{i}_{t})$ 

Here, $p^{\mathrm{s}}$ , $p^{\mathrm{n}}$ , and $p$ denote the next token distributions under the text skill, non-skill, and soft prompt, respectively.

First, we define the positive gain $G$ induced by the skill on the base model as follows.

 $\displaystyle G_{t}^{i}=\log p_{t}^{\mathrm{s}}(y_{t}^{i})-\log p_{t}^{\mathrm{n}}(y_{t}^{i})$ 

(3)

at position $t$ of the teacher trajectory, it measures how much the probability of the successful token $y_{t}$ increases after adding the text Skill, compared with the no-skill condition.
Next, we define the distributional shift $JS$ induced by the skill on the base model as follows.

 $\displaystyle JS_{t}^{i}=\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(p_{t}^{\mathrm{s}}\;\|\;m_{t}^{i}\right)+\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(p_{t}^{\mathrm{n}}\;\|\;m_{t}^{i}\right)$ 

(4)

(5)

at position $t$ of the teacher trajectory, it measures how much the full next-token distribution changes after adding the text Skill, compared with the no-skill condition. By combining the two metrics, we define the localization score $U_{t}^{i}=G_{t}^{i}JS_{t}^{i}$ at each position. We then select the top $k\%$ of positions as the training targets.

At the selected core positions, we minimize the full vocabulary KL divergence between the predictive distributions under the text skill and soft skill conditions. At the unselected preservation positions, we use the token distribution of the no-skill model as a behavioral anchor, encouraging the soft-prompt model to preserve the original predictive behavior of the base model as much as possible.

## 4 Experiment

Figure 1: 
Aggregate concentration on 61 successful training trajectories.
Positive gold token gain is highly concentrated under teacher forcing.

## 4.1 Setup

We conduct our experiments on SpreadsheetBenchMa et al. (2024). We use GPT-5.5 to generate the successful teacher trajectories. All experiments use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as the frozen student model, with all parameters fixed during training. Each soft prompt has a length of 8 and is initialized using the embeddings of the first same tokens of the full text skill.

During evaluation, we use greedy decoding with a maximum of 4,096 token cost and set the execution timeout for each task to 600 seconds. A task is considered successful only if the generated output passes all SpreadsheetBench checks.

## 4.2 Main Result

We use the Behavioral Locator to select key positions and optimize both a shared soft prompt across tasks and task-specific soft prompts for individual tasks.
As shown in Figure 1, the positive gain is highly concentrated in a small subset of trajectory positions. Selecting only 10% of the tokens captures 96.12% of the total positive Skill effect. This motivates us to use a sparse set of relevant tokens as supervision for soft skill learning.

OPCD is an important on-policy distillation baseline that trains online rather than relying on fixed teacher trajectories. Our method instead relies on lower cost offline teacher trajectories. Under the shared prompt setting, our method improves over full-trajectory SoftSkill, although it remains below the on-policy OPCD baseline. More importantly, under task-specific condition, selecting the top 10% localized positions achieves 57.38%, outperforming both Text Skill and OPCD. title: GuideEvolve: Self-Evolving Agent Framework with Expert Guidance and 3Ts Mechanisms
abstract: This study introduces GuideEvolve, a self-evolving agent framework incorporating expert guidance and three autonomous regulatory mechanisms, collectively termed the 3Ts: Think Fast and Slow, Throwback, and Termination by choice. The framework addresses critical limitations in extant self-evolving agent paradigms through dual innovations: (1) a task-specific expert-evaluation-driven evolutionary pipeline, and (2) the integration of 3Ts mechanisms to facilitate cognitive optimization, performance recovery via temporal rollback, and adaptive termination protocols. Empirical validation across the MGSM and MMLU benchmarks demonstrates that GuideEvolve attains performance metrics comparable to current state-of-the-art models (89.8% accuracy versus Gödel Agent's 90.6% on MGSM; 89.1% versus 87.9% on MMLU), while exhibiting notably reduced variance (25-59%) and enhanced robustness. Furthermore, the framework achieves a 100% evolution success rate, superior to the baseline's 82%, diminishes required optimization iterations by approximately 50% (from 30 iterations in baseline to 15.1 and 13.4 across tasks), and provides improved stability for production deployment.
