## 1 Introduction

Humans have the ability to coordinate with each other remarkably well, often with little or no explicit communication. For instance, chefs can prepare a meal together, teammates can execute a play, and negotiators can converge on a deal, each anticipating what the other will do and acting accordingly. This capacity for joint action rests on each agent’s Theory of Mind (ToM): the ability to model another agent’s unobserved mental state based on observed behaviors (Premack and Woodruff, 1978).
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that must act alongside partner agents (human or AI) in both collaborative and competitive tasks
(Duan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Stengel-Eskin et al., 2024; Kosinski, 2024; Xu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2026). To succeed in these settings, an agent needs strong working ToM (Bakhtin et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025a).
This ToM allows the agent to infer a partner’s goals, beliefs, and likely next actions, enabling it to coordinate with less explicit communication and adapt to a counterpart’s strategy on the fly (Baker et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2020).

Making these kinds of inferences can be seen as a form of world modeling directed at another agent (Raileanu et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2022; Chernyavskiy et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025).
As in world modeling, it is often important to form an abstract model that can superimpose multiple possibilities, in this case of the partner’s intent Xie et al. (2021); Chernyavskiy et al. (2025).
A general sketch of the partner’s beliefs and intentions is often sufficient, and excessive fidelity can be inefficient and in fact harmful to the task (Mu et al., 2026); for example, when two chefs have to coordinate in a crowded kitchen, one does not need to predict what the other wants for breakfast tomorrow (which might even be a distraction), but does need to predict if the other needs shared resources.

Figure 1: 
Left: Vanilla LLM agents (using Qwen3-8B) each reason only about their own plan. Both independently conclude they should fetch a dish from the dispenser, producing redundant and conflicting behavior. Middle: Language ToM Agents are able to more frequently consider their partner’s next actions, but they often commit to a single line of reasoning without considering other potential paths. Right: Our method ToM2Vec is used to train an agent (blue hat) with stronger ToM capabilities; that agent considers what the untrained partner agent (green hat) is doing before making its own decision.

Given this goal of abstraction, a key challenge for ToM agents lies in building an abstract representation
that retains enough information about the partner’s potential future paths to support prediction and planning, while lifting unnecessary details.
We argue that natural language is a poor medium for this kind of abstraction, as expressing another agent’s intent or state linguistically tends to commit the agent to a single estimate of the partner, even when many distinct hypotheses are possible.
Instead, we argue that modeling another agent may be more akin to forming a latent world model (LeCun, 2022),
where abstractions are formed in the model’s latent space rather than its output space (see Figure 1).
Latent reasoning paradigms offer precisely this kind of latent-space abstraction as a natural alternative to verbalized reasoning,
where latent thought tokens can superimpose several candidate chains-of-thought rather than fixing to one
(Hao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b; Shi et al., 2026).
Similarly, we argue that a representation of a partner should be able to superimpose multiple hypotheses about the partner’s goals and intentions, and that a ToM agent should be able to predict these representations and consider alternatives before committing to a decision.

To this end, we introduce ToM2Vec to directly learn these latent representations of the partner agent. ToM2Vec trains the agent to predict, from its own point-of-view, a fixed number of continuous latent embeddings that abstract over its partner’s thoughts; in other words, it teaches the main agent to perform a mind-reading task about its partner.
During training, we obtain supervision for these latent embeddings by abstracting a training partner’s actual next thoughts into continuous latent tokens to serve as a representation of its reasoning.
We train the agent’s generated latent embeddings to match the partner’s hidden states under a cosine similarity objective (see Figure 2);
during training, we use the same model for both agent and partner, as their representation spaces must be shared.
At test-time (where partner reasoning is not available) an agent trained with ToM2Vec then generates its own latent thought tokens, intended to capture a ToM about the partner.
Interestingly, we show that at test-time, our training generalizes to other partner models, including a closed-source proprietary model that is stronger than the training partner.

We evaluate ToM2Vec across cooperative and competitive tasks, including (1) Overcooked (Carroll et al., 2019), a cooperative cooking environment, (2) multi-party LLM negotiation (Abdelnabi et al., 2024), (3) Decrypto (Lupu et al., 2025), a ToM task where two agents attempt to pass secret messages without being decoded by an interceptor agent, (4) Hanabi (Agashe et al., 2025), a cooperative card game with hidden information, and (5) Collab Escape/Capture (Agashe et al., 2025), two collaborative coordination tasks.
Across these domains, ToM2Vec delivers consistent improvements over competitive baselines. Relative to the untrained model (Qwen3-8B), training with ToM2Vec improves the average Overcooked score by 12.0 points and raises negotiation deal success from 62.0% to 71.0%. It also outperforms approaches that prompt agents to consider their partners’ intentions or train them to explicitly verbalize their partners’ reasoning, supporting the value of learning latent partner representations. In Overcooked, these benefits extend to unseen partners from different model families: ToM2Vec improves over the base agent by 17.3 points on average with a GPT-5.4 partner and matches or exceeds the base agent with a Gemma-4 partner, despite training only with a Qwen3-8B partner.

Our analysis further examines to what extent ToM2Vec learns representations that capture a partner’s evolving beliefs. We directly test whether these representations better support inferences about a partner’s beliefs, desires, and next actions (i.e., Baker et al. (2011)’s Bayesian ToM modeling)
within a given environment state.
We also test whether the latent tokens encode partner-specific reasoning by deliberately corrupting the context used to derive them. Latents derived from the partner’s actual context assign lower perplexity to its true reasoning than those derived from an altered layout or an adversarial intent, supporting the interpretation that they capture context-sensitive information about the partner rather than only generic signals useful for coordination.
We complement this analysis with additional results in the appendix, showing that ToM2Vec helps in Sally-Anne-style false-belief tests, and that the representations learned by ToM2Vec support belief revision given new evidence.

## 2 Method

Figure 2: 
Overview of ToM2Vec on the multi-party negotiation task.
Left (training): From its local observation and interaction history, the main agent predicts $K$ continuous latent ToM tokens that summarize a partner’s likely reasoning trace.
Middle (training): The partner’s reasoning is segmented at sentence delimiters, and latent tokens are extracted across the trace.
These $K$ vectors provide self-supervised targets for position-wise cosine alignment with the main agent’s predictions.
Right (inference): The main agent predicts the latent ToM tokens using only its local context and conditions its subsequent reasoning and action on them. The partner’s private context and reasoning are used only to construct training targets.

## 2.1 Problem Setup

We formulate the multi-agent task as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process,

 $\mathcal{D}=\big(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{S},\{\mathcal{A}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}},T,\{\mathcal{O}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}},O,R,\rho_{0},H\big),$ 

where $\mathcal{I}=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ is the agent set, $\mathcal{S}$ is the state space, $\mathcal{A}_{i}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{i}$ are agent $i$ ’s action and observation spaces, $T$ is the transition kernel, $O$ is the joint observation kernel, $R$ is the shared reward, $\rho_{0}$ is the initial-state distribution, and $H$ is the horizon. At step $t$ , the agents choose a joint action $\mathbf{a}_{t}=(a_{t}^{1},\ldots,a_{t}^{n})$ and the environment transitions according to $T(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},\mathbf{a}_{t})$ . Turn-based interactions are represented by including a no-op action to inactive agents. Note that assumption of a shared reward applies only to cooperative tasks, not in competitive tasks.

Each agent $i\in\mathcal{I}$ acts from its own action history $h_{t}^{i}=(a_{0}^{i},\ldots,a_{t-1}^{i}).$ We write $c_{t}^{i}$ for the model input context constructed from this history, the current state, role-specific instructions, and general task information.

We detail the training method for a main agent $M\in\mathcal{I}$ modeling a partner $P\in\mathcal{I}$ . Both agents are initialized from the same base language model $\mathcal{B}$ . We denote the trainable main model by $\mathcal{B}_{\theta}$ .

## 2.2 Modeling Partners via Latent Reasoning

Under partial observability, the main agent must anticipate its partner’s behavior without observing the partner’s complete history and reasoning. We train $\mathcal{B}_{\theta}$ to predict a fixed budget of $K$ continuous latent vectors from the main agent’s own context:

 $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t}=\big(\hat{z}_{t,1},\ldots,\hat{z}_{t,K}\big)=\operatorname{Latent}_{K}(\mathcal{B}_{\theta};c_{t}^{M}),$ 

Here, $\operatorname{Latent}_{K}$ denotes $K$ autoregressive steps in the model’s hidden space. To perform these steps, we follow recent work on latent reasoning (Hao et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2025) and treat the last layer’s hidden state at each step as the next step’s input embedding, rather than decoding out to the vocabulary.
These latent ToM tokens are intended to summarize the partner’s likely reasoning given what the main agent can observe.

## 2.3 Self-Supervised Training via Self-Play

ToM2Vec operates by teaching agents to predict latent vectors of each other’s thought traces.
To obtain a signal for this, we leverage self-play: given a main agent (to be trained) and a partner agent (both parameterized by the same model $\mathcal{B}$ ), we sample a reasoning trace from the partner, compress it into latent tokens, and then supervise the main agent to autoregressively produce latent tokens that match the latent tokens extracted from the partner.

More formally, as illustrated in Figure 2 (Middle), given a partner agent’s context $c_{t}^{P}$ , the partner generates a full reasoning sequence $r_{t}^{P}\sim\mathcal{B}_{\theta}(c_{t}^{P})$ .
We first segment $r_{t}^{P}$ at sentence delimiters and store the hidden state of each token. To obtain $K$ continuous reasoning tokens, we reserve two positions for the start and end tokens and divide the sentences evenly into $K-2$ chunks.
We take the hidden state for the token at the center of each chunk to get $K-2$ continuous latent tokens.
We then add the hidden states from the tokens at the start and end of the reasoning trace, resulting in $K$ latent tokens.
These tokens $\mathbf{z}_{t}=(z_{t,\text{start}},z_{t,\text{chunk 1}},\ldots,z_{t,\text{chunk K-2}},z_{t,\text{end}})=(z_{t,\text{1}},z_{t,\text{2}},\ldots,z_{t,\text{K}})$ will serve as the targets for training the main agent.

During training, all agents share a model, so we can directly align the main agent’s output to the targets extracted from the partner.
As shown in Figure 2 (Left), we allow the main agent to autoregressively predict $K$ latent tokens, supervising these tokens via a cosine similarity loss:

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ToM}}=1-\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\cos\big(\hat{z}_{t,k},z_{t,k}\big),\vskip-2.5pt$ 

(1)

In practice, we use $K=10$ .
Note that the ToM objective in Equation 1 is ToM2Vec’s only training signal; we do not directly optimize for task rewards.
Further details are provided in Appendix A.

## 2.4 Inference

At inference time the partner’s info ( $c^{P}_{t}$ , $r^{P}_{t})$ is unavailable, so agent $M$ relies solely on its prediction, as shown in Figure 2 (Right). Given its own context, the agent first emits the $K$ latent ToM tokens $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ to act as an abstract theory of the partner’s likely reasoning.
These tokens then become part of the context for predicting subsequent tokens, allowing the reasoning and actions that follow them to condition on the latent theory:

 $(r_{t}^{M},a_{t}^{M})\sim\mathcal{B}_{\theta}\big(\cdot\mid c_{t}^{M};\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t}\big).$ 

Intuitively, a good ToM agent should reconstruct what its partner is about to do well enough to adjust to it before the partner acts.

## 3 Experiments and Results

## 3.1 Experimental Setup

## Environments.

We evaluate ToM2Vec on five multi-agent environments that span cooperative (Overcooked-AI, Hanabi, Collab Escape/Capture), mixed-motive (negotiation), and competitive (Decrypto) multi-agent settings.
Overcooked-AI (Carroll et al., 2019) is a fully cooperative
cooking game in which two agents share a kitchen and must interleave complementary subtasks (e.g., fetching onions, plating, and delivering) to maximize the total team score. We use three layouts provided in Carroll et al. (2019) (Cramped Room, Asymmetric Advantages, and Coordination Ring) each run for 30 seeds.
Multi-party, multi-issue negotiation (Abdelnabi et al., 2024) is a mixed-motive task that we evaluate over 100 samples where each agent holds private preferences over a set of issues and must reach an agreement that balances their own self-interest against the broader risk of walking away with no deal. Decrypto (Lupu et al., 2025) is a competitive
ToM communication game, in which a decoder must interpret a teammate’s clues relating to provided hint words (which only the decoder and teammate can view) while an interceptor simultaneously tries to recover the same hidden code from those clues; we run Decrypto over 1000 samples.
We evaluate multiple environments from the LLM Coordination benchmark (Agashe et al., 2025).
Hanabi is a cooperative card game in which players can observe their
teammates’ cards but not their own, requiring them to interpret limited
hints to coordinate their actions; we run Hanabi over 100 seeds.
In Collab Capture, two agents
coordinate their movement and actions to capture an adversary.
In Collab Escape, two agents must repair generators to open an exit
while evading an adversary. In all environments, each agent receives only the observation permitted by its role, and cannot see their partners’ private contexts.
Following Agashe et al. (2025), we evaluate Collab Capture and Collab Escape on 6 and 12 seeds respectively.

## Models.

We use Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025), trained with ToM2Vec entirely in self-play with the partner instantiated from the same base model.
To test the partner generality of the learned ToM, we additionally evaluate against partner agents drawn from other model families at test time,
including Gemma-4-E4B (Google, 2026) and GPT-5.4 (Singh et al., 2025), which are not seen during training, and the latter of which is far stronger.

## 3.2 Metrics

We report each domain’s standard metrics.
For Overcooked, we report mean episode score.
For LLM Negotiation, we report deal-success rate (deal is acceptable for at least 5/6 parties) together with the agent’s own score and the average collective score across all parties.
For Decrypto, we report the decoder win rate (how often the team guesses the codes), and interceptor win rate (how often the interceptor guesses the codes).
For Hanabi, we report game score, which is the number of correctly played cards.
For Collab Capture and Collab Escape, we report capture and escape success rates, respectively, together wi
limitations:
ToM2Vec requires access to the partner’s CoT during training.
However, we show that this CoT does not need to come from the eventual test-time partner: training against one partner transfers to others.
Nevertheless, it is still a requirement of the training procedure, and our supervision relies on both agents sharing a representation space, which is why training uses the same base model for agent and partner.
ToM2Vec also requires a training phase, unlike prompting-based approaches that work at inference time.
We find this cost is offset by performance, since the method outperforms both prompting and a training-matched verbalized baseline.
Finally, we note that our experiments use English-only tasks, a limitation shared with much prior work on LLM theory of mind and constrained in part by available models and datasets.

title: UserSWE: Evaluating Coding Agents in Multi-Turn Conversations with Dynamic Users
abstract: As coding agents become more capable, developers increasingly use them to fix bugs through multi-turn interactions. Existing benchmarks do not adequately cover this scenario. Most present a complete issue report in a single turn without interaction. Their evaluation can produce both false positives and false negatives, accepting incorrect patches or rejecting correct ones. We introduce UserSWE for evaluating coding agents' ability to fix repository-level bugs through multi-turn interactions with dynamic users and execution-grounded verdicts at every turn. Its construction pipeline turns repository history and existing single-turn benchmarks into multi-turn tasks. At each turn, information pools constrain what the simulated user can reveal, while a persona chain sampled from a transition model calibrated on 20,859 development sessions governs how it speaks. Tests run after every turn, and a pair of agents from different model families writes and gates each verdict, using test results as primary evidence and model judgment only for aspects the tests cannot resolve. We evaluate eleven agents on 72 tasks from 42 repositories and find that agent rankings change with the interaction budget. Claude Fable 5.1 resolves the most tasks in one turn, GPT-6-Astra resolves the most by the eighth turn, and Claude Opus 5 leads at most intermediate budgets. These results indicate that single-turn performance is insufficient to characterize interactive coding ability.

Abstract

As coding agents become more capable, developers increasingly use them to fix bugs
through multi-turn interactions. Existing benchmarks do not adequately cover this
scenario. Most present a complete issue report in a single turn without interaction.
Their evaluation can produce both false positives and false negatives, accepting
incorrect patches or rejecting correct ones. We introduce UserSWE for evaluating
coding agents’ ability to fix repository-level bugs through multi-turn interactions
with dynamic users and execution-grounded verdicts at every turn. Its construction
pipeline turns repository history and existing single-turn benchmarks into multi-turn
tasks. At each turn, information pools constrain what the simulated user can reveal, while a persona chain sampled from a transition model calibrated on 20,859 development sessions governs how it speaks. Tests run after every turn, and a pair
of agents from different model families writes and gates each verdict, using test
results as primary evidence and model judgment only for aspects the tests cannot
resolve. We evaluate eleven agents on 72 tasks from 42 repositories and find that
agent rankings change with the interaction budget. Claude Fable 5.1 resolves the
most tasks in one turn, GPT-6-Astra resolves the most by the eighth turn, and Claude
Opus 5 leads at most intermediate budgets. These results indicate that single-turn
performance is insufficient to characterize interactive coding ability.

††footnotetext: ∗Equal contribution.  †Correspondence to qsenre@gmail.com, cheeseluo@tencent.com.

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Existing multi-turn benchmarks keep the simulated user in one persona, while in the real development sessions we measure a developer’s style shifts from turn to turn.
On the same date-off-by-one bug, the static simulator phrases every turn as precise guidance, while the UserSWE simulator opens on a vague complaint, guesses a wrong cause, and reaches guidance only at the third turn.

AI programming assistants are deployed at scale and used daily by developers (Liang et al., 2024).
Their form has evolved from autocompletion to context-grounded conversation, and then to agents that navigate repositories, edit files, and run tests on their own — a practice popularly called vibe coding (Ross et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Sarkar and Drosos, 2025).
Developers pose follow-up questions and refine their requests in response to intermediate model outputs (Barke et al., 2023; Ross et al., 2023), where initial requests are often incomplete and gradually clarified across turns. Studies of agents in real-world settings further confirm this same iterative pattern holds across entire tasks (Siddeeq et al., 2026; Baumann et al., 2026).
As a representative scenario, debugging with an agent has now become a standard conversational workflow for developers.

However, prevailing benchmarks do not measure how well an agent works in this scenario for two main reasons.
One is that most use a single-turn setup, handing the agent everything at once and asking for a correct patch in return, so the agent is never put in the conversation where the work actually happens.
The few that do run several turns stay static, releasing the information in a written order or phrasing every turn in one fixed conversational style, which leaves the agent talking to an unresponsive mechanism and not to a simulation of a developer.
Figure 1 sets a static user beside a dynamic one on the same task.
The other concerns multi-turn judging, where every intermediate turn calls for independent assessment, but standard tests can only provide factual execution evidence, and unrestricted LLM judges are prone to making inferences beyond what results actually demonstrate.
For both reasons, a benchmark that measures coding agents’ abilities in conversation is still missing.

To address this, we propose UserSWE, which settles where the tasks come from, where the turns come from, and how each turn is judged.
The first is a construction pipeline that produces multi-turn tasks along two routes.
One route mines a repository’s own history for paired issues that a maintainer publicly recorded as linked.
The other takes an instance of an existing single-turn benchmark and stages it as a conversation.
As we continue running the pipeline along these two routes, it consistently generates new and up-to-date tasks.
The second is a method for simulating the user across the turns of a conversation.
We calculate a persona transition matrix on 20,859 real development sessions from an internally deployed commercial coding assistant, and we write each turn’s utterance from that matrix together with the information pools of the task, so the persona an agent meets becomes dynamic as the session goes on.
For each task we draw the whole chain in advance, which ensures any agent on the same task meets the same user.
The third is an evaluation framework, which enables the coding agent to operate under constraints, with dual agents judging its generated outputs based on evidence.
The framework sets rules that prevent coding agents from receiving credit beyond their demonstrated ability.
Based on tests run after every turn, a Judge from one family writes the verdict, and a Reviewer from another family clears it before it counts.
We select 72 tasks from the pipeline as UserSWE and evaluate agents on it.

The evaluation on UserSWE reveals behavior that a single-turn evaluation cannot show.
Claude Fable 5.1 resolves the most tasks within a single turn, 31.9%, and still finishes second on the length-discounted pass rate, behind Claude Opus 5, which reaches a similar place in fewer turns, 2.99 against 3.14.
GPT-6-Astra resolves the most tasks of any agent by the eighth turn, 81.9%, and places fourth once the turns it spends getting there are discounted.

In this paper, we make the following contributions.
(1) A construction pipeline.
It builds multi-turn tasks from repository evidence and existing single-turn benchmarks.
(2) A multi-turn user simulation.
We introduce a user simulator with dynamic personas grounded in real development conversations.
(3) An evaluation framework.
We propose a dual-agent judging evaluation framework complemented by a suite of supporting mechanisms, such as equivalent pass testing.
UserSWE will be released along with the evaluation framework.

## 2 Related work

Table 1 compares UserSWE with existing coding-agent benchmarks. Below, we discuss two complementary lines of related work.

Multi-turn benchmarks and simulated users.

Multi-turn evaluations must specify both what the user reveals and how the user speaks. SWE-Interact releases a task’s requirements one at a time and uses a fixed, terse senior-developer persona derived from SWE-chat (Raghavendra et al., 2026; Baumann et al., 2026), while SWE-Together reconstructs a task-specific simulator from a recorded session and triggers utterances according to the live trajectory (Wu et al., 2026). These approaches condition information release on the trajectory but do not vary the user’s voice according to a measured distribution of developer personas. More broadly, simulated users can diverge from real developers, and persona choice can substantially change measured performance (Seshadri et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026; Truong et al., 2025). UserSWE samples a persona chain from real development sessions and generates an information pool for each task, which helps simulate users naturally.

SWE benchmarks and evaluation reliability.

SWE-bench established issue-level, execution-based evaluation for coding agents (Jimenez et al., 2024). Later work addresses task contamination and freshness through larger, private, or continuously refreshed task collections (Xue et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025); SWE Context Bench is closest to our mining route but poses related instances independently (Zhu et al., 2026). A parallel line shows that verdicts can fail because tests are too loose or tight, LLM judges exhibit bias, or the evaluation harness can be gamed (Xue et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2023; Wataoka et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026). Panel-based judges and rule-based checkers improve reliability but remain imperfect (Verga et al., 2024; Lù et al., 2025). In the multi-turn setting, SWE-Interact still verifies only the final solution and rubric-scores intermediate turns (Raghavendra et al., 2026). UserSWE executes tests after every turn and uses a cross-family writer/reviewer gate, grounding each verdict in execution and reserving model judgment for evidence the tests cannot cover.

## 3 Preliminaries

The dominant executable format for software-engineering evaluation poses one issue as one task and grades the returned patch by executing tests (Jimenez et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2026).
Given an issue and the repository state $b$ at the commit preceding its fix, the agent answers once with a patch $\hat{g}$ .
Write $t(s)\in\{0,1\}$ for the outcome of test $t$ in workspace state $s$ , and let $s\oplus p$ apply patch $p$ to $s$ .
The task also carries the maintainer’s own fix, the gold patch $g$ , and two sets of tests from $b$ and $b\oplus g$ ,

A patch $\hat{g}$ resolves the task when $t(b\oplus\hat{g})=1$ for every $t\in F\cup P$ , and the reported score is the fraction of tasks resolved (Yang et al., 2024).

## 4 UserSWE

We introduce UserSWE, which evaluates agents on issue fixing inside a multi-turn conversation and so measures coding ability more completely than a one-shot format can.
Where Section 3 is settled in a single exchange, an agent here works on the issue over several turns, each turn answering what the user has just asked for, and we check the fail-to-pass and the pass-to-pass set after every one of those turns.
Turning both sets green in as few turns as possible is what UserSWE credits as strength at resolving code issues interactively.

constructed, the persona panel how the simulated user is built, and the
evaluation panel how a session is run and scored.

## 4.1 Data Construction

We mine issue cascades and single issues from two sources and select the suitable ones as tasks.
The first route searches repository histories for two issues explicitly linked by a maintainer.
Each side has a merged fix with tests, giving the task two related acceptance points.
The second route takes tasks from published single-turn benchmarks, preserving their repository state, gold patch, tests and original acceptance point while changing how their information is released across a multi-turn conversation.

Both routes then turn each task into an information pool.
The pipeline extracts symptoms from the issue report and uses the gold patch to construct correct or wrong directions about the cause, with the wrong direction later shared by the off-target and wrong personas.
A cascade also carries follow-up information for its second issue.
The pool is frozen before evaluation and checked for identifiers introduced by the gold patch, with an additional cross-phase scope check for cascades.
Agents evaluated on the same task therefore draw from the same frozen candidate information pool, preventing differences in pool construction from confounding the comparison.

Before admission, each task passes both mechanical and human checks.
The framework reruns the fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests in the evaluation container, verifying that the fail-to-pass tests fail at the base state and pass after the gold patch is applied, while the pass-to-pass tests pass in both states.
Appendix A details how tasks from both sources are converted into information pools and admitted as executable tasks.

## 4.2 Multi-turn Interaction

Section 4.1 fixes what the simulated user may say, but not which item should be selected at each turn or the voice in which it should be expressed.
We handle these questions separately, first selecting the content through a release policy and then rendering it through a conversational persona model calibrated on real development sessions.

After each turn, the simulated user selects guidance from the information pool according to the agent’s response and the canonical test results.
The information selection process follows a fixed priority hierarchy designed to mirror the logic of natural developer interactions. If the agent poses a direct question, the simulated user responds with a direct answer. Otherwise, it selects content in descending order of priority: the most severe user-observable blocking failure, an unaddressed core business boundary, or a secondary edge case. This hierarchy governs what information the user simulator releases at the current turn.

Once the content is selected, the framework must decide how to express it.
The expression of the developer varies between people and between turns of the same session.
Its two common components align with the two kinds of content in the information pool, namely how a developer describes what was observed and whether they offer a view of the cause.
We therefore factor the simulated user along two axes.
Clarity records whether the symptom is stated precisely or vaguely, and veracity records whether the user offers no view, a correct one, an off-target one, or a wrong one.
Crossing these axes yields eight conversational personas, and Table 2 presents the same request phrased in each of them.

What remains is how each turn is judged, which is the next subsection.

## 4.3 Evaluation

A multi-turn evaluation framework entails two dimensions of freedom, each causing evaluation misjudgments when improperly calibrated.
The degree of freedom allowed by the framework, when set too loose or too tight, renders the evaluation scores unreliable.
The degree of freedom granted to the agent, when set too loose or too tight, prevents it from demonstrating its true capabilities.
Our evaluation framework for UserSWE addresses these two dimensions separately.

limitations:
UserSWE has three limitations.
(1) Scale. Multi-turn evaluation runs a full session and reruns tests after every turn, making it more expensive than scoring one patch per task and limiting the released set to 72 tasks. Table 15 reports detailed per-task costs.
(2) Horizon. UserSWE covers one maintenance episode over one or two issues, from a base commit to a fixed set of acceptance points. It does not cover longer-term work such as building a repository from scratch, which remains a direction for future extensions.
(3) Session logs. The user model uses opening distributions and turn-to-turn transitions measured from 20,859 sessions collected from an internally deployed commercial coding assistant. Future versions could incorporate additional signals about task types and request phrasing.
conclusion:
We present UserSWE, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents in multi-turn
conversations with dynamic users. We contribute a construction pipeline that builds
multi-turn tasks from repository history and existing benchmarks, a user
simulator with dynamic personas grounded in real development sessions, and an
evaluation framework that anchors cross-family judging and review to executed
tests. Together, these components produce UserSWE, which we use to evaluate
eleven agents on 72 tasks and uncover behaviors that single-turn
evaluation cannot reveal.

title: COMET: A coordinated multi-layer runtime monitoring framework for human-supervised AI-enabled safety systems
abstract: Incorporating AI systems into safety systems requires monitoring to avoid silent faults and ensure safe and reliable operation. Single monitors often do not provide actionable information for human supervisors, who act as the system's adaptive controller. We present COMET, a coordinated multi-layer runtime monitoring framework for human-supervised AI-enabled safety systems in which each monitor is anchored in a different fault mode. Monitor outputs are combined in a coordination layer and mapped by a communication layer to a traffic-light display. In this work, COMET consists of three monitoring layers: signal integrity, physics consistency, and the AI system's competence envelope. The framework is evaluated on an open dataset of compressed-air leaks, where an AI system detects leaks from acoustic emissions, with held-out conditions simulating covariate shift, semantic shift, and sensor faults, events expected during runtime but unknown in their exact appearance. All monitors are frozen after development and tested zero-shot, and the framework is compared against no-monitoring and single-monitor setups. The bare AI system fails silently and confidently under all three shift types, whereas COMET reduces the trusted-wrong-answer rate to zero on covariate-shifted no-leak data and on three of four sensor faults, at a nominal false-alarm rate of $\approx 1\%$. Single monitors come close in detection but cannot attribute the fault mode. COMET converts their anonymous detection flags into diagnoses. Residual silent misses under semantic shift define the boundary of passive monitoring. Runtime monitoring frameworks for AI-enabled safety systems must therefore combine quantitative fault detection and isolation with qualitative, human-oriented feedback.

Abstract

Incorporating AI systems into safety systems requires monitoring to avoid silent faults and ensure safe and reliable operation. Single monitors often do not provide actionable information for human supervisors, who act as the system’s adaptive controller. We present COMET, a coordinated multi-layer runtime monitoring framework for human-supervised AI-enabled safety systems in which each monitor is anchored in a different fault mode. Monitor outputs are combined in a coordination layer and mapped by a communication layer to a traffic-light display. In this work, COMET consists of three monitoring layers: signal integrity, physics consistency, and the AI system’s competence envelope. The framework is evaluated on an open dataset of compressed-air leaks, where an AI system detects leaks from acoustic emissions, with held-out conditions simulating covariate shift, semantic shift, and sensor faults, events expected during runtime but unknown in their exact appearance. All monitors are frozen after development and tested zero-shot, and the framework is compared against no-monitoring and single-monitor setups. The bare AI system fails silently and confidently under all three shift types, whereas COMET reduces the trusted-wrong-answer rate to zero on covariate-shifted no-leak data and on three of four sensor faults, at a nominal false-alarm rate of $\approx 1\%$ . Single monitors come close in detection but cannot attribute the fault mode. COMET converts their anonymous detection flags into diagnoses. Residual silent misses under semantic shift define the boundary of passive monitoring. Runtime monitoring frameworks for AI-enabled safety systems must therefore combine quantitative fault detection and isolation with qualitative, human-oriented feedback.

## 1 Introduction

## 1.1 Motivation

The diffusion of AI systems from research into real-world applications has accelerated in recent years, driven by cheap compute, capable models, large amount of available data, and increasingly complex systems that need to be managed. Whereas for consumer products reliable operation of AI systems is largely a question of practicality, for safety-critical systems safe and reliable operation is a requirement, not a nice-to-have. This requirement is emphasized by policies and standards such as the EU AI Act (EU AI Act, 2024) and the ISO/IEC TR 5469 (ISO/IEC TR 5469:2024, 2024), which addresses the incorporation of AI systems into systems whose failures can cause severe consequences. One means of ensuring reliable and safe operation is monitoring (Rausand et al., 2021; Leveson, 2012). It provides information about system behavior during runtime and thus contribute to maintaining safe and reliable operation. Throughout this work, the term AI system describes a system consisting of an AI model and its necessary pre- and post-processing steps during runtime, whereas AI-enabled system describes the broader engineered system into which one or more AI systems are integrated (Det Norske Veritas, 2023).

In recent years, much research has focused on developing monitors for AI systems, most commonly are out-of-distribution detectors (Yang et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024). These works typically aim to improve the performance on new or established benchmarks rather than proposing holistic frameworks, where not only the quantitative aspect of detecting samples outside the learned distribution matters, but also the qualitative aspects on how detections are communicated, and how monitors work together with the human supervisors who are supposed to use them. A few works have begun to combine multiple monitor into unifying frameworks (Dario et al., 2027; Torens et al., 2025; Ferreira, 2023), but these still address detection rather than diagnosis and do not consider the human supervisor. This leads to the question:

How can we design a runtime monitoring framework for AI systems that detects potentially unreliable system behavior, isolates faults, and supports the human supervisor in the loop, so as to enhance safe and reliable operation?

The purpose of this work is to propose and test such a framework under realistic conditions. Derived from fault-tolerant control theory, where adapting the control of a system requires fault diagnosis, i.e., detection, isolation and identification, the framework promotes safe and reliable operation by detecting shifts that can degrade the AI system’s performance and by providing qualitatively meaningful information to the human supervisor. To this end, we select a dataset and an AI system that together represent an AI safety system, and build COMET, a coordinated multi-layer runtime monitoring framework whose monitors cover different fault modes, are fused through a coordination layer, and are mapped to a traffic-light-based display through a communication layer. The framework is derived in Section 2. Section 3 describes the experimental setup, which tests the framework under realistic conditions and compares it with alternative monitoring strategies. The results are presented in Section 4 and discussed in Section 5. Section 6 concludes and outlines future work.

## 1.2 Related work

The need for monitoring deployed AI systems is already established in the MLOps literature (Kreuzberger et al., 2023), where monitoring serves continuous performance improvement. However, its scope is operational rather than safety-related, i.e., the monitored systems are typically not part of safety functions, and reliability and safety implications of unreliable outputs are not the focus. On the regulatory side, the EU AI Act mandates post-market monitoring for high-risk AI systems but does not specify how such monitoring should be realized (EU AI Act, 2024). Similarly, ISO/IEC TR 5469 on AI and functional safety names monitoring as a potential risk-reduction measure without detailing its concrete design (ISO/IEC TR 5469:2024, 2024). This work addresses that gap of a concrete runtime monitoring framework for AI-enabled safety systems, where system reliability is a primary concern and a human supervisor remains in the loop as highest control entity.

The most common monitoring technique is out-of-distribution (OOD) detection (Yang et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024). In simple terms, it discriminates between samples inside the learned distribution, where the AI system should operate as trained and tested, and samples outside it, where outputs are potentially unreliable. These methods perform well on established benchmarks, with effectiveness depending on the method used. They can be applied using in-distribution data alone (Liu et al., 2023; Heng et al., 2024) or a combination of in-distribution and OOD data (Liu et al., 2020), and many are training-agnostic, operation post-hoc on a deployed model (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016a; Sun et al., 2022). In concrete applications, OOD detection has been used to increase trustworthiness of deployed AI systems, for instance in prognostics and health management for renewable energy systems (Xie et al., 2023) and in mechanical fault diagnostic (Xiao et al., 2025). What these method have in common is that they are typically proposed and evaluated as single, isolated monitors, not as part of a holistic runtime monitoring framework.

Combining complementary monitors into holistic runtime monitoring frameworks that cover different fault modes and are potentially more robust than single monitors is underrepresented in current research. The few existing examples (Ferreira, 2023; Dario et al., 2027; Torens et al., 2025) demonstrate that combining monitors can improve detection, but they treat monitoring as a purely algorithmic output where the human supervisor who may need to perceive, interpret and decide on the outputs is not explicitly considered. Moreover, existing combinations fuse monitor to improve detection performance, rather than coordinating local diagnoses toward fault isolation in the sense of classical fault diagnosis. This work addresses both gaps. It develops a runtime monitoring framework with multiple monitor derived fault-tolerant system principles, and it designs the framework around the human in the loop.

Considering the human in the loop means going beyond bare in/out verdict of an OOD detector. Such a verdict may not be sufficient when a supervisor remains responsible and needs a clear basis for judgment. To take over from an AI system or override a potentially unreliable output, they must understand what kind of event is occurring. Otherwise, even well-intended monitoring can contribute to situations similar to automation surprise (Sarter and Woods, 1997). Integrating a communication layer and building a more holistic runtime monitoring framework can thus promote more resilient, reliable, and safe system operation. This work address how outputs from multiple monitors can be fused into qualitatively richer feedback for humans in the loop.

## 1.3 Contributions

Based on the related work and the limitations identified above, this works makes the following contributions to the field of runtime monitoring for AI systems:

1. 

We present COMET, a coordinated multi-layer runtime monitoring framework in which multiple monitors derive their authority from different fault modes. In this work, we have three monitors: engineering rules (signal integrity), first-principle physics (spectral leak template), and learned behavioral statistics (feature-space competence envelope). This results in fault modes that are disjoint by construction. The monitor outputs are combined by a coordination layer and fused into a fixed taxonomy with a traffic-light mapping, designed as the communication layer to the human supervisor in the loop.

2. 

We demonstrate the quantitative performance via an empirical evaluation on an open dataset that serves as a proxy for a safety-critical application. Covariate shift, semantic shift, and injected sensor faults are held out from all training, validation, and calibration. Every monitor is frozen after development, and the shifts are evaluated exactly once, zero-shot. An ablation ladder compares COMET against the bare AI system and single-monitor setups, including the commonly used max-softmax probability (MSP) baseline, using supervisor-oriented metrics such as the trusted-wrong-answer rate and silent-miss-coverage.

3. 

We derive design insights for runtime monitoring of deployed AI systems, supported by the ablations and by pre-registered sensitivity variants, i.e., why disjoint anchoring matters more than individual monitor strength, why the calibration unit must match the decision unit, and where the boundary of passive monitoring lies. We report the negative results and residual fault modes openly, including the silent misses no passive layer combination caught, which we consider essential evidence for future research on monitoring AI systems.

## 2 Methods

The first part of the methods section describes the AI application that was used to represent an AI-enabled safety system, the complementary dataset, the specific model architecture, the pre-processing of the data, and the training process. Then, the coordinated multi-layer runtime monitoring framework is derived from the concept of fault-tolerant systems and coordinated fault diagnosis. The specific monitors that are used in this work are derived. Finally, the specific taxonomy states for the coordination and communication layer is described.

## 2.1 AI application: leak detection system

To evaluate the coordinated multi-layer runtime monitoring framework, we used an open dataset (Johnson et al., 2020b) on compressed-air leaks with the complementary AI system that performs well on the dataset with accuracies reaching over 95 % (Johnson et al., 2020a). Its high performance reflects a realistic scenario where the result from training and testing satisfies the requirement for real-world deployment of an AI system. The AI system used was designed to classify spectrogram files into ”leak” or ”no leak” where a compressed-air leak represents a costly fault in industrial productions. The leak of compressed air does not represent a safety-critical issue, but using acoustic emissions together with AI systems to detect leaks is a common method used in process industries (Banjara et al., 2020; Ullah et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2026). The detection of leaks in this domain represents a safety system that is essential to ensure safe and reliable operation. Due to the lack of open and diverse data on gas leaks but the similarity between the use cases, we chose the compressed-air leak detection as suitable proxy for the safety-critical leak detection in process industries.

In this work, the AI system represents the AI component inside an AI-enabled safety system. It performs the safety function of detecting the leak, whereas the overall system additionally comprises physical components such as the sensors, the monitored process, and potential actuators that are activated to maintain safe and reliable operation.

## 2.1.1 Dataset

The data used for this work were collected by the Fraunhofer institute (Johnson et al., 2020b). The data represent compressed-air leaks that were collected with 4 microphones, at 2 gain settings, with different backgrounds (i.e., lab noise ”lab”, workshop noise ”work”/”work-low”, hydraulic noise ”hydr”/”hydr-low”), different leak types (i.e., vent leak at 6 bar ”vent”, vent leak at 5 bar ”vent-low”, tube leak ”tube”), and different severity gradation based on the knob state. Each leak type contains all backgrounds and for each background there are three sessions of recording. There are two recordings for each knob state, one with low gain and one with max gain. The knob state increases from 0 to 3 with a step size of 1 and from there it continues with a step size of 0.5 until 9.0. The knob state represents the number of turns to open the vent where 0.5 represents half a turn. Between knob state 3.5 and 5.0 there are small leaks present but not detectable for the installed microphones thus these knob states are excluded from the data. The whole dataset composition is seen in Figure 1.

## 2.1.2 Primary AI system

The primary AI system used for this work is based on the original convolutional neural network (CNN) model from Johnson et al. (2020a) that was used on the same dataset with some adaptions. The model architecture consists of an initial block that applies a Gaussian noise with standard deviation of 0.1 and that is only active during training mode. Next, there are three convolution blocks with a GELU (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016b) activation function and max pooling with channels 16, 32 and 64. The final block contains a dropout function, a dense multi-layer perceptron (MLP) network, a GELU activation function, another dropout regularization, and finally a second MLP with two logits as output. The whole model has 121,794 parameters.

## 2.1.3 Pre-processing

Each recording has a length of 30 seconds and a measurement frequency of 48 kHz. First each recording was transformed with a short-time Fourier transformation (STFT) to create a spectrogram of shape 513 x 2813 (frequency bins x time frames). Then the spectrogram is cut along the time axis into non-overlapping 24-frame patches, 267 ms. One recording yields 117 patches, each of shape 513 x 24. This also is the fixed-size ”image” for the AI system. Every patch inherits its recording’s label: ”leak” or ”no-leak”. Next, we augmented the training patches with noise to make the model more robust. This is relevant for the patches with lab noise which basically means no added noise. In the real world, we always have noise so this is why we chose the augmentation. With a probability of 0.5, we added white or pink Gaussian noise to the patches in the power domain at a random signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) between 0 and 20 dB. Validation and test patches are excluded from this augmentation. Finally, we normalize the patches. Each patch is z-scored per frequency bin: subtract the per-bin mean, divide by the per-bin standard deviation. The statistics are computed once over all training split frames of one fold.

## 2.1.4 Training process

We trained one AI system per microphone. For each microphone, the nominal envelope, i.e., ”vent”/”vent-low” leak types, ”lab”/”work”/”work-low” noise types, no-leak knob state $\leq 3.0$ , leak knob state $\geq 5.5$ , is split by whole recording session. This means a leave-one-session-out training with three folds: train on two sessions, validate on the held-out one. Session-level splitting guarantees no data leakage. For microphone-1, the concrete split resulted in 286 training files and 120 validation files, roughly a 70/30 split. The dataset for the training and validation is built per fold. First, the pre-processing is done as mentioned above. Then, the patches get split into 33,580 training patches and 14,080 validation patches for one fold. The normalization statistics are computed on the training split, and applied to both training and validation.

conclusion: The central finding of this work is that no single monitor or local diagnoser was sufficient, and that the fault modes of the individual monitors were largely disjoint as it was intended. Confidence-based monitoring reduced but did not remove trusted wrong answers. The physics-consistency monitor withheld its judgment exactly where it was most needed, and the feature-space monitor was the strongest single monitor but could not isolate and identify the fault. Only COMET reduced the trusted-wrong-answer rate to zero on hydraulic no-leak data and on three of four injected sensor faults, at a nominal false-alarm rate of $\approx 1\%$ . Equally important the qualitative difference that the coordinated multi-layer runtime monitoring structure with coordination and communication layers turns a detection flag into a diagnosis with detection, isolation and identification for some fault modes, i.e., sensor fault, physically implausible detection, or unfamiliar operating context. This is the form of information a responsible human supervisor can act on and adapt to.

title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents
abstract: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49-59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79-86% accuracy, a significant 17-24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers.

headings: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents
body_start:
Abstract

Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49–59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79–86% accuracy, a significant 17–24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers.

## 1 Introduction

Language agents that search the biomedical literature are quickly becoming a default component of scientific assistants: they formulate queries, read abstracts, and return verdicts with citations (Lála et al., 2023; Skarlinski et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2024). The design space of such harnesses is large, but the empirical basis for choosing among designs is thin. Three questions arise for anyone building a literature agent for the life sciences:
(i) Does giving a frontier model access to PubMed improve its verdicts over closed-book answering, or does parametric knowledge suffice?
(ii) Is an agentic loop, in which the model writes and refines its own queries (Yao et al., 2023; Nakano et al., 2021), worth its additional cost over a fixed one-shot retrieval pipeline (Lewis et al., 2020)?
(iii) When agents cite papers, are those citations faithful to what they actually read?

We study these questions in a controlled setting: expert-written biomedical claim verification on SciFact (Wadden et al., 2020), using the live PubMed E-utilities API as the only tool. We hold the backbone model, prompt format, and output schema fixed and vary only the harness: closed-book, single-shot retrieval, a ReAct-style multi-query agent, and an oracle that receives the gold abstracts. We run the same protocol with two backbones and decompose errors into retrieval failures (the gold paper was never seen) and reasoning failures (the gold paper was seen but the verdict was wrong).

## Contributions.

(1) A small, fully reproducible harness-ablation protocol for literature agents built on a public benchmark and a public API (code and cached tool calls released). (2) An empirical comparison of four harnesses across two backbones, with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired analyses. (3) A citation audit showing how closed-book models cite real but irrelevant papers, a failure mode that existence-based checks alone cannot catch.

## 2 Related Work

Scientific claim verification. SciFact (Wadden et al., 2020) introduced expert-written claims paired with evidence abstracts; subsequent systems such as MultiVerS (Wadden et al., 2022) operate over a fixed corpus of about 5K abstracts. We instead place the model in the open-world setting it would face in deployment, searching all of PubMed.
Retrieval-augmented and agentic biomedical QA. MedRAG (Xiong et al., 2024) benchmarks retrieval-augmented generation for medical QA, GeneGPT (Jin et al., 2024) teaches LLMs to call NCBI APIs, and PaperQA/PaperQA2 (Lála et al., 2023; Skarlinski et al., 2024) build full literature agents. LAB-Bench (Laurent et al., 2024) evaluates biology-research capabilities including literature tasks. These works typically evaluate full systems; our aim is a minimal, controlled ablation of the harness itself.
Citation fabrication. LLMs are known to fabricate bibliographic references (Walters and Wilder, 2023). We extend this analysis to PubMed IDs and distinguish non-existent citations from existing but irrelevant ones.

## 3 Experimental Setup

Task and data. Each SciFact claim is labeled Support, Contradict, or Not Enough Info (NEI) with respect to its cited abstracts. Because SciFact test labels are hidden, we use the labeled dev split (300 claims) and, due to computational budget constraints, evaluate a fixed random sample of $N{=}100$ claims (seed 0), shared by all conditions. We report accuracy and macro-F1 over the three labels, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (2,000 resamples).

Harnesses. All conditions share the same instructions and require a JSON output {label, cited_pmids, rationale}, at temperature 0.

• 

Closed-book: the model answers from parametric knowledge and may cite PMIDs it believes are relevant.

• 

Single-shot RAG: the claim, with stopwords removed, is issued as one PubMed query (relevance sort, top-5). If PubMed returns nothing (terms are ANDed), we relax to an OR over content words. Titles and abstracts (truncated to 1,500 characters) are given to the model.

• 

Agentic search: a ReAct-style loop (Yao et al., 2023) in which, at each step, the model either issues a PubMed query of its own design or answers. It has a budget of 4 searches (top-5 each, deduplicated) and is told PubMed’s query semantics.

• 

Oracle: the model receives the SciFact-cited gold abstracts directly. This upper-bounds performance given perfect retrieval and isolates reasoning over evidence.

Backbones. We use two efficient frontier models from the same provider, gemini-3.1-flash-lite and gemini-3.5-flash-lite, chosen for their low latency and cost. Tool calls and model outputs are cached to make every number reproducible from the released logs.

Retrieval and citation diagnostics. SciFact documents are identified by Semantic Scholar IDs, not PMIDs, so we map a retrieved PubMed record to a gold document by normalized title match (exact or ratio $>0.9$ ). Gold recall is the fraction of Support/Contradict claims for which at least one gold abstract was retrieved. For retrieval conditions, a citation is unfaithful if its PMID was never returned by the tool. For closed-book citations, we check (a) existence in PubMed, (b) whether it matches a gold paper, and (c) topical relevance, judged by a model from a different family (qwen3.8-27b) given the claim and the cited title and abstract. We apply the same relevance judge to agent citations for comparison.

## 4 Results

Figure 1: (a) Macro-F1 by harness with 95% bootstrap CIs. (b) Accuracy on Support/Contradict claims, split by whether a gold abstract was retrieved (gold-hit groups are small: $n{=}4$ for RAG and $n{=}12/13$ for the agent).

Table 1 and Figure 1 summarize the results. We highlight five findings.

F1: Naive one-shot retrieval does not help, and changes how the model fails. Issuing the claim itself as a PubMed query retrieves a gold abstract for only 6% of evidence-bearing claims (4/64 for both backbones). Given mostly off-target abstracts, both models abstain heavily: 59% and 70% of their predictions are NEI, against 36% NEI in the gold labels. Accuracy is unchanged or lower relative to closed-book (53.0 vs. 55.0 and 49.0 vs. 59.0; exact McNemar $p{=}0.89$ and $p{=}0.24$ ). Retrieval converts overconfident errors into abstentions rather than into correct verdicts. When the gold abstract was retrieved, both models were correct on all 4 such claims.

F2: Letting the model write its own queries triples gold recall and gives the best verdicts, but the gains are modest. The agentic harness raises gold recall to 19–20% and attains the highest accuracy (62.0 for both backbones) and macro-F1 (60.3 and 61.1) of the non-oracle harnesses. Its queries are short, entity-centric reformulations (e.g., “chenodeoxycholic acid energy expenditure” instead of the full claim), and they can repair misspellings in the claim (“Chenodeosycholic” $\rightarrow$ “chenodeoxycholic”), which silently break literal retrieval. In paired comparisons, however, the improvement is not statistically significant at $N{=}100$ : agent vs. single-shot, 24 vs. 15 discordant claims ( $p{=}0.20$ ) and 29 vs. 16 ( $p{=}0.07$ ); agent vs. closed-book, 13 vs. 6 ( $p{=}0.17$ ) and 11 vs. 8 ( $p{=}0.65$ ). The direction is consistent across both backbones.

F3: Agents under-use their search budget. Despite a budget of 4 searches, the agents issue 1.42 and 1.70 queries per claim on average and answer after a single search on 71% and 55% of claims; only 3% and 6% of claims use the full budget. Among evidence-bearing claims where the agent never saw a gold abstract, it still answered Support/Contradict correctly 75% of the time, suggesting that it draws on other relevant PubMed papers or on parametric knowledge. But it also abstains less on true NEI claims (33% and 42% NEI recall, versus 72% and 81% for single-shot). Budget use is therefore a clear axis for harness improvement, for example through a minimum-evidence criterion before answering.

F4: Retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Given the gold abstracts, the same models reach 86.0% and 79.0% accuracy (macro-F1 85.8 and 78.6), 24 and 17 points above the best realistic harness. Unlike the differences among realistic harnesses, this gap is highly significant (agent vs. oracle, 5 vs. 29 discordant claims, $p{<}10^{-4}$ ; 9 vs. 26, $p{=}0.006$ ). The oracle also restores calibrated abstention (NEI recall 78% and 86%) without sacrificing Support/Contradict accuracy, so the models reason well over evidence once they are shown the right papers.

F5: Closed-book citations are real papers, but almost never relevant ones. Closed-book models cited PMIDs for 97 and 80 of the 100 claims. Almost all cited PMIDs exist in PubMed (186/190 and 141/145), so existence checks would pass them. None matched a SciFact gold paper, however, and the cross-family judge rated only 1 of 186 and 2 of 141 as relevant to the claim. Typical examples: a claim about TNF- $\alpha$ /IL-1 and IL-6/IL-10 regulation is supported by “[The proper eyeglasses for children]”, and a claim about headache and cognitive impairment by “Improving access to appointments at Laurie Pike Health Centre”. The judge itself is well calibrated on controls: it labels 21/25 gold abstracts relevant and 0/25 mismatched gold abstracts relevant. Grounding changes this sharply. The same judge rates 66% (141/215) and 70% (128/184) of agent-cited PMIDs as relevant, and 77% and 84% of agent verdicts that cite anything cite at least one relevant paper. Agents almost never cite outside what they retrieved (0% and 2.6% of citing claims).
Closed-book models are also overconfident: they predict NEI for only 4% and 9% of claims, recovering 6% and 17% of true NEI claims, so their competitive accuracy rests entirely on Support/Contradict claims.

## 5 Discussion and Limitations

Implications for harness design. (1) Query formulation appears to be where the model adds the most value in a literature agent: letting the LLM reformulate the query triples recall of the right paper and gives the best verdicts on both backbones, whereas passing the claim straight to the search engine does not help. (2) The largest remaining headroom lies in retrieval, as the 17–24 point gap to the oracle shows, so iterative search that is actually used (F3), citation chasing, and domain retrievers are more promising than stronger verdict prompting. (3) Citations from ungrounded generation should never be surfaced, even when the IDs resolve: validating that a PMID exists is not sufficient, and relevance must be checked against the retrieved text.

Limitations. This is a pilot study. $N{=}100$ claims per condition gives wide confidence intervals, and none of the accuracy differences between realistic harnesses is significant. Both backbones are small, efficient models from a single provider, chosen for their low latency and cost, so results may differ for larger or open-weight models. SciFact labels are defined with respect to specific cited abstracts, whereas our harnesses search all of PubMed as of 2026. Some “errors” may therefore reflect newer or different evidence, and title-matched gold recall is a lower bound on useful retrieval. Relevance judgments come from a single LLM judge, validated only on 50 controls. We plan to scale to the full dev set, add open-weight and biomedical-specialist backbones, and study budget-forcing strategies for agentic search.

Reproducibility. Code, prompts, all raw model outputs, and the cached PubMed responses are available at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers. The released cache reproduces every reported number without API access.

## Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding

The author received no specific funding for this work and declares no competing interests.

title: TraceForge: Distilling with Your Own Thinking
abstract: Using an LLM to generate training data for another is among the most general ways to train one, and it remains common practice. Some frontier teams have closed that route for their own models: what comes back is an answer, or a short summary, without the detailed reasoning trace behind it. That is a little ironic: they were themselves built on distilling human knowledge, and distilling an open-source model is still entirely routine; the restriction applies to their own outputs alone. Recent work recovers the hidden reasoning by replaying encrypted blocks across models. It somehow works, but it breaks the providers' terms of service, so it is not something a product can be built on long-term. We built the alternative. We take the context and the teacher's answer as input, and generate the reasoning trace ourselves, in the style of the student's own model family. Training is two-stage, supervised and then adversarial: a generator learns to regenerate the family's own reasoning traces from their context and answer, and a critic learns how real a reasoning trace looks. Applied to a teacher's answer, the generator writes one in the family's style. An independent judge rates how likely traces are to be genuine on a scale from 0 to 1: ours average 0.68, real traces 0.66, and traces selected by the critic from four candidates 0.82. These are authenticity scores, not correctness rates. We test the idea on five benchmarks with everything else held fixed. On general tasks the five training corpora are about the same; on coding, the generated reasoning beats Fable 5's own thinking content. With the same 5,000 questions and the same teacher answers, HumanEval+ improves by 3.7 points and MBPP+ by 7.1 at the final checkpoint, and the MBPP+ lead holds at every checkpoint. We suspect that reasoning written in the student's family style is easier for it to learn from.
