Adversarial training and the reconstruction target.
body_start:
Abstract

Using an LLM to generate training data for another is among the most general ways to train one, and it
remains common practice. Some frontier teams have closed that route for their own models: what comes
back is an answer, or a short summary, without the detailed reasoning trace behind it. That is a little ironic: they were themselves built on distilling human knowledge, and distilling an open-source model is
still entirely routine; the restriction applies to their own outputs alone. Recent work recovers the
hidden reasoning by replaying encrypted blocks across models Panfilov et al. [2026]. It somehow
works, but it breaks the providers’ terms of service, so it is not something a product can be built on
long-term.

We built the alternative. We take the context and the teacher’s answer as input, and generate the
reasoning trace ourselves, in the style of the student’s own model family. We call the result a “family-native” trace. Training is two-stage,
supervised and then adversarial: a generator learns to regenerate the family’s own reasoning traces from their context and answer, and a critic learns how real a reasoning trace looks. Applied to a teacher’s answer, the generator writes one in the family’s style. A closed judge scores the family-native traces at 68% against 66% for the real ones, and at 82% once
the critic picks the best of four.

We test the idea on five benchmarks with everything else held fixed. On general tasks the five training corpora are about the same; on coding, the generated reasoning beats Fable 5’s own thinking
content. With the same $3{,}500$ questions and the same teacher answers, HumanEval+ improves by $3.7$ 
points and MBPP+ by $7.1$ at the final checkpoint, and the MBPP+ lead holds at every checkpoint.
Intuitively, we attribute this to the student and the family-native traces coming from the same model
family: the student can absorb them without unlearning its own habits, so adaptation costs less and
catastrophic forgetting is smaller.

Figure 1: Same answers, better traces. HumanEval+ (left) and MBPP+ (right) across training. Against the model trained on Fable 5’s own traces, ours with Fable 5’s answers wins at nearly every checkpoint. Both of our models, with Fable 5 and with GPT-6.1-SOL as the teacher, are far better than the one trained with Qwen3.8-Max as teacher.

## 1 Introduction

Using an LLM to generate training data for another is among the most general ways to train one. A strong
model answers a set of questions, a weaker one is trained on those answers and, better still, on the
reasoning that led to them, and the gap closes DeepSeek-AI [2025]. This is not a loophole. Training a model on another model’s output is how this field has advanced from the start.

Some labs have decided to stop this. The strongest models now return an answer, or a short summary of
their reasoning, and nothing more. The stated reasons are safety and intellectual property; the effect
is a moat, and the moat is the point. Others have tried to go around it by hacking the reasoning traces directly:
recent work shows that the encrypted reasoning blocks returned by providers are interchangeable across
models and can be replayed to recover a hidden reasoning trace verbatim Panfilov et al. [2026]. It works, but
it breaks the terms under which those APIs are sold, so it is not something to build on long term.

We propose a legal alternative: do not recover the teacher’s reasoning: generate the missing reasoning
ourselves. We train a generator to regenerate the reasoning traces of the student’s own model family from their context and answer, and a critic to keep those reasoning traces indistinguishable from the family’s real ones. Applied to a teacher’s answer, the generator writes the reasoning that arrives at it, in the family’s style. The two are trained against each other, and at inference
the critic picks the best of several candidates, with no labels and nothing that violates a provider’s
terms. We call the result a family-native trace.

We train Qwen3.5-9B-Base on reasoning traces produced in different ways. On the two coding benchmarks,
replacing Fable 5’s reasoning trace with a family-native one raises pass@1 by $3.7$ and $7.1$ points at the final
checkpoint, and the MBPP+ lead holds at every checkpoint we measured; on the three general-knowledge
tasks, which do not test reasoning, the result is about the same. Reasoning traces synthesized from GPT-6.1-SOL’s
answers reach a similar level. Family-native traces also beat training on the family’s strongest model directly: with Qwen3.8-Max’s own reasoning traces and answers, the same student trails our corpus by $21$ and $35$ points on the same two benchmarks. The teacher’s capability sets the ceiling for the student’s.

One might be surprised that the generated reasoning traces beat Fable 5’s own. We attribute it to the source of the
form: a reasoning trace written by the student’s own family is data the student can absorb without unlearning its
own habits, so adaptation costs less and catastrophic forgetting is smaller than when the same capability
arrives in a foreign hand.

Our contribution is easy to state. Training on another model’s output is an old and open technique; the only line that matters is whether the data was obtained legally. We use the word
distillation without apology, and we stay on the right side of that line. The community can now learn
from the best models without asking permission and, on the evidence here, end up with a better
student than those models’ own reasoning traces would have produced.

## 2 Method

Figure 2: The pipeline. A conversation is a system prompt, user turns, tool calls and
responses, an answer, and the reasoning trace that sits before the answer. Training the generator
(blue) takes the conversation with the reasoning trace removed and restores it as the target (green). The critic
(purple) is shown a real reasoning trace and a generated one and must say which is which. The generator is then
trained against the critic’s verdict (arc).

## 2.1 Problem

Figure 2 shows the object we work with, a conversation written as a message list. Let
 $R$ be the reasoning trace and let $S$ , $U$ , $A$ and $T$ be everything else: the system prompt, the user
turns, the answer, and any tool call or response. The generator models

 $P(R\mid S,U,A,T),$ 

the reasoning trace a model would write given the rest of the exchange.

Training uses conversations from the student’s own family only. For the roughly ten thousand reasoning traces we
collected from Qwen3.8-Max, all five elements are present, so $R$ is supervised directly and no
teacher is involved. At inference we take $S,U,A,T$ from a closed-source model, which supplies
everything except the reasoning trace, and sample the reasoning trace the family would have written. The teacher therefore
enters only at inference, and only as the source of those four inputs.

## 2.2 Supervised training of the generator

The generator is a model from the Qwen family. It is fine-tuned on those ten thousand conversations to
maximize $\log P(R\mid S,U,A,T)$ : the reasoning trace is removed from the input, everything else is kept, and
the loss falls on the reasoning trace alone. This is the blue path in Figure 2. Two details carry
the design. The target is always a reasoning trace the family itself wrote, so the form is learned from data
rather than requested in a prompt. And the answer is part of the input and never part of the output, so
the model learns a derivation that ends at $A$ rather than a restatement of it.

One consequence is worth stating, because it is easy to misread the result. The reasoning traces we train on were
written for the family’s own answers. When we later ask the generator for a reasoning trace to accompany a
teacher’s answer, it cannot be reproducing a reasoning trace it has seen. It is doing what it was trained to do:
writing a derivation that ends at that answer, in the family’s voice. We call the result a family-native trace. No provider gives us the real
reasoning trace anyway, and none is needed.

After this stage we ask an outside judge, GPT-6.1-SOL, for the probability that a reasoning trace is real. Real
family reasoning traces average $0.66$ ; the generator’s average $0.54$ . That gap is what the rest of the section
addresses.

## 2.3 Supervised training of the critic

The critic is trained to tell real reasoning traces from generated ones, the purple path of
Figure 2. For each of the ten thousand samples the generator produced one matched
negative, and training stops once the critic assigns the positive a probability at least $0.2$ higher
than that negative, rather than driving the margin as far as it will go.

We made one mistake here that is worth recording. We assumed that a smaller model could judge a larger
one. It cannot: within a few hundred steps the critic fitted shortcuts, scored well on held-out pairs,
and gave the generator nothing to learn from. The critic is therefore at least as large as the
generator.

## 2.4 Adversarial co-training

We then run five rounds of online co-training, the arc at the bottom of Figure 2. In
each round the generator produces $5{,}000$ reasoning traces, which are shown to the critic alongside the
corresponding real reasoning traces. A reasoning trace that fools the critic becomes critic training data; a reasoning trace that
does not becomes a preference pair for the generator. At the end of each round we re-score a held-out set with GPT-6.1-SOL.

The score stops improving after five rounds, and we stop there. At that point the generator alone scores
 $0.68$ , above the $0.66$ of real reasoning traces, and selecting the best of four candidates with the critic
scores $0.82$ .

## 3 Evaluation

The point of this work is to break the moat of the closed-source model providers, so the test that
settles it is a simple one: is a student trained on family-native traces as good as a student trained on
the real ones? Everything in this section follows from that question. We hold the base model, the
training recipe and the budget fixed, vary only where the reasoning trace and the answer come from, and we simply want to see how the two students compare.

## 3.1 Setup

## Models.

Every student is fine-tuned from
Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B-Base, the pretrained
checkpoint, so that the only difference between two students is their training data.

## Data.

We distil from 5,000 Claude Code trajectories that carry Fable 5’s real reasoning traces and answers, at a 256K context window. The source is confidential, but the pool is fixed: every corpus below uses the same prompts and the same Fable 5 answers. From this single pool we build five training corpora that differ only in where the reasoning trace
and the answer come from.

• 

S1, Fable 5 reasoning $+$ answer. The original data, used as is: for each of the 5,000 prompts, Fable 5’s real reasoning trace together with its own answer.

• 

S2, family-native $+$ Fable 5 answer. As S1, with the reasoning trace replaced by a
family-native trace from the generator and critic of Section 2; the answers are
unchanged. S1 and S2 therefore differ only in who wrote the reasoning trace.

• 

S3, Qwen-Max reasoning $+$ answer. The prompts of S1 (all context) are
given to Qwen3.8-Max, the strongest legal model in the student’s own
family, and its reasoning traces and answers are used for training.

• 

S4, TraceInversion $+$ Sol answer. We have no GPT-6.1-SOL data carrying real reasoning traces, so
we mimic S3: we collect GPT-6.1-SOL’s answers on the same prompts and
synthesize a reasoning trace for each with TraceInversion (Sol below), the inversion method of
Zhang et al. Zhang et al. [2026].

• 

S5, family-native $+$ Sol answer. As S2, applied to S4: our reasoning traces over GPT-6.1-SOL’s answers.
S4 and S5 share the answers and differ only in the synthesizer.

## Training.

Teacher-forced SFT with the prompt masked from the loss. No truncation: every row
is under 262,144 tokens, and packed sequences may reach that length. Full parameters, BF16, AdamW with
weight decay $0.1$ and gradient clipping $1$ , learning rate $2\times 10^{-5}$ under a cosine schedule
with 5% warmup down to $2\times 10^{-6}$ , micro-batch $1$ , eight H20 GPUs with TP4/PP2 and sequence
parallelism, seed $42$ , no shuffling. One step is one packed-batch update. The adversarial stage adds
five rounds of online preference data, used with the standard DPO objective.

## Evaluation.

We use three multiple-choice tasks, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge and BoolQ, to test
general ability in a non-reasoning mode, and two code benchmarks, HumanEval+ and MBPP+, to test coding
ability in a reasoning mode.

## 3.2 Main comparison

Table 1 gives the final checkpoint. The three knowledge benchmarks do not separate the five
corpora: every value sits within $1.6$ points of every other, and no setting leads on all three. That is
what we expect of tasks that never ask for a reasoning trace, and we set them aside here. The code benchmarks are a different picture,
with a spread of more than sixty points.

The first surprise is that S2 beats S1. Replacing the teacher’s own reasoning trace with a family-native one adds
 $3.7$ points on HumanEval+ and $7.1$ on MBPP+, and Table 2 shows the MBPP+ lead
holding at every checkpoint. S1 is the textbook recipe, built on the assumption that the strongest
available reasoning trace is the best training signal. On these two benchmarks it is not.

The second surprise is S3. Qwen-Max is a far stronger model than the student, so we expected it to be
almost as good a teacher as Fable 5, perhaps a little behind. It is nowhere near: $18$ points behind on
HumanEval+ and $28$ on MBPP+. A capable teacher writing in its own hand transfers much less than a
stronger teacher whose answers are re-expressed in the student’s hand. Teacher capability turns out to
be necessary but not sufficient.

TraceInversion is the weakest of the five, at $3.66$ and $6.61$ , and this one did not surprise us once
we read its output. Its reasoning traces are recognisably synthetic: they narrate the solution in a generic voice,
use numbered steps the family never writes, and often restate the answer rather than derive it. The
score matches what a glance at the data already suggests.

S5 closes the argument with a second teacher. Given exactly the same GPT-6.1-SOL answers as S4, our
reasoning traces reach $59.15$ and $60.05$ against $3.66$ and $6.61$ : $55$ and $53$ points with nothing varying but
the synthesizer. Set beside S2, which shares the synthesizer and differs only in whose answers it writes,
S5 is $9$ points behind on HumanEval+ and level on MBPP+. That is about the gap one would expect between
the two teachers themselves, and it matches the common view of how the two model families compare.

## 3.3 Further analysis

We also want to know how each corpus behaves over training, not only where it ends.
Table 2 reports every intermediate checkpoint on the two code benchmarks, and the
trajectories say more than the endpoints do.

S1 is not stable. It reaches $66.46$ on HumanEval+ at step 600, falls to $33.54$ at step 1,200, and
recovers to $64.63$ by the end; we re-ran the 1,200-step evaluation twice to rule out a scoring error,
and the number held. A 33-point drop that repairs itself is not noise. Our reading is that the teacher’s
reasoning trace style sits far enough from the family’s own that fitting it moves the parameters a long way, and a
long move is a move that can overshoot.

S2 and S5 go the other way. S2 rises steadily to $68.29$ and $59.52$ , and S5 rises at every single
checkpoint on both benchmarks, from $0.61$ and $10.32$ to $59.15$ and $60.05$ ; on the average of the two,
S5 edges past S1.

S5 starts last and finishes near the front. It has the same reasoning traces as S2 and different answers, so the
answers are where the difference must come from. Qwen3.5’s mid-training is widely said to have used a lot
of Claude-family data and very little GPT-family data, which would make GPT-6.1-SOL’s answer style new to
the base model: it needs steps to adapt to it before the reasoning trace can help. The reasoning trace style is not new, which
is why the climb, once it starts, never reverses.

We also have some interesting findings on S3 and S4. Both had their moment and both ended badly: S3
reaches $48.78$ on HumanEval+ inside the first 300 steps and never gets back, and S4 peaks at $21.95$ and
 $42.59$ at step 900 before falling to $3.66$ and $6.61$ . Reading their outputs,
conclusion:
The result is easy to state. Our reasoning traces beat the strongest model we are allowed to distil from,
and they beat it by a wide margin: against Qwen-Max’s own reasoning traces and answers we are $21$ and $35$ 
points ahead. They also edge past the teacher’s own reasoning traces, by $3.7$ and $7.1$ points with the
questions and answers held fixed. A comparison from schooling fits. The best student is not produced by the best teacher alone, but by that teacher teaching in the way the student learns best. Our traces are
that lesson plan: the strongest teacher’s content, delivered in a way that students are familiar with.

Neither the generator nor the critic has ever seen a Claude or an OpenAI token. Every training example comes from Qwen3.8-Max, a model whose terms permit this
use, so the pipeline violates no provider’s agreement.

One more option, for teams that still see risk in handling Claude or OpenAI answers at all. Generate the
family-native trace, hand it to the strongest legally-distillable model in the same family such as Qwen3.8-Max, and let that
model write the answer. Then train on the family-native trace and that answer together. No Claude or
OpenAI token is backpropagated at any point, which removes both the legal exposure and the provenance
question: the pipeline yields data that is, on every count, the family’s own. We have run this variant, and it performs essentially the same as S2.

title: From Association to Decision Value: Testing Paired Instruction Dependence for VLA Corpus Selection
abstract: Choosing among robot demonstration corpora is a ranking problem: an upstream diagnostic must preserve which candidates produce better downstream policies, not merely correlate with average performance. We study paired instruction dependence, the rate at which a demonstrator changes its first decision when only the goal changes. Across 136 independently seeded quadruped-navigation corpora, predictions developed on 56 corpora are evaluated prospectively on 80 held-out corpora. The audit is reliable and associated with downstream paired correctness, and lowers mean absolute prediction error when added to a correctness-aware baseline, but the primary proper-log-score increment is +0.059 nats (95% corpus-bootstrap CI [-0.027, 0.133]) and the prespecified top-20% comparison does not establish an incremental selection gain. An exploratory response decomposition suggests a structural source of this predictive-ranking mismatch: under the tested predictor specification, separating both-correct and both-wrong responses yields larger held-out gains than their unsigned switch statistic. Seed-to-seed agreement indicates that the held-out endpoint retains recoverable rank signal. These results show that counterfactual response structure can be reliable and predictive while providing limited incremental decision value in this setting when compressed into an unsigned statistic, motivating diagnostics that preserve outcome-relevant structure and are validated against the decisions they are intended to support.

Testing Paired Instruction Dependence for VLA Corpus Selection

Nurmukhambet Serikbayev

Abdul Basit

headings: 3.2 What does the switch rate contain?
5.1 Reliability, association, and incremental value diverge

body_start:
Abstract

Choosing among robot demonstration corpora is a ranking problem: an upstream diagnostic must preserve which candidates produce better downstream policies, not merely correlate with average performance. We study paired instruction dependence, the rate at which a demonstrator changes its first decision when only the goal changes. Across 136 independently seeded quadruped-navigation corpora, predictions developed on 56 corpora are evaluated prospectively on 80 held-out corpora. The audit is reliable and associated with downstream paired correctness, and lowers mean absolute prediction error when added to a correctness-aware baseline, but the primary proper-log-score increment is $+0.059$ nats (95% corpus-bootstrap CI $[-0.027,0.133]$ ) and the prespecified top-20% comparison does not establish an incremental selection gain. An exploratory response decomposition suggests a structural source of this predictive–ranking mismatch: under the tested predictor specification, separating both-correct and both-wrong responses yields larger held-out gains than their unsigned switch statistic. Seed-to-seed agreement indicates that the held-out endpoint retains recoverable rank signal. These results show that counterfactual response structure can be reliable and predictive while providing limited incremental decision value in this setting when compressed into an unsigned statistic, motivating diagnostics that preserve outcome-relevant structure and are validated against the decisions they are intended to support.

Figure 1: Why prediction is not yet selection; (a) A schematic third-person view illustrates the same-observation goal swap used to test whether the demonstrator changes its first response. (b) In the primary held-out test, adding $A_{d}$ lowers MAE $.110\!\to\!.096$ while Spearman falls $.589\!\to\!.490$ . (c) The prespecified top-20% rule ranks 80 corpora and selects 16, so ordering determines utility.

## 1 Introduction

The downstream value of a robot demonstration corpus is usually known only after a vision–language–action (VLA) policy has been fine-tuned on it. Evaluating every candidate therefore pays much of the cost that an upstream diagnostic is meant to avoid. The practical question is consequently decision-focused: can a measurement rank candidate corpora well enough to select the ones that will produce better policies?

Language-conditioned behavior creates a tempting diagnostic. If two goals require opposite turns from the same observation, a demonstrator that follows language should usually change its decision when the goal changes. We call the resulting switch rate paired instruction dependence, $A_{d}$ . Unlike ordinary correctness, it uses a controlled same-state intervention and tests whether the response depends on the instruction. This distinction is relevant to generalist VLAs, whose success can otherwise conceal shortcut policies that weakly use language (Geirhos et al., 2020; Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025).

Dependence, however, is unsigned. A demonstrator can switch in the correct direction for both goals or in the wrong direction. With binary left/right responses, $A_{d}$ is exactly the sum of these both-correct and both-wrong cases; the observed halt action makes that identity approximate rather than exact in our data. The relevant question is therefore narrower than whether language sensitivity matters in general: does unsigned same-state response structure improve prediction and selection after marginal demonstrator correctness is known?

This question also separates four criteria that are often conflated:

 $\text{reliable measurement}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{association}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{incremental prediction}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{decision value}.$ 

A signal may track broad outcome differences or lower mean error while failing to preserve the ordering near a selection cutoff. Figure 1 illustrates this decision-value gap.

We test it prospectively on 136 independently seeded quadruped-navigation corpora. Nested probabilistic predictors are developed on 56 corpora, while 80 disjoint corpora form the held-out test population. The correctness-aware baseline $M_{0}$ uses per-goal demonstrator correctness and corpus entropies; $M_{1}$ adds only $A_{d}$ . We train 544 adapters across Qwen2.5-VL-3B and Qwen3.5-VL-0.8B and evaluate in-distribution and under a controlled scene shift. The primary selection endpoint is paired first-decision correctness; closed-loop evaluation separately tests how this local endpoint relates to full navigation. Predictors, held-out corpus identifiers, and the top-20% operating point were prespecified before held-out outcomes were revealed.

The study makes three main contributions:

1. 

A prospective decision-value evaluation: we separate reliability, association, proper probabilistic prediction, and top- $k$ selection for a same-state robot-data diagnostic, using the corpus as the unit of inference.

2. 

Correctness-resolved response structure locates a candidate source of the predictive–ranking mismatch: the unsigned switch statistic mixes both-correct and both-wrong behavior; separating them yields larger exploratory held-out gains under the tested predictor specification.

3. 

Decision resolution and practical alternatives: a cross-seed resolution benchmark establishes recoverable corpus ordering, while demonstrator and proxy baselines locate the audit relative to realistic selectors.

## 2 Related Work

## Vision–language–action learning:

Language-conditioned robot learning spans task-specific imitation (Lynch and Sermanet, 2021; Mees et al., 2022; Nair et al., 2022), large pretrained embodied models (Driess et al., 2023; Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025), and heterogeneous robot corpora (O’Neill et al., 2024). Physical VLM-to-VLA transfer is increasingly practical (Hancock et al., 2026); NaVILA separates language-level navigation decisions from low-level legged control (Cheng et al., 2025), as we do. We study the preceding data decision: which fixed demonstration corpus should train a policy?

## Language grounding and counterfactual evaluation:

Vision-and-language navigation established grounded instruction following (Anderson et al., 2018), but success can hide instruction-insensitive shortcuts. Controlled tests expose memorized action sequences and semantic failures (Fei et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Hou and Zhao, 2026; Yu et al., 2026), while mismatched instructions can supply corrective supervision (Kondoh et al., 2026). Our intervention similarly holds the state fixed while changing the goal, but it measures a data-generating demonstrator and predicts a separately trained learner. Crucially, we distinguish unsigned response change from correctness-resolved response structure.

## Robot-data selection and valuation:

Robot policies are sensitive to demonstration composition and scale (Mandlekar et al., 2022; Saxena et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025). Data valuation uses marginal contribution, training dynamics, gradients, or standardized retraining (Ghorbani and Zou, 2019; Swayamdipta et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2024; Gadre et al., 2023). DemInf scores demonstrations through state–action mutual information (Hejna et al., 2025); DataMIL learns policy-aware datamodels (Dass et al., 2026). Unlike end-to-end selectors such as DataMIL, we test whether an interpretable pre-training corpus diagnostic retains incremental value at the downstream selection decision. Our unit is an entire candidate corpus, and the nested comparison conditions on marginal demonstrator correctness.

## Proxy selection and decision-aware evaluation:

Selection via Proxy uses a smaller model to rank data efficiently (Coleman et al., 2020); compute-aware selection makes the appropriate proxy depend on its cost (Yin and Rush, 2025). Small training runs can preserve data-recipe rankings inconsistently across proxy configurations (Wang et al., 2026). Upstream probes can correlate with control (Dong et al., 2026), and proxy environments can be judged by absolute prediction and rank preservation (Quevedo et al., 2026). Prior work therefore distinguishes absolute prediction quality from rank preservation and selection utility. We extend this distinction to prospective robot-corpus selection with prespecified decisions, a proper-score test, a seed-based resolution benchmark, and direct comparison with practical selectors.

## 3 Method

Figure 2 summarizes the prospective comparison and the disjoint roles of audit, training, and held-out evaluation data.

## 3.1 Same-state goal-swap audit

For each audit state, we query the demonstrator twice with an identical visual observation and action history. Only the object goal changes, and the two goals require opposite branches. Let $d$ index a corpus, $u$ a state, $x^{-},x^{+}$ the goals, and $B_{d}(u,x)$ the first response. For a deterministic demonstrator, paired instruction dependence is

 $A_{d}=\frac{1}{n_{A}}\sum_{u=1}^{n_{A}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[B_{d}(u,x^{-})\neq B_{d}(u,x^{+})\right].$ 

(1)

It is an unsigned response statistic: changing correctly for both goals and changing incorrectly for both goals can each increase $A_{d}$ . Under the balanced deterministic intervention, each unequal pair identifies the goal and contributes one bit, so Eq. 1 equals state-averaged conditional mutual information (Appendix A). This equivalence does not make $A_{d}$ a correctness or downstream-value measure.

The audit requires counterfactual access to a queryable demonstrator and is unavailable from a fixed corpus containing only one instruction per state. It is therefore applicable in settings such as automated simulation or online data generation, where the same state can be replayed under alternate goals before committing to a large collection. The study therefore concerns this access model rather than arbitrary human demonstrations.

## 3.2 What does the switch rate contain?

Let $a_{d}$ , $b_{d}$ , and $c_{d}$ be the fractions of audit states for which both goal responses are correct, both are wrong, or exactly one is correct. Marginal per-goal demonstrator correctness is

 $p_{d}=a_{d}+\tfrac{1}{2}c_{d}=\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}(a_{d}-b_{d}).$ 

(2)

If responses are restricted to left/right, opposite required branches imply $A_{d}=a_{d}+b_{d}$ . Thus, in the binary case, $(p_{d},A_{d})$ is an invertible reparameterization of $(a_{d},b_{d})$ : $p_{d}$ contains their signed difference, whereas $A_{d}$ contains their unsigned sum. Our demonstrators may also emit halt; this breaks the exact $A_{d}=a_{d}+b_{d}$ identity in our data, although Eq. 2 remains exact. The decomposition makes the primary question precise: does unsigned joint response structure improve prediction beyond marginal correctness and corpus composition?

Figure 2: Prospective test of paired response structure; Audit states and training trajectories are disjoint, and only the goal changes within an audit pair. Baseline $M_{0}$ uses marginal per-goal correctness and corpus entropies; $M_{1}$ adds the same-state switch rate $A_{d}$ . Both models predict paired learner correctness and rank the same held-out corpora.

## 3.3 Nested prediction test

After fine-tuning with learner seed $s$ , let $C_{d,s}\in\{0,\ldots,m\}$ count evaluation states where the VLA predicts the correct branch for both goals. This conjunction rejects constant-side policies. We compare nested beta–binomial predictors:

 $\displaystyle C_{d,s}$ 
 $\displaystyle\sim\mathrm{BetaBinomial}(m,\mu_{d,s},\rho),$ 

(3)

 $\displaystyle M_{0}:\quad\mathrm{logit}(\mu_{d,s})$ 
 $\displaystyle=\alpha+\beta^{\top}W_{d}+\gamma_{s},$ 

(4)

 $\displaystyle M_{1}:\quad\mathrm{logit}(\mu_{d,s})$ 
 $\displaystyle=\alpha+\beta^{\top}W_{d}+\eta A_{d}+\gamma_{s}.$ 

(5)

 $W_{d}$ contains marginal per-goal demonstrator correctness, training-goal entropy, and coarse training-action entropy. Both predictors therefore use the same 48 demonstrator responses; $M_{1}-M_{0}$ isolates pairing structure rather than extra queries. The crossed seed effect $\gamma_{s}$ is a nuisance term and $\rho$ captures extra-binomial variation.

Feature scaling and the ridge penalty are learned on development corpora. The primary $M_{1}$ shares $M_{0}$ ’s penalty so that adding $A_{d}$ does not also add a hyperparameter search. Test-audit uncertainty is marginalized by resampling the 24 paired states. Exploratory checks separately tune the ridge penalty for each response parameterization, decompose $A_{d}$ into $a_{d}$ and $b_{d}$ , and add existing rollout features. None changes the prespecified endpoint or primary result.

## 3.4 Prediction, ranking, and selection

The primary estimand is the equal-corpus improvement in proper log score,

 $\bar{\delta}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{d\in\mathcal{B}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\left[\log p_{1,d,s}(C_{d,s})-\log p_{0,d,s}(C_{d,s})\right],$ 

(6)

where $\mathcal{B}$ is the held-out corpus population and $\mathcal{S}$ the two learner seeds. A corpus-cluster bootstrap supplies the 95% interval. The prespecified primary rule requires its lower bound to exceed zero. The $0.105\approx-\log(0.9)$ -nat magnitude reference corresponds to multiplying the geometric-mean assigned probability by approximately 1.11; it is not a universal utility threshold. Log score (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007) evaluates the full predictive distribution and penalizes confident errors.

For selection, model $M_{j}$ ranks each corpus by predicted mean correctness,

 $\widehat{q}_{j}(d)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbb{E}_{M_{j}}[C_{d,s}/m],$ 

(7)

and selects $K=16$ of 80 corpora. We report selected correctness, regret relative to the realized oracle set, and oracle overlap. The operating point was prespecified before outcome reveal; its confidence interval is exploratory. No held-out outcome enters fitting, tuning, or ranking.

## 3.5 Resolution and comparator analyses

Finite evaluation states and learner seeds limit any ranking method. We use cross-seed ranking as an empirical resolution benchmark and compare against demonstrator and proxy selectors. We also repeat $M_{0}/M_{1}$ comparisons after excluding the two least mature checkpoints. These exploratory analyses do not alter the prespecified primary test.

## 4 Experimental Setup

## 4.1 Corpus population

We study Unitree Go2 object-goal navigation in Isaac Lab (Mittal et al., 2023). Given forward RGB, instruction text, and action history, the VLA emits a discrete navigation command for a fixed low-level controller; only that controller sees proprioception. Every corpus uses a separately trained tabular Q-learning demonstrator with unique training, layout, physics, and rendering seeds. Checkpoints span 10, 50, 250, 1,000, and 50,000 episodes. The held-out population has 16 corpora per level; development has 12 at 10 episodes and 11 at each remaining level. Checkpoint maturity is excluded from the deployable baseline because it is an experimental assignment, not a property available for an arbitrary corpus.

Each corpus contains 24 paired audit states, 48 unpaired multi-step training trajectories, and 48 paired in-distribution (ID) evaluation states. Audit, training, and evaluation packets are disjoint at the state, image, and trajectory levels. All 6,528 attempted training rollouts passed prespecified structural-validity checks, so acceptance is constant across corpora and cannot explain their ranking; first-branch correctness instead ranges from $.375$ to $.813$ . Appendix I gives the complete validity checklist.

Across 136 corpora, the study contains 6,528 training trajectories (43,084 steps), 3,264 audit states, and 6,528 ID evaluation states. The 56 development and 80 held-out corpora share no demonstrator seeds or scene realizations. Figure 3 summarizes the data roles and evaluations.

The audit requires 48 demonstrator queries and costs a median 4.18 GPU-min per corpus. A Qwen2.5 fit and ID evaluation average 11.46 GPU-min for one seed, or $2.74\times$ the audit cost. Appendix Table 16 reports the complete measured cost comparison.

## 4.2 VLA training and evaluation

The primary learner is Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025); Qwen3.5-VL-0.8B is both a supporting backbone and an exploratory proxy selector (Qwen Team, 2026). Within each backbone, only corpus and learner seed vary. We hold the vision tower fixed and train rank-8 LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2022) on language-model projections. Outputs are left/right turns, forward, halt, or done; invalid generations are errors. The full factorial gives 544 adapters. A Qwen2.5 fit averages 10.68 GPU-min and Qwen3.5 averages 13.41 GPU-min over the measured runs.

Figure 3: Experimental design across simulation and hardware; (a) Paired states span three semantic families with RGB fixed across goals. (b) Audit, training, and evaluation observations are disjoint. (c) Controlled scene shift balances a $2\!\times\!2$ geometry/appearance design. (d) Stationary real images evaluate 16 adapters; 48 physical runs describe two deployed adapters.

## ID and controlled shift:

The ID endpoint has 48 paired states per corpus; both goals must receive the required branch. The 24-state shifted set crosses two spawn/target geometries with two lighting settings, six states per cell. Camera, warehouse, objects, prompt, action space, and controller remain fixed, so this is controlled rather than open-world shift.

## Closed-loop simulation:

For 16 held-out corpora at evenly spaced $A_{d}$ ranks, the first Qwen2.5 seed runs 24 scenes and both goals (768 episodes). We record first-command correctness, target reach, collision/fall, path efficiency, and recovery. These aggregate rates and exploratory rank correlations describe the stratified subset, not all 80 held-out corpora.

The audit requires counterfactual demonstrator access and is tested on one simulator, one tabular demonstrator family, short corpora, and a largely maturity-driven population. The resulting claim is specific to this controlled corpus population. Generalization to different demonstrator families, corpus-generation mechanisms, and larger real-world corpora remains untested.

conclusion: Paired instruction dependence provides a controlled case study of how proxy structure can be lost through compression. The switch rate is measured with substantial reliability and associated with learner behavior, but its unsigned form mixes both-correct and both-wrong responses; correctness-resolved parameterizations yield larger exploratory held-out gains under the tested predictor specification. Cross-seed agreement shows that corpus ordering remains recoverable. Together, these results motivate preserving outcome-relevant structure in counterfactual data diagnostics and validating them against the decisions they are intended to support.

title: Parallel Thinking for Large Language Model with Path Diversity
abstract: Parallel thinking has emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by exploring multiple reasoning paths simultaneously. However, we identify that parallel thinking via Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically suffers from the mode collapse of reasoning paths, where parallel thinking trajectories degenerate into similar ones. This homogeneity undermines the fundamental motivation of parallel thinking, that is, maintaining multiple hypotheses concurrently to prevent premature loss into a suboptimal solution. In this paper, we propose Diverse Parallel Thinking (DPT), a simple yet effective RL approach for parallel thinking designed to encourage path diversity. DPT rewards the model to develop distinct reasoning strategies by penalizing the prefix similarity of parallel thinking paths, thereby enhancing a more comprehensive exploration of the reasoning space. We conduct various experiments and analyses across multiple reasoning benchmarks to demonstrate the effectiveness of DPT. Results show that DPT successfully outperforms previous parallel thinking methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance over baselines. We validate path diversity as a key element to improve parallel thinking. Our code is available at https://github.com/JiaruQian/DPT.

headings: Parallel Thinking for Large Language Model with Path Diversity
body_start:
Abstract

Parallel thinking has emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by exploring multiple reasoning paths simultaneously. However, we identify that parallel thinking via Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically suffers from the mode collapse of reasoning paths, where parallel thinking trajectories degenerate into similar ones. This homogeneity undermines the fundamental motivation of parallel thinking, that is, maintaining multiple hypotheses concurrently to prevent premature loss into a suboptimal solution. In this paper, we propose Diverse Parallel Thinking (DPT), a simple yet effective RL approach for parallel thinking designed to encourage path diversity. DPT rewards the model to develop distinct reasoning strategies by penalizing the prefix similarity of parallel thinking paths, thereby enhancing a more comprehensive exploration of the reasoning space.
We conduct various experiments and analyses across multiple reasoning benchmarks to demonstrate the effectiveness of DPT. Results show that DPT successfully outperforms previous parallel thinking methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance over baselines. We validate path diversity as a key element to improve parallel thinking.
Our code is available at https://github.com/JiaruQian/DPT.

## 1 Introduction

Parallel thinking has emerged as a transformative paradigm for augmenting the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly in challenging tasks like mathematical reasoning (Wen et al., 2025a; Zheng et al., 2025b; Wu et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2025; Tu et al., 2025). The practical efficacy of this approach has been recently epitomized by Google’s Gemini at the IMO (18), where the integration of parallel and sequential thinking proved instrumental to its success (Huang and Yang, 2025). Beyond empirical gains, parallel thinking aligns with principles in cognitive science as human experts often engage in divergent thought, maintaining multiple hypotheses concurrently to prevent premature loss into a suboptimal solution (Clark, 1993; Jackendoff, 2003). By synthesizing these concurrent paths into a coherent conclusion, parallel thinking enables a more structured and deliberate reasoning process.

Figure 1: Comparison of Traditional Sequential Thinking, Naive Parallel Thinking (RL with outcome reward), and Ideal Parallel Thinking.

Despite this promise, we observe mode collapse of reasoning paths in a reproduced parallel-thinking model trained with outcome rewards. Standard RL reward formulations (Yu et al., 2025b; Gao et al., 2024; Eschmann, 2021) optimize for correct final answers without directly rewarding diversity among internal paths. Exploitation of reliable patterns can therefore leave multiple paths highly redundant. As illustrated in Figure 1, paths that repeatedly cover the same approach provide limited additional exploration. Our goal is to discourage this redundancy within a trajectory while preserving task correctness.

The pursuit of path diversity in parallel thinking presents two key challenges. First, the evaluation of reasoning path diversity is difficult. Second, naively maximizing diversity risks sacrificing correctness. A straightforward way is to employ lexical-level similarity like Jaccard (Niwattanakul et al., 2013) between entire paths as a metric in the training reward to encourage diversity across paths. However, such method is strongly influenced by factors such as overall path length and lexical choice, computing the reward at the whole-path level did not yield satisfactory results. Another way is to use a reward model to score the reasoning path diversity. However, it is costly and susceptible to reward hacking (Eisenstein et al., 2023; Khalaf et al., 2025).
Therefore, how to develop a simple yet effective metric that captures path diversity of parallel thinking remains an open problem.

In this paper, we propose Diverse Parallel Thinking (DPT), a simple yet effective RL approach for parallel thinking that enforces path diversity as an intrinsic optimization objective, thereby exploring multiple hypotheses concurrently to prevent premature convergence on suboptimal solutions. DPT integrates diversity into the reward signal through a token-level diversity metric that shifts the focus to the early part of each reasoning path. By explicitly encouraging greater diversity in the tokens generated at the beginning, we aim to steer the reasoning trajectories in different directions, allowing them to branch out and explore a broader solution space. DPT can be integrated into existing RL pipelines without requiring architectural modifications, making it applicable to parallel thinking frameworks. We evaluated DPT across a diverse range of reasoning benchmarks and various LLMs. Our results show that DPT consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) baseline, with ablation studies further revealing that path diversity is the primary driver behind these performance gains. These results establish path diversity as a design principle for parallel thinking in LLMs. Our main contribution can be summarized as follows:

• 

We identify and formally analyze the path mode collapse problem in parallel thinking, showing theoretically that outcome-supervised RL inherently drives parallel paths toward identical trajectories due to exploitation dynamics.

• 

We propose DPT, a general diversity-aware RL framework for parallel thinking. DPT introduces prefix-based diversity metrics grounded in autoregressive strategy anchoring, requiring zero additional computational overhead.

• 

Extensive experiments validate that DPT outperforms existing SOTA parallel thinking approaches, establishing path diversity as a key design principle for parallel thinking.

Figure 2: Path Mode Collapse in Naive Parallel Thinking.

## 2 Motivation

In this section, we analyze the parallel thinking models trained with the existing RL approach (Zheng et al., 2025b). Despite the intuitive appeal of parallel exploration, our findings suggest that existing RL training for parallel thinking leads to the mode collapse of reasoning paths.

Empirical Evidence. We sampled 1,156 parallel reasoning blocks from validation rollouts of the reproduced Parallel-R1 model at training step 200 on AIME24, AIME25, AMC23, and MATH. Each included <Parallel> span contains $K=2$ parsed <Path> spans; malformed or incomplete spans are excluded. GPT-5-mini (GPT-5-Mini, 2025) judges solution approach, reasoning structure, mathematical technique, expression style, and overall strategy diversity. Figure 2 (left) shows that 61.81% of path pairs receive similarity scores $\geq 0.9$ . This is a judge-based indication of overlap whose reliability depends on the evaluation protocol; Appendix H distinguishes this assessment from lexical diagnostics and states its validation limits.

The result reveals a pervasive mode collapse of parallel thinking paths in the reasoning space, which converge onto identical semantic manifolds. Figure 2 (right) provides an example of this phenomenon in a math reasoning task. Both paths anchor on the same insight, i.e., concluding that vertex alignment constrains the probability to $1/8$ . Although the phrasing fluctuates, the underlying logical heuristic remains monolithic. The model essentially learns to produce high-reward paraphrases rather than exploring the disjoint solution spaces that parallel thinking is intended to cover.

Theoretical Analysis.
Why does standard RL drive parallel reasoning paths toward mode collapse, as observed in Figure 2? The failure arises from the exploitation dynamics inherent in maximizing the expected reward under outcome-supervision.
Consider a generator $\pi_{\theta}$ that produces an ordered tuple of $K$ latent reasoning paths $\mathcal{T}=(\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{K})$ given an input $x$ . A deterministic aggregation function $\hat{y}(\mathcal{T})$ extracts the final answer from the summary of all paths. The standard RL objective maximizes:

 $\mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[r\!\left(\hat{y}(\mathcal{T}),\;y^{*}\right)\right]\right],$ 

(1)

 $\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{J}$ 
 $\displaystyle\approx\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathcal{T}|x)$ 

(2)

 $\displaystyle\cdot\underbrace{r(\hat{y}(\mathcal{T}),y^{*})}_{\text{Reward Signal}}].$ 

where $y^{*}$ is the ground truth and $r(\cdot,\cdot)$ is a binary correctness metric. Crucially, the reward depends on $\pi_{\theta}$ only through $\hat{y}(\mathcal{T})$ and is agnostic to the diversity of $\mathcal{T}$ .

The core problem stems from the exploitation dynamics inherent in maximizing Eq. (1). Let $\tau^{*}$ denote the “safe mode”, i.e., the single reasoning pattern with the highest marginal probability of yielding the correct answer under the current policy. Because all $K$ paths are sampled from the same shared policy $\pi_{\theta}$ , the gradient reinforces whichever pattern most reliably produces the correct answer. This drives the marginal distribution $\pi_{\theta}(\tau|x)$ to concentrate on $\tau^{*}$ , causing all path slots to simultaneously collapse:

 $\pi_{\theta}(\tau_{k}|x)\to\mathbb{I}[\tau_{k}=\tau^{*}],\quad\forall k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}.$ 

(3)

Since all generated paths share the same policy, the model is not incentivized to diversify and instead converges toward $\tau^{*}$ .

Analysis Result. Our analysis reveals a critical design principle: Path diversity must be an explicit optimization constraint rather than an emergent byproduct. To unlock the true potential of parallel thinking to align with its motivation, we must penalize redundancy in the latent reasoning space, specifically at the prefix level, where early strategic decisions are made.

Figure 3: Overview of DPT. (I) Format learning teaches the parallel thinking format via SFT on easy problems. (II) Diverse parallel thinking develops autonomous parallel thinking on hard problems with combined rewards.

## 3 Related Work

Enhancing LLM Reasoning Capability via RL.
RL has become a central technique for enhancing LLM reasoning, with advances in policy optimization (Shao et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025a; Yu et al., 2025a), on/off-policy learning (Dong et al., 2025), self-improvement without explicit labels (Zuo et al., 2025), and search-augmented reasoning (Jin et al., 2025). LTE (Tang et al., 2026) further explores trial-and-error learning to overcome exploration stagnation. More recently, RL with rollout diversity has gained attention. DivPO (Lanchantin et al., 2025), unlikeliness reward (He et al., 2025), and EVOL-RL (Zhou et al., 2025) encourage rare, high-quality generations through reward shaping or preference optimization, while PODS (Xu et al., 2025), DARLING (Li et al., 2025), and DQO (Chen et al., 2025) improve rollout selection and aggregation. However, these methods still treat each rollout as a sequential generation process, motivating RL for parallel inference.

Parallel Thinking.
Parallel thinking has recently emerged as a promising area in LLM reasoning. A set of works (Brown et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025) explores test-time compute scaling by generating multiple reasoning samples per input and aggregating them to improve answer quality. However, they typically rely on post-hoc sampling as well as simple aggregation, and tend to generate redundant or low-value traces. Recent works (Jia et al., 2025; Tu et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2025a; Wu et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025b) aim to endow models with native parallel reasoning capabilities, producing and integrating multiple thought trajectories within a single inference process. Among them, SFT-based methods such as SSFT (Jia et al., 2025) and ParaThinker (Wen et al., 2025a) inevitably lead to superficial parallel thinking, where models merely imitate parallel patterns without genuine parallel reasoning. RL-based methods such as NPR (Wu et al., 2025) and Parallel-R1 (Zheng et al., 2025b) enable models to autonomously explore parallel reasoning, but often suffer from path mode collapse.
To this end, we propose DPT to enforce path diversity while maintaining high reasoning accuracy in parallel thinking.

## 4 Diversity Parallel Thinking

We present DPT, an RL approach that enforces path diversity in parallel thinking while maintaining reasoning accuracy. We first formalize parallel thinking as a structured generation process that produces multiple independent reasoning paths within a single trajectory. We then introduce DPT’s training algorithm, which integrates cold-start initialization with SFT and employs a diversity-aware RL reward function to explicitly penalize mode collapse among reasoning paths. An overview of the DPT framework is shown in Figure 3.

## 4.1 Parallel Thinking Formulation

Given a reasoning problem $x$ , parallel thinking generates $K$ distinct reasoning paths $\{\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\ldots,\tau_{K}\}$ within a single coherent generation trajectory. Unlike traditional beam search or sampling that produces independent sequences, parallel thinking enables the model to adaptively decide when to branch into multiple exploration threads during the reasoning process.

We implement this behavior through three special control tags that structure the generation:

• 

<Parallel>...</Parallel>: Marks the parallel exploration phase, indicating where the model suspends the main reasoning chain to explore multiple solution strategies concurrently.

• 

<Path>...</Path>: Delimits an internal reasoning thread intended to explore a solution approach. Information isolation depends on the attention mode.

• 

<Summary>...</Summary>: Synthesizes insights across parallel paths and resolves conflicts before resuming the main reasoning chain.

Formally, let $z$ denote the complete generation trajectory for problem $x$ . The model autoregressively generates tokens according to policy $\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)$ . When the model emits a <Parallel> token, it spawns $K$ parallel paths $\{\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{K}\}$ within separate <Path> blocks. Each path $\tau_{i}$ is intended to explore a distinct reasoning strategy. In the “Unseen” mode, structural attention masking enforces true information isolation between paths; in the “Seen” mode, paths may attend to prior paths. A <Summary> block then integrates the parallel explorations before resuming the main trajectory.

The objective of parallel thinking is twofold: exploring multiple strategies increases the probability of finding correct answers, and diverse paths enable multi-perspective verification. However, standard RL optimizes only for correctness without penalizing redundancy, causing paths to collapse into identical strategies. DPT addresses this by explicitly rewarding diversity among parallel paths.

## 4.2 Training Algorithm

We train DPT through a two-stage curriculum that addresses the cold-start problem in parallel thinking. The model first learns the basic format and structure of parallel reasoning on simpler problems with supervised finetuning, then transitions to reinforcement learning on challenging tasks to enhance performance with path diversity.

## 4.2.1 Cold Start Initialization

Since pretrained language models have not encountered the special control tags (<Parallel>, <Path>, <Summary>) during pretraining, they cannot generate valid parallel thinking trajectories for RL exploration. We address this cold-start problem through supervised fine-tuning on a curated dataset of parallel thinking examples constructed from the GSM8K training set. We prompt a capable language model to generate solutions in the parallel thinking format and filter outputs to retain only those with valid tag structure. This phase instills familiarity with the parallel thinking format—when to trigger <Parallel> blocks, how to structure independent <Path> segments, and how to synthesize conclusions in <Summary> blocks—enabling subsequent RL exploration on harder tasks.

## 4.2.2 Reinforcement Learning

After cold-start initialization, we train the model using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024), a well-known policy gradient method designed for grouped samples.

Training Objective. For each problem $x$ , GRPO samples $N$ trajectories $\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{N}\}$ from the policy $\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)$ and computes rewards for each trajectory. The policy gradient estimates the advantage function using group-relative normalization:

 $\hat{A}(z_{i})=\frac{R(z_{i})-\bar{R}}{\sigma_{R}+\epsilon},$ 

(4)

where $\bar{R}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}R(z_{j})$ and $\sigma_{R}$ are the mean and standard deviation of rewards within the group, and $\epsilon$ is a small constant for numerical stability. This normalization reduces variance compared to absolute rewards.
The policy is updated via:

 $\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},z_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[\hat{A}(z_{i})\log\pi_{\theta}(z_{i}|x)\right],$ 

(5)

subject to a KL divergence constraint $\text{KL}(\pi_{\theta}||\pi_{\text{ref}})<\delta$ to prevent the policy from deviating too far from the reference model $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ . We use the pretrained base model as the reference.

Reward Modeling. The reward function $R(z_{i})$ determines what behaviors the model learns. Here $z_{i}$ denotes the complete generation trajectory, which may contain multiple parallel paths $\{\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{K}\}$ . Standard RL for reasoning uses only a correctness reward $r_{c}(z_{i})=\mathbb{I}[\hat{y}(z_{i})=y^{*}]$ , where $\hat{y}(z_{i})$ is the final answer extracted from trajectory $z_{i}$ and $y^{*}$ is the ground truth. Existing parallel thinking approaches also introduce format reward $r_{f}(z_{i})$ :

 $\displaystyle r_{f}(z_{i})=\mathbb{I}[$ 
 $\displaystyle\text{At least one correct}$ 

 $\displaystyle\text{{<Parallel>} block in }z_{i}].$ 

However, opti
limitations: Our study focuses on text-based reasoning tasks with verifiable answers, including mathematics, coding, and knowledge reasoning. Extending DPT to multimodal inputs and interactive reasoning would further broaden its application scope. We evaluate a small set of internal path counts and keep the path count fixed within each configuration. An adaptive allocation policy that selects the number of paths according to problem difficulty and inference budget could provide greater flexibility. We leave these directions for future work.
conclusion:
In this paper, we first discover the problem of path mode collapse in parallel thinking, where multiple parallel reasoning paths degenerate into similar ones, contradicting the core motivation of parallel thinking. Therefore, we propose a simple but effective RL approach, DPT, to address path mode collapse in parallel thinking for LLMs. Specifically, DPT enforces path diversity through a token-level diversity metric that detects early reasoning divergence, combined with a two-stage training curriculum that balances correctness and exploration. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DPT consistently outperforms the best-performing baseline on mathematical reasoning, coding and knowledge reasoning benchmarks.
The results establish that path diversity is a key component for effective parallel thinking.
By addressing path mode collapse, we take a step toward realizing the full potential of parallel thinking, unlocking the test-time scaling.

## An Exact 93-Move Solution to a

Nonlocal Crystal-Exchange Puzzle

Zilai Wang

Email: wzlfly87@gmail.com

October 21, 2026

body_start:
Abstract

We determine the minimum number of directional commands needed to solve a
level of Order of the Sinking Star, modeled as a crystal-exchange
puzzle on an $11\times 11$ board. A command swaps
the player with the nearest crystal in the selected row or column, regardless
of distance; only an empty ray permits an ordinary unit walk. Two gates admit
the player to the exit exactly while all sixteen crystals occupy their target
cells. We give an explicit 93-command solution and exclude every shorter
solution by an exact, cost-bounded breadth-first search. The search represents
a position by its seventeen occupied cells and one active cell. Its admissible
heuristic partitions command costs between a compressed core abstraction and
residual motion, strengthened by a necessary activation detour and a corner
visit condition. The completed computation retained 605,349,215 occupied sets
and 1,863,925,136 states. We prove the reductions and pruning conditions,
describe the exact storage scheme, and provide source code, execution logs,
and a reproduction driver. The result is a computer-assisted proof for the
specified instance, with an explicit implementation trust boundary.

## 1 Introduction

We study a crystal-exchange level from the puzzle game
Order of the Sinking Star.
Nonlocal exchanges make familiar geometric intuitions unreliable in
shortest-path puzzles. A single command can move the player across an entire
row, while placing every crystal on a target need not finish the puzzle:
the player must still reach an exit. The position of the player at the moment
the gates open is therefore part of the optimization problem.

The level was supplied as a diagram together with
its movement rules. Section 2 gives a self-contained
mathematical specification, so the result does not depend on access to a
particular game implementation. Our main result is an exact minimum of
93 directional commands. We give a witness and a computational exclusion
of all routes of length at most 92.

The computational method uses established principles of admissible search.
Pattern databases store exact distances in abstractions of a state
space [1]. Additive pattern databases and action-cost
partitioning permit several lower bounds to be summed when their allocated
costs do not exceed the cost of a real action [2, 3].
Here the partition is fixed and binary: a command contributes to exactly
one of two cost components. We specialize these principles to nonlocal
exchange by retaining occupied points, rather than crystal identities,
and deriving a residual-motion bound from the need to activate an
off-target occupied point.

Our contribution is the exact solution of this instance and a documented
search formulation that makes the result reproducible. We do not claim a
new general-purpose search algorithm, a complexity classification of the
puzzle family, or a proof checked by a formal proof assistant.

## 2 The instance and its exact state space

Rows and columns are numbered from 1 to 11, with rows increasing downward.
Let

 $V=\{1,\ldots,11\}^{2},\qquad K=\{4,\ldots,8\}^{2},$ 

and let the sixteen target cells form the perimeter

 $T=\{(r,c)\in K:r\in\{4,8\}\ \text{or}\ c\in\{4,8\}\}.$ 

The exit is $E=(11,11)$ , the gates are
 $G=\{(10,11),(11,10)\}$ , and the initial positions are

 $p_{0}=(10,10),\qquad C_{0}=(T\setminus\{(4,4)\})\cup\{(1,1)\}.$ 

(1)

Crystals are indistinguishable. A state consists of a player cell $p$ 
and a sixteen-element set $C$ , with $p\notin C$ .

11223344556677889910101111P $\times$ $\times$ ECrystalTargetPPlayer $\times$ GateEExit

Figure 1: The initial instance, redrawn from its mathematical specification.
The target at $(4,4)$ is empty; the displaced crystal is at $(1,1)$ .
Both gates are initially closed.

## Commands.

The four directions are denoted $U,D,L,R$ . The gates are open if and
only if $C=T$ ; their status is not latched. In a selected
direction, scan the ray from $p$ , stopping at the board boundary or a
closed gate. If the ray contains a crystal, let $q$ be the nearest one
and replace the state by

 $\bigl(q,\ (C\setminus\{q\})\cup\{p\}\bigr).$ 

If the ray contains no crystal, move the player one cell in that direction,
provided that cell is in $V$ and is not a closed gate. Each command costs
one, including a long-distance exchange. Invalid commands can be omitted
from a shortest route; if interpreted as idle commands, deleting them
does not change any subsequent state. The objective is the player’s
first entry into $E$ .

Lemma 2.1 (Goal characterization).

On first entry into $E$ , the crystal set is $T$ .

Proof.

Initially $E$ has no crystal. The only operation that could place a
crystal there is an exchange from a player already at $E$ . Thus a first
entry cannot be an exchange; it is a walk from one of the two gates.
Entering that gate requires $C=T$ . From either gate, its row and column
contain no target cells. While the player remains on a gate or walks
between it and $E$ , no exchange can alter $T$ . Hence $C=T$ on entry.
∎

Definition 2.2 (Occupied-set representation).

Write $U=C\cup\{p\}$ and $s=(U,p)$ .
Then $|U|=17$ , $p\in U$ , and $C=U\setminus\{p\}$ .

An exchange changes only the active cell $p$ . A walk from $p$ to $q$ 
replaces $U$ by $(U\setminus\{p\})\cup\{q\}$ . This is an exact
representation, not an abstraction. By Lemma 2.1, the required
terminal state is

 $s_{*}=(T\cup\{E\},E).$ 

(2)

Theorem 2.3 (Main result; computer-assisted).

For the instance and rules specified above, the minimum number of commands
from $(C_{0}\cup\{p_{0}\},p_{0})$ to first entry into $E$ is exactly $93$ .

The upper bound is explicit in Section 7. The lower bound
combines the mathematical reductions below with the exhaustive
computation reported there.

## 3 Partitioning command costs

For a one-dimensional coordinate $k\in\{1,\ldots,11\}$ , define

 $\pi(k)=\min\{6,\max\{0,k-3\}\},\qquad\eta(k)=\begin{cases}k-3,&k<3,\\
0,&3\leq k\leq 9,\\
k-9,&k>9.\end{cases}$ 

(3)

Apply both maps coordinatewise to cells. The map $\pi$ compresses the
board to $Q=\{0,\ldots,6\}^{2}$ ; $\eta$ records the signed residual
displacement outside the interval $[3,9]$ . In one dimension,
 $k=\pi(k)+\eta(k)+3$ .

Table 1: Every adjacent pair changes exactly one of $\pi$ and $\eta$ 
by one. The identity $k=\pi(k)+\eta(k)+3$ alone would not establish
this property; the adjacent values do.

Lemma 3.1 (Disjoint cost partition).

A unit walk changes exactly one coordinate of either $\pi(p)$ or
 $\eta(p)$ , by one. Charge every exchange and every $\pi$ -changing walk
to cost $\alpha$ , and every $\eta$ -changing walk to cost $\beta$ .
For every route of length $L$ , $L=\alpha+\beta$ .

Proof.

In one dimension the edges $3\leftrightarrow 4,\ldots,8\leftrightarrow 9$ 
change only $\pi$ ; the remaining four edges change only $\eta$ .
A grid walk changes only one original coordinate. The asserted partition
therefore assigns each walk to exactly one class, and exchanges are
assigned to $\alpha$ by definition.
∎

## Stationary labels under exchange.

Temporarily label the seventeen occupied points. A label stays at its
cell during an exchange; only which label is active changes. During a walk,
the active label moves with the player. These are bookkeeping labels of
occupied points, not persistent identities of crystals. Consequently,
only walks move labels, and only $\beta$ -walks change their residual
coordinates. At completion, sixteen labels have residual coordinate
 $(0,0)$ , and one has residual coordinate $(2,2)$ . This observation
permits a displacement lower bound on $\beta$ , even though the
player itself can change residual coordinates in a single exchange.

## 4 A compressed-core lower bound

Let $Q^{\circ}=\{1,\ldots,5\}^{2}$ be the interior of $Q$ .
The abstraction of $s=(U,p)$ is

 $A(s)=(M,a,e),\qquad M=\pi(U\cap K),\quad a=\pi(p),\quad e=\pi(E)=(6,6).$ 

The endpoint corner $e$ is stored explicitly because the pattern table
uses all square symmetries. The integer $n_{\mathrm{out}}=17-|M|$ 
counts occupied points outside $K$ , including the player
when appropriate. Their individual positions are forgotten. Valid states
satisfy $|M|\leq 17$ , $a\in M$ when $a\in Q^{\circ}$ , and $n_{\mathrm{out}}\geq 1$ 
when $a\in\partial Q$ .

## 4.1 Abstract transitions

The following directed transitions have unit cost. Gates are ignored.
Rays exclude their starting cell.

1. 

Exchanges from the interior.
If $a\in Q^{\circ}$ , an exchange may reach the first point of $M$ 
on a chosen ray. If there is none, it may reach the boundary cell on
that ray, provided $n_{\mathrm{out}}\geq 1$ .

2. 

Exchanges from the boundary.
If $a\in\partial Q$ , an exchange may reach the first point of $M$ 
on a ray. It may also reach any other boundary cell on that ray before
a point of $M$ , provided $n_{\mathrm{out}}\geq 2$ .
Exchanges preserve $M$ .

3. 

Walks.
The active cell may move to an adjacent $b\in Q$ if the ray from
 $a$ in that direction contains no point of $M$ . Remove $a$ from
 $M$ if $a\in Q^{\circ}$ , and add $b$ if $b\in Q^{\circ}$ .
Only valid resulting states are retained.

These rules permit configurations of exterior points that need not be
simultaneously realizable on the original board. That extra freedom is
intentional. Exchanges whose endpoints have the same projection need no
abstract transition.

Lemma 4.1 (Simulation).

Every real $\alpha$ -command maps to one abstract edge or no change.
Every real $\beta$ -command maps to no change.

Proof.

A real exchange cannot pass a nearer interior crystal. If it reaches an
exterior point, the corresponding boundary destination is allowed by
the occupied-point count: an exterior-to-exterior exchange uses two
distinct exterior points. Projection preserves row or column alignment
and order along the noncollapsed part of a ray. Thus every exchange
with distinct projected endpoints is included.

A real walk is allowed only when its entire unblocked ray has no
crystal. The only cells hidden behind closed gates are gate cells and
exit-side boundary cells; none belongs to $K$ . Hence there is no
interior occupied point ahead of a legal walk. A $\pi$ -changing walk
satisfies the abstract walk rule, with precisely the stated
update of $M$ . An $\eta$ -changing walk stays outside $K$ , does not
change $\pi(p)$ , and leaves $M$ fixed.
∎

Let $T^{\prime}=\pi(T)$ , and define the base pattern distance

 $d(A)=\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal{A}}\bigl(A,(T^{\prime},e,e)\bigr),$ 

where $\mathcal{A}$ is the directed abstract graph. Reverse
breadth-first search from the abstract goal computes $d$ .
Lemma 4.1 gives $d(A(s))\leq\alpha$ for every
completion of $s$ .

## 4.2 A necessary northwest visit

Let $N=\{1,2,3\}^{2}$ , whose projection is the northwest corner $o=(0,0)$ .
If $U\cap N\neq\varnothing$ , at least one currently occupied point in
 $N$ must eventually move: neither a target nor the exit lies there.
Before its first walk, that point must be active. Thus the projected
player must visit $o$ , with a visit at the current time permitted.

For an abstract state $A=(M,a,e)$ , let $o(e)$ be the corner opposite
 $e$ , and define

 $d_{N}(A)=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}B=(M^{\prime},o(e),e)\\
B\text{ valid}\end{subarray}}\bigl[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal{A}}(A,B)+d(B)\bigr].$ 

(4)

This value is computed by reverse Dijkstra search, seeding each such
 $B$ with its base distance $d(B)$ . Set

 $H_{\alpha}(s)=\begin{cases}d_{N}(A(s)),&U\cap N\neq\varnothing,\\
d(A(s)),&U\cap N=\varnothing.\end{cases}$ 

(5)

Proposition 4.2.

For every completion of $s$ , $H_{\alpha}(s)\leq\alpha$ .

Proof.

Without the northwest condition this is the simulation lemma. With that
condition, split the projected route at an occurrence of $o$ .
The abstract prefix and suffix have total length at most the real
 $\alpha$ -cost and are candidates in (4).
∎

## 4.3 Symmetry and pattern-table representation

The group $D_{4}$ acts on the abstract board. We transform $M,a,e$ 
together; $o(e)$ transforms with $e$ . Canonicalizing the mask alone
without retaining goal orientation would not justify the distance lookup.
After choosing a representative mask, the implementation minimizes the
pair $(a,e)$ over the mask’s stabilizer.

There are 4,211,744 orbits of all $2^{25}$ masks under $D_{4}$ .
Each mask representative has $49\cdot 4=196$ addressable player/corner
slots, so each byte-valued distance array contains 825,501,824 slots.
The arrays include unused and noncanonical addresses. Each generated
array has 584,039,298 entries different from the sentinel 255.
These are storage counts, not counts of all real positions.
For the bound-93 computation, sentinel 255 is sufficient to reject a
state: all abstract paths of cost at most 92 are represented by the
reverse searches. Values at or beyond the sentinel need not be
distinguished. The initial core lower bound used in the search is 65.

## 5 Residual motion and activation detours

Fix labels $1,\ldots,17$ on the occupied points of the current state.
Write $r_{i}=\eta(u_{i})$ , and let $i_{p}$ be the active label.
For each possible exit-assigned label $e$ , put

 $z_{i}^{(e)}=\begin{cases}(2,2),&i=e,\\
(0,0),&i\neq e,\end{cases}\qquad D_{e}=\sum_{i=1}^{17}\left\lVert r_{i}-z_{i}^{(e)}\right\rVert_{1}.$ 

Every completion induces one such assignment. Since each $\beta$ -walk
moves exactly one residual coordinate by one,

 $D_{0}=\min_{e}D_{e}=\sum_{i}\left\lVert r_{i}\right\rVert_{1}+\min_{e}\bigl(\left\lVert r_{e}-(2,2)\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert r_{e}\right\rVert_{1}\bigr)$ 

(6)

is a lower bound on its residual-motion cost.

## 5.1 One necessary activation

Consider an inactive label $v$ with $r_{v}\neq(0,0)$ and $u_{v}\neq E$ .
It is currently on neither a target nor the exit and must eventually
move. Before its first walk, some distinct active label $j$ must exchange
with it. Until that first activation, $u_{v}$ remains fixed. Just before
the activating exchange, $u_{j}$ and $u_{v}$ share a row or column.
In particular, one residual coordinate of $j$ equals the corresponding
coordinate of $r_{v}$ .

For a possible terminal residual coordinate $z$ , define the excess
length forced by this necessary alignment:

 $\delta_{j}(z;v)=\min_{\ell\in\{1,2\}}\left(|r_{j,\ell}-r_{v,\ell}|+|r_{v,\ell}-z_{\ell}|-|r_{j,\ell}-z_{\ell}|\right).$ 

(7)

It is nonnegative by the triangle inequality. Alignment in residual
coordinates is only a necessary condition for real alignment; weakening
the condition can only decrease this bound.
Allowing every possible exit assignment and approaching label gives

 $D_{v}=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}e\in\{1,\ldots,17\}\\
j\neq v\end{subarray}}\left[D_{e}+\delta_{j}\bigl(z_{j}^{(e)};v\bigr)\right].$ 

(8)

In particular, the approaching label is allowed to be the exit-assigned
label. Excluding that possibility would not be justified.
Define

 $\mathcal{V}(s)=\{v:v\neq i_{p},\ r_{v}\neq(0,0),\ u_{v}\neq E\}$ 

and

 $H_{\beta}(s)=\max\bigl(\{D_{0}\}\cup\{D_{v}:v\in\mathcal{V}(s)\}\bigr).$ 

(9)

Proposition 5.1 (Residual lower bound).

For every completion of $s$ , $H_{\beta}(s)\leq\beta$ .

Proof.

Fix the actual exit assignment $e$ . For any $v\in\mathcal{V}(s)$ ,
let $j\neq v$ be the label that first activates it. The residual path
of $j$ , from $r_{j}$ to $z_{j}^{(e)}$ , passes through a point with at
least one coordinate equal to that of $r_{v}$ . Its length is therefore
at least its direct Manhattan distance plus
 $\delta_{j}(z_{j}^{(e)};v)$ . Every other label requires at least its direct
distance. Summing these disjoint label motions gives the expression
inside (8) for this particular $e,j$ , and hence
 $\beta\geq D_{v}$ . The same reasoning without a detour gives
 $\beta\geq D_{0}$ . Taking the maximum proves the claim.
∎

The maximum in (9) is essential: one motion may help
activate several points, so their detour bounds cannot in general be
added. The implementation computes the strongest two obligations and
the cell identifying the strongest one. This permits the active label’s
obligation to be omitted for any choice of $p$ in the same $U$ .

Lemma 5.2 (Safe reuse along walks).

For a legal walk $s\to s^{\prime}$ , the residual bound is unchanged if the
walk has $\alpha$ -cost. If the walk has $\beta$ -cost, then
 $\lvert H_{\beta}(s^{\prime})-H_{\beta}(s)\rvert\leq 1$ .

Proof.

The active label remains the same and all inactive labels remain fixed.
Thus the candidate set $\mathcal{V}$ and the activation coordinates
are unchanged. For fixed $e,j,v$ and choice of alignment coordinate,
the expression $D_{e}+\delta_{j}(z_{j}^{(e)};v)$ is a sum of path lengths.
If the active label is $j$ , its contribution is a path through a
fixed coordinate; otherwise its contribution is a direct distance.
Changing its residual start coordinate by one changes either length
by at most one. If its residual coordinate does not change, neither
does the expression. Minima and maxima preserve these properties.
The same argument applies to $D_{0}$ .
∎

Corollary 5.3 (Admissible combined heuristic).

The function $h(s)=H_{\alpha}(s)+H_{\beta}(s)$ is a lower bound on the
length of every completion of $s$ .

Proof.

Apply Propositions 4.2 and 5.1 to the
same completion and use $L=\alpha+\beta$ .
∎

The search uses an initial value $h(s_{0})=65+10=75$ .
A separate analytic argument proves that every complete route from
the initial state has $\beta\geq 12$ 
(Appendix A); that stronger initial-state statement
was not used as a statewise residual heuristic in the reported search.

## 6 Exact bounded search

Fix a strict bound $B=93$ . Breadth-first search processes states in
nondecreasing prefix length $g$ , enumerating all four legal commands.
A successor at depth $g+1$ is discarded when

 $(g+1)+h(s^{\prime})\geq B.$ 

(10)

Previously visited states need not be inserted again. The mathematical

title: RubricOpt: Self-Revision of Semantic Rubrics for Preference Optimization
abstract: A model's failures can reveal gaps in the behavioral criteria guiding its training. We introduce RubricOpt, a framework that lets a policy revise these criteria within preference optimization. The policy diagnoses its own rubric-free outputs, retains requirements already covered by the rubric, and edits clauses that leave recurring failures unaddressed. A shared semantic representation connects task demands, preference-data contrasts, and rubric clauses, while a deterministic gate checks evidence references and fixed semantic anchors. The rubric then guides Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) during training, with preference pairs, labels, and the objective held fixed, and is removed at evaluation. Our analysis relates the local effect on rubric-free success to semantic alignment and a residual beyond the measured factors. Experiments on capability and open-ended generation benchmarks show that rubric conditioning can improve outcomes over ordinary DPO, with gains and regressions varying across models and datasets. A matched continuation isolates the contribution of revision from additional training and finds mixed incremental effects for the tested edit, whose feedback overlaps the evaluation set. RubricOpt thus brings the behavioral specification itself into the policy's feedback loop.
