body_start:
Abstract

A model’s failures can reveal gaps in the behavioral criteria guiding its training.
We introduce RubricOpt, a framework that lets a policy revise these criteria within preference optimization.
The policy diagnoses its own rubric-free outputs, retains requirements already covered by the rubric, and edits clauses that leave recurring failures unaddressed.
A shared semantic representation connects task demands, preference-data contrasts, and rubric clauses, while a deterministic gate checks evidence references and fixed semantic anchors.
The rubric then guides Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) during training, with preference pairs, labels, and the objective held fixed, and is removed at evaluation.
Our analysis relates the local effect on rubric-free success to semantic alignment and a residual beyond the measured factors.
Experiments on capability and open-ended generation benchmarks show that rubric conditioning can improve outcomes over ordinary DPO, with gains and regressions varying across models and datasets.
A matched continuation isolates the contribution of revision from additional training and finds mixed incremental effects for the tested edit, whose feedback overlaps the evaluation set.
RubricOpt thus brings the behavioral specification itself into the policy’s feedback loop.

## 1 Introduction

Language models can supply rewards for their own iterative preference training (Yuan et al., 2024).
They can also improve their judgment skills by assessing their own judgments (Wu et al., 2025a).
The corresponding question for semantic training rubrics is how revising their behavioral requirements affects learned behavior, including when a revision yields gains beyond continuing training with the existing rubric.

Written rubrics specify desired response properties and can supply reward signals (Gunjal et al., 2025) or guide the construction of synthetic preference data (Gallego, 2025).
EvoRubrics jointly trains a policy and a rubric generator to adapt rubric-based rewards as learning proceeds (Ding et al., 2026).
SERPO co-evolves response evidence, query-specific rubrics, and policy parameters, using rubric scores as rewards for test-time reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2026a).
We study rubric revision in Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023), holding the pairs, labels, and objective fixed while changing the rubric context.
A matched continuation with the existing rubric measures the edit’s incremental contribution.

Figure 1: The RubricOpt loop. (a) Task demand and preference-data supply share eight factor axes. (b) Matched Prefer/Avoid clauses condition both responses during DPO. (c) Rubric-free evaluation supplies feedback for policy self-revision and the next refine/keep decision. Dashed frames group stages. Green boxes denote computation.

We introduce RubricOpt to study how a model revises its own training rubric across preference-training rounds (Fig. 1).
Fine-grained evaluation describes response quality through explicit skills (Ye et al., 2024).
We use a fixed eight-factor ontology to connect the model’s task failures, the contrasts in its preference data, and the rubric’s Prefer/Avoid clauses.
Diagnosis-guided self-evolution uses failure histories to direct subsequent learning (Wei et al., 2026).
RubricOpt applies this diagnostic idea to rubric revision, with the current policy reading task outcomes, self-judged factor scores, and judge feedback on its own outputs to attribute recurring failures to the eight factors.
It retains explicit requirements for further learning and proposes clause edits where the wording leaves recurring failures uncovered.
A deterministic gate checks evidence references, factor anchors, and edit size before carrying the rubric into the next round.
Training-only Semantic Rubric Steering uses the resulting rubric to condition both responses of a preference pair during DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023), with the pairs, labels, and objective held fixed.
Its exposure decreases during training, and evaluation uses the resulting policy without the rubric.
This use of training-only information has a precedent in privileged-information learning (Vapnik & Vashist, 2009).
Our analysis relates the extra update induced by a rubric to rubric-free success through its alignment with task demand (Sec. 3.3).

The experiments evaluate how changes to the training specification affect comprehensive capability and open-ended generation.
Fixed-state probes and criterion comparisons show that rubric text changes the learning update and can alter rubric-free outcomes (Sec. 4.1).
Across model families and preference corpora, rubric conditioning improves some capability and generation evaluations over ordinary DPO, with gains and regressions varying by setting (Tabs. 1 and 2).
The dataset comparison relates these effect profiles to the behavioral contrasts available in each corpus (Sec. 4.2).
A matched continuation separates revision from further optimization and finds mixed incremental results from the tested edit (Tab. 3).

RubricOpt makes the behavioral specification itself an object of policy-driven revision within preference learning.
Shared semantic coordinates connect failure diagnosis and preference-data contrasts to editable rubric clauses, while training-only steering connects those clauses to subsequent parameter updates.
This closes the loop from learned behavior to the specification of further learning, with the effect of revision evaluated independently of additional training.

## 2 Related Work

## Preference Optimization and Credit Assignment.

The family descends from RLHF, in which a reward model is fit to pairwise human judgements (Stiennon et al., 2020) and a policy is then optimised against it at assistant scale (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022).
DPO instead fits chosen–rejected pairs with a classification objective (Rafailov et al., 2023), whose implicit reward is the log density ratio between the policy and the reference (Sugiyama et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2025).
Later objectives change one component of that recipe: IPO replaces it with a squared loss on the pairwise margin (Azar et al., 2024), KTO drops the pairing requirement by scoring each response against a reference point (Ethayarajh et al., 2024), and SimPO removes the reference model and normalises the margin by length (Meng et al., 2024).
Two analyses place the family in a wider frame: one connects these objectives to imitation learning (Xiao et al., 2025), and one disentangles how their update suppresses the rejected response and preserves the chosen one (Chen et al., 2026).
A complementary line assigns credit inside a response rather than to the response as a whole: TDPO reweights tokens by a forward-KL penalty (Zeng et al., 2024), TIS-DPO reweights them by importance sampling against an estimated weight (Liu et al., 2025), SEPO selects tokens using a token-level reward estimate (Yang et al., 2025b), T-REG uses a token-level reward as a regulariser (Zhou et al., 2025), and TIDPO guides the update by token importance (Yang et al., 2026).
RubricOpt operates at a different level: a semantic factor names a behavioral distinction that can span several tokens or reasoning steps, while the pairwise loss itself is left unchanged.

## Criteria and Behavioral Diagnosis.

Written criteria already enter learning through several interfaces.
As reward signals, Rubrics as Rewards scores on-policy responses against a rubric (Gunjal et al., 2025).
As data, Configurable Preference Tuning builds rubric-conditioned synthetic preference pairs (Gallego, 2025).
And as weights, CoRT contrasts rubric-conditioned with rubric-free replays to form token-level weights (Zhang et al., 2026).
Criterion-conditioned training also has close relatives outside preference optimisation: learning using privileged information trains on a signal that is absent at test time (Vapnik & Vashist, 2009).
Context distillation trains on a context and then evaluates without it, introduced as an alignment technique (Askell et al., 2021) and developed as a standalone method (Snell et al., 2022).
And classifier-free guidance interpolates between conditioned and unconditioned predictions (Ho & Salimans, 2022).
On the diagnostic side, fine-grained evaluation describes response quality through interpretable skill sets and error taxonomies—FLASK by grading along skill dimensions (Ye et al., 2024), EvalTree by profiling weaknesses as a hierarchical capability tree (Zeng et al., 2025), and ErrorMap and ErrorAtlas by charting the failure landscape into error categories (Ashury-Tahan et al., 2026)—and diagnosis-driven post-training then acts on what those tools find, with DiagEvo feeding diagnosed errors back into self-evolution through a hierarchical error memory (Wei et al., 2026) and APTER turning expert-grounded rubrics into post-training supervision (Wang et al., 2026b).
RubricOpt uses shared semantic coordinates to connect task diagnosis, preference-data contrasts, and edits to the training rubric.

## Self-Improvement and Recursive Feedback.

Self-improvement methods differ in the component they revise and how that revision enters subsequent behavior.
Self-Refine edits outputs from self-feedback (Madaan et al., 2023), and automatic prompt optimisation edits inference-time text from feedback (Pryzant et al., 2023).
In parameter learning, Self-Rewarding uses the model to generate its own reward signals (Yuan et al., 2024), Meta-Rewarding trains judgment skills through a meta-judge (Wu et al., 2025a), and self-play preference optimisation regenerates preferences (Wu et al., 2025b).
Rubric evolution also enters the reward interface through joint policy–generator learning (Ding et al., 2026) and co-evolving query-specific rubrics during test-time reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2026a).
RubricOpt places self-revision in the semantic rubric that conditions preference training.
The current policy proposes clause edits from feedback about its own behavior, then learns under the resulting rubric in the next round.
The initial clause bank, factor ontology, task outcomes, and fixed scoring prompt provide the reference points for revision.

## 3 RubricOpt: Method and Analysis

RubricOpt alternates preference learning under a written rubric with revision of that rubric by the resulting policy.

## Problem Setup.

We study preference optimization on a fixed dataset $\mathcal{D}=\{({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}^{+},{\bm{y}}^{-})\}$ of chosen–rejected pairs, with a trainable policy $\pi_{\theta}$ and a frozen reference $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ trained by DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023),

 $\mathcal{L}=-\mathbb{E}\left[\log\sigma\left(\beta\left[\bar{\ell}_{\theta}({\bm{y}}^{+}\mid{\bm{x}})-\bar{\ell}_{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{y}}^{+}\mid{\bm{x}})-\bar{\ell}_{\theta}({\bm{y}}^{-}\mid{\bm{x}})+\bar{\ell}_{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{y}}^{-}\mid{\bm{x}})\right]\right)\right],$ 

(1)

with $\bar{\ell}({\bm{y}}\mid{\bm{x}})=L^{-1}\log\pi({\bm{y}}\mid{\bm{x}})$ averaged over the $L$ response tokens.
The pairs, labels, and objective are held fixed; only the text that conditions a pair may change, which is the degree of freedom RubricOpt introduces.

Behavior is described by a fixed eight-factor ontology $\mathcal{F}=\{f_{1},\ldots,f_{8}\}$ (appendix A.2), on which a blind judge returns one ordinal score per factor, $z_{k}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})\in\{0,\ldots,4\}$ (appendix A.3).
Every behavioral quantity here is a contrast between two groups of these scores, and only two contrasts are used.

title: PreCoMem: Predictive Cognitive Memory for Self-Evolving Long-Term Dialogue Agents
abstract: Long-horizon dialogue agents need to keep user memories stable enough for personalization while adapting when the user genuinely changes. Existing memory systems often append every observation or overwrite old entries by heuristic rules, which makes transient noise hard to distinguish from real belief drift. We introduce PreCoMem, a memory consolidation framework inspired by predictive coding that represents memory as confidence-weighted beliefs about the user's state. Its core signal, Effective Surprisal, combines semantic deviation and contradiction evidence, then downweights this signal when retrieval is diffuse and unreliable. According to effective surprisal, a two-threshold gate maps each turn to one of three deterministic updates: MAINTAIN reinforces supported beliefs, PROFILE stores ambiguous cues as low-confidence hypotheses, and CORRECT softly decays reliably contradicted facts. The PROFILE stage acts as an explicit waiting room, preventing premature commitment to noisy evidence. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and PersonaMem-v2 show consistent state-of-the-art accuracy; our new DiMoBench confirms that PreCoMem adapts to non-stationary belief drift without over-reacting to noise. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhongWishing/PreCoMem.

body_start:
Abstract

Long-horizon dialogue agents need to keep user memories stable enough for personalization while adapting when the user genuinely changes. Existing memory systems often append every observation or overwrite old entries by heuristic rules, which makes transient noise hard to distinguish from real belief drift. We introduce PreCoMem, a memory consolidation framework inspired by predictive coding that represents memory as confidence-weighted beliefs about the user’s state. Its core signal, Effective Surprisal, combines semantic deviation and contradiction evidence, then downweights this signal when retrieval is diffuse and unreliable. According to effective surprisal, a two-threshold gate maps each turn to one of three deterministic updates: MAINTAIN reinforces supported beliefs, PROFILE stores ambiguous cues as low-confidence hypotheses, and CORRECT softly decays reliably contradicted facts. The PROFILE stage acts as an explicit waiting room, preventing premature commitment to noisy evidence. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and PersonaMem-v2 show consistent state-of-the-art accuracy; our new DiMoBench confirms that PreCoMem adapts to non-stationary belief drift without over-reacting to noise. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhongWishing/PreCoMem.

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Memory evolution case study (coffee $\rightarrow$ tea). PreCoMem autonomously manages the lifecycle of facts and hypotheses, achieving a stable transition between conflicting belief states without manual intervention.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are moving from stateless responders toward long-term partners that interact with the user over hundreds or thousands of turns [32, 39, 44]. Such partners need more than stored transcripts; they require a user model to sustain personalized interaction [51, 15].
To formalize the core units of this user model, we define a belief as a compact, actionable claim about the user’s preferences, goals, or life context, paired with a confidence weight that can be reinforced or revised over time.
This user model underpins both agent personalization and behavioral self-correction, thereby redefining the role of long-term memory: rather than merely serving as simple context extension [30, 41], long-term memory enables the agent to maintain consistent behavior across sessions.

The harder question is not whether information can be stored, but how it should be consolidated and revised. A practical memory consolidation mechanism must decide which observations to retain, how strongly to trust them, and when to maintain, revise, or correct stored items without explicit supervision. We refer to this as the memory stability–plasticity problem: the agent should preserve stable user traits while remaining plastic enough to adapt when those traits change [6]. Long-horizon interaction makes the problem hard for three coupled reasons. First, most turns carry little signal, while a small fraction may contain cues indicative of more persistent user states. Second, user preferences and life facts evolve over time [5], so the system must adapt under non-stationarity and belief drift [49, 7]. Third, corrective feedback is rarely explicit [14], and noisy retrieval over long contexts further blurs the picture [48, 25, 4, 43]. Therefore, the brittle memory update mechanism causes two opposite failures: premature correction from noise, or persistent over-reliance on outdated memories, which we call old-memory pull, a phenomenon related to loss of plasticity and retrieval interference in continual adaptation systems [6, 11].

Recent memory systems have made impressive progress on retrieval and storage organization. Hierarchical and OS-style stores [30, 23, 10], structured indices with timestamps or topic shards [34, 40, 21, 38], and agentic retrievers [45, 46] all sharpen what the system can recall. However, the question of when to update is still often handled by recency overwriting, fixed-threshold importance, or one-shot append rules [51, 2]. These triggers cannot reliably separate persistent drift from transient noise [11], so they collapse the stability–plasticity trade-off precisely where long-horizon dialogue stresses it most. A fuller literature discussion is provided in Appendix Appendix A.

We draw inspiration from predictive coding, which posits that learning is driven by mismatch between expectation and reality, i.e., prediction error [8, 3]. In information theory the same quantity is called surprisal [19, 29]. We use this view as a design principle for the update path rather than as a claim that dialogue memory is a fully specified probabilistic model. The resulting criterion is simple: events consistent with current memory should be reinforced, while surprising events may require learning or correction [33, 36]. Crucially, surprisal must be paired with a measure of retrieval reliability, so that update decisions stay conservative when recall itself is uncertain or noisy [18, 48].

Building on this view, we propose PreCoMem (Predictive Cognitive Memory), a self-evolving long-term memory framework for conversational LLM agents. PreCoMem operates in two active phases over a shared memory store. In memory leveraging, it retrieves confidence-weighted beliefs to condition response generation. In memory evolution, it compares new observations with recalled evidence and computes Effective Surprisal $S_{\mathrm{eff}}$ , a reliability-adjusted mismatch score. A two-threshold gate then routes each update to MAINTAIN, PROFILE, or CORRECT, corresponding to consistent, ambiguous, and reliably contradictory evidence. Figure 1 illustrates this loop on a coffee-to-tea preference shift, where a low-confidence hypothesis is gradually promoted to a fact while the contradicted old fact is softly decayed.

In summary, we (i) propose PreCoMem, a memory consolidation framework that casts long-term memory as a dynamic prediction of the user’s state; (ii) introduce a reliability-weighted surprisal signal that gates each update through MAINTAIN, PROFILE, or CORRECT; and (iii) evaluate on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, PersonaMem-v2, and DiMoBench/DiMoBench-XL, controlled write-path stress tests with gradual drift and decoy retrieval. PreCoMem outperforms the strongest contemporary baselines while keeping effective memory stable across 1050 turns.

## 2 PreCoMem

## 2.1 Framework overview

Figure 2: The PreCoMem framework. Two active phases operate over a shared memory store. Phase 1, Memory Leveraging: a confidence-modulated retrieval score combines semantic, lexical, and topic signals to select Top- $K$ beliefs $\mathcal{C}_{t}$ for response generation. Phase 2, Memory Evolution: the effective surprisal $S_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and a two-threshold gate route each turn to MAINTAIN, PROFILE, or CORRECT, illustrated by representative low/medium/high- $S_{\mathrm{eff}}$ turns. Memory Store: an editable Belief Store $\mathcal{B}$ of FACT/HYPO nodes with confidence weights, linked by provenance to an immutable Episodic Cache $\mathcal{E}$ under a shared topic index; belief items are updated independently, and the drawn links are provenance pointers and topic groupings (Appendix Section C.11).

As illustrated in Figure 2, PreCoMem operates as a closed loop of two active phases around a shared memory store. Memory Leveraging retrieves confidence-weighted beliefs and uses them to condition response generation. Memory Evolution then revises the memory state in light of the new interaction: it computes Effective Surprisal $S_{\mathrm{eff}}$ against recalled evidence, and routes the update to one of three deterministic operators—MAINTAIN, PROFILE, or CORRECT. This read–write loop differs from prior memory systems in two ways. First, every belief item carries a continuous confidence weight $w_{t}(m)\!\in\![0,1]$ that is reinforced or softly decayed by the operators, instead of relying on discrete commit decisions such as Add/Ignore/Update in O-Mem [40] or binary expiry intervals in EverMemOS [10]. Second, PROFILE buffers ambiguous observations as low-confidence hypotheses, letting weak evidence accumulate across turns before it is committed or discarded.

In implementation, each operator pairs a closed-form update rule with a fixed-prompt LLM sub-agent. The sub-agent only identifies which items are relevant and emits one bounded scalar, such as evidence_strength, severity, or initial_confidence. The deterministic layer then plugs these scalars into Equations 7, 8 and 10. Thus the LLM proposes local magnitudes, while the gate, confidence bounds, and closed-form $w$ updates control when and how memory changes accumulate. Algorithm 1 (Appendix Section B.4) gives the per-turn pipeline.

## 2.2 Memory primitives

Dialogue and memory state. At turn $t=1,2,\ldots$ , the user input is $u_{t}$ , the agent response is $y_{t}$ , and $Q_{t-1}$ is a rolling working-memory window. Long-term memory is $\mathcal{M}_{t}=(\mathcal{B}_{t},\mathcal{E}_{t},\mathcal{T}_{t})$ . The belief store $\mathcal{B}_{t}$ contains editable facts and hypotheses with confidence weights. The episodic cache $\mathcal{E}_{t}$ stores immutable raw dialogue traces with source pointers. The optional topic table $\mathcal{T}_{t}$ is only a retrieval prior. This keeps beliefs editable and evidence traceable.

Items, confidence, and hypothesis lifecycle. A memory item $m$ has content $c(m)$ , type $\tau(m)\in\{\texttt{FACT},\texttt{HYPOTHESIS}\}$ , and retrieval metadata such as embeddings, topic labels, entities, timestamps, and source pointers into $\mathcal{E}_{t}$ . For belief items, $w_{t}(m)\in[0,1]$ is an operational support score. Episodic traces are fixed at $w_{t}(e)\equiv 1$ and used only as provenance, not in confidence-weighted Top- $K$ ranking. A HYPOTHESIS is a provisional belief: it is reinforced under supporting evidence, decayed when evidence stays absent, and promoted to FACT when confidence crosses $\tau_{\mathrm{promote}}$ . Type transitions are one-way. Contradicted facts are softly decayed by CORRECT (Section 2.4) rather than demoted, yielding low-confidence “deprecated” facts that confidence-weighted retrieval naturally deprioritizes. Appendix Section C.7 confirms this retention is accuracy-neutral.

## 2.3 Memory leveraging: evidence recall and response generation

In Memory Leveraging, PreCoMem recalls a compact evidence set from long-term memory and leverages it to generate the current response.

Evidence recall. Given $u_{t}$ and short-term context $Q_{t-1}$ , PreCoMem ranks candidates in $\mathcal{B}_{t}$ with a confidence-modulated score. The score combines three retrieval signals: semantic similarity, lexical overlap (BM25), and topic relevance. Omitting $Q_{t-1}$ in the notation,

 $s(u_{t},m)=w_{t}(m)\sum_{j=1}^{3}\alpha_{j}s_{j}(u_{t},m),\quad m\in\mathcal{B}_{t},$ 

(1)

where $(s_{1},s_{2},s_{3})=(s_{\mathrm{sem}},s_{\mathrm{fact}},s_{\mathrm{topic}})$ and $\boldsymbol{\alpha}=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3})^{\top}$ is a convex weight vector. The multiplier $w_{t}(m)$ biases retrieval toward high-confidence items. The Top- $K$ belief items form $\mathcal{C}_{t}=\{m_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}$ with retrieval scores $\mathbf{s}_{t}$ . Linked episodic traces from $\mathcal{E}_{t}$ are appended as provenance context, but they do not participate in Top- $K$ ranking. The same scores $\mathbf{s}_{t}$ are retained for the reliability estimate in Section 2.4.

Evidence-conditioned response. The recalled evidence texts $\{c(m)\mid m\in\mathcal{C}_{t}\}$ , together with $u_{t}$ and the short-term window $Q_{t-1}$ , condition the response model:

 $y_{t}=\texttt{Respond}(u_{t},Q_{t-1},\mathcal{C}_{t}).$ 

(2)

We reuse the same recall outputs $(\mathcal{C}_{t},\mathbf{s}_{t})$ to perform memory evolution in Section 2.4.

## 2.4 Memory evolution: regime-gated belief updating

Given the recall outputs $(\mathcal{C}_{t},\mathbf{s}_{t})$ and the new interaction $(u_{t},y_{t})$ ,
PreCoMem computes a prediction-error signal adjusted by retrieval reliability,
and applies a regime-gated update to the belief store.
It also writes the new turn back into the episodic cache for future provenance and recall.

Retrieval reliability. Surprisal computed against recalled evidence can be misleading when recall is uncertain, so we derive a reliability coefficient from the entropy of retrieval scores. Let $\mathbf{s}_{t}=\{s_{i}\}_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{C}_{t}|}$ denote the Top- $K$ retrieval scores returned with $\mathcal{C}_{t}$ , and let $\hat{s}_{i}=(s_{i}+\epsilon)/\sum_{j}(s_{j}+\epsilon)$ be the smoothed normalization. We define the normalized entropy $H_{t}$ and the reliability coefficient $\rho_{t}$ as

 $H_{t}=\frac{-\sum_{i}\hat{s}_{i}\log\hat{s}_{i}}{\log\max\{|\mathcal{C}_{t}|,2\}}\in[0,1],\qquad\rho_{t}=1-H_{t}.$ 

(3)

Because $H_{t}$ is minimized when one item dominates and maximized under near-uniform scores, $\rho_{t}$ measures score concentration as a proxy for evidence precision. Diffuse recall (small $\rho_{t}$ ) downweights deviation signals to avoid over-updating; concentrated recall (large $\rho_{t}$ ) preserves them for correction. Thus the gate becomes aggressive only when recall is concentrated and the raw contradiction/deviation signal is large. Since $\rho_{t}$ enters only multiplicatively, it can defer an update but never trigger one on its own; whether CORRECT fires still depends on the contradiction term below, and Appendix Section C.8 verifies empirically that $\rho_{t}$ tracks evidence precision. The constant $\epsilon>0$ ensures numerical stability.

Raw surprisal proxy. We define:

 $S_{\mathrm{raw}}(u_{t})=\lambda\,d_{\mathrm{sem}}(u_{t},\mathcal{C}_{t})+(1-\lambda)\,d_{\mathrm{conf}}(u_{t},\mathcal{C}_{t}),$ 

(4)

where $\lambda\in(0,1)$ , $d_{\mathrm{sem}}$ is the normalized semantic deviation between $u_{t}$ and score-weighted recalled evidence, and $d_{\mathrm{conf}}$ is a verifier-based contradiction score quantifying how strongly $u_{t}$ conflicts with recalled beliefs (see Appendix Section B.2).

Effective surprisal. We define:

 $S_{\mathrm{eff}}(u_{t})=\rho_{t}\,S_{\mathrm{raw}}(u_{t}),$ 

(5)

which corresponds to a precision-weighted prediction error that becomes conservative when recall is unreliable.
We use $x_{t}:=S_{\mathrm{eff}}(u_{t})$ as the scalar gate score below. Appendix Section B.1 gives an optimization view that interprets $x_{t}$ as a Monte Carlo surrogate of a long-horizon predictive objective.

Regime-gated evolution. Given two ordered thresholds $\theta_{\mathrm{low}}<\theta_{\mathrm{high}}$ , PreCoMem maps the gate score $x_{t}$ into three regimes:

 $a_{t}=\begin{cases}\texttt{MAINTAIN},&x_{t}\leq\theta_{\mathrm{low}}\\
\texttt{PROFILE},&\theta_{\mathrm{low}}<x_{t}\leq\theta_{\mathrm{high}}\\
\texttt{CORRECT},&x_{t}>\theta_{\mathrm{high}}.\end{cases}$ 

(6)

Two-threshold gate. Low, medium, and high $x_{t}$ correspond to consistent, ambiguous, and reliably contradictory evidence. PROFILE handles the middle regime that a binary maintain/correct rule must either ignore or overwrite. We fix $(\theta_{\mathrm{low}},\theta_{\mathrm{high}})=(0.2,0.6)$ throughout the main experiments to keep behavior controllable and the comparison reproducible across benchmarks; the cost-sensitive break-even derivation, operator ablations, threshold sensitivity, and dynamic-threshold variant are in Appendix Sections B.3, C.4, C.5 and C.5.

## MAINTAIN (reinforcement).

When surprisal is low, PreCoMem strengthens supported beliefs in $\mathcal{C}_{t}$ via:

 $w_{t+1}(m)=w_{t}(m)+\eta_{t}(m)\,(1-w_{t}(m)),\quad m\in\mathcal{C}_{t}\cap\mathcal{B}_{t},$ 

(7)

where $\eta_{t}(m)\in(0,1]$ is the per-item evidence_strength returned by the Maintain-Agent; weakly supported items barely move, while strongly supported ones are pulled toward $1$ . The optimization view in Appendix Section B.3 treats $\eta_{t}(m)$ as a scalar step size.

## PROFILE (hypothesis writing).

When surprisal is medium, the observation is novel but not decisively contradictory. PreCoMem generates a low-confidence hypothesis $h$ and writes it as a HYPOTHESIS belief:

 $\displaystyle h$ 
 $\displaystyle=\texttt{GenerateHypothesis}(u_{t},\mathcal{C}_{t}),\qquad\tau(h)=\texttt{HYPOTHESIS},$ 

(8)

 $\displaystyle b_{t}^{(c)}$ 
 $\displaystyle=w_{\min}^{(c)}+\sigma(x_{t})\bigl(w_{\max}^{(c)}-w_{\min}^{(c)}\bigr),\qquad w_{0}(h)=\tfrac{1}{2}\,b_{t}^{(c)}+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{clip}\bigl(q_{t},[w_{\min}^{(c)},w_{\max}^{(c)}]\bigr),$ 

where GenerateHypothesis is the Profile-Agent under a fixed prompt, $\sigma(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})$ , $c\!\in\!\{\textsc{explicit},\textsc{latent}\}$ is the class label assigned by the agent, and $q_{t}$ is the agent’s initial_confidence, clipped to the class band $[w_{\min}^{(c)},w_{\max}^{(c)}]$ . The gate score thus supplies a reproducible prior $b_{t}^{(c)}$ inside the band, and the agent scalar can shift $w_{0}$ by at most half the band width. Explicit-event hypotheses paraphrase stated facts or actions and use the band $[0.60,0.70]$ . Latent-inference hypotheses capture deduced traits, moods, or hidden goals and use $[0.50,0.59]$ . These initial values are low relative to stable FACTs, which sit at $w\!\geq\!0.80$ and meet the promotion threshold $\tau_{\mathrm{promote}}\!=\!0.80$ . A fresh hypothesis therefore ranks below committed facts in confidence-weighted retrieval (Equation 1) and still needs repeated support to graduate. In later turns, hypotheses are reinforced under MAINTAIN when supported and decayed when evidence remains absent:

 $w_{t}(h)\leftarrow w_{t}(h)\exp\bigl(-\gamma\,a_{t}(h)\bigr),\qquad a_{t}(h)=t-\ell(h),$ 

(9)

where $\ell(h)$ is the turn at which $h$ was created or last received supporting evidence and $\gamma>0$ is a decay rate. The rule is applied once per turn to unsupported hypotheses: any supporting update resets $\ell(h)$ and skips the decay in that turn, and hypotheses flagged as decay_protection by the agent (explicit events) are exempt, so the compounding decay over cons
conclusion: PreCoMem treats long-horizon conversational memory not as a transcript to be stored, but as confidence-weighted beliefs about the user’s state that must be continually checked. A reliability-adjusted surprisal signal routes each turn into MAINTAIN (reinforce supported beliefs), PROFILE (buffer ambiguous cues as low-confidence hypotheses), or CORRECT (softly decay contradicted facts). The PROFILE waiting room is the central design choice: it lets evidence accumulate before commitment, so the agent stays consistent under noise without freezing under genuine drift. Across LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, PersonaMem-v2, and DiMoBench, this discipline yields the best overall accuracy while keeping memory bounded over a thousand turns; qualitative case studies (Appendix Section C.11) show calibrated recommendations beyond retrieval-only baselines. We see continuous confidence and explicit hypothesis lifecycles as a useful baseline for long-term memory systems, where what to commit matters as much as what to recall. Our evaluation covers English dialogue benchmarks; other languages and modalities are left for future work.

title: Events, Not Pixels: Where World Models Get the Return Wrong
abstract: World models are increasingly used for planning, where a planner ranks candidate actions by returns imagined by the model. However, these models are judged mainly by how well they render frames, even though a visually faithful rollout can still assign the wrong return. To identify where this mismatch arises, we introduce a transition-level diagnostic that replaces imagined transitions with real ones and measures the reduction in return error against a budget-matched random control. Our analysis yields two findings. (1) Event transitions, the few steps where a reward is earned or an episode ends, are rendered as well as other steps (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error. In contrast, restoring transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error removes less than a random choice. Across the 44 Atari-100k model--collection pairs that pass our reliability checks, including three released families, event patches outperform random patches in 39 (sign test p=1.4 x 10^{-7}), with a median gain of +44 percentage points. (2) The remaining error is structured: a complementary patch separates errors at true events from those elsewhere, while an eight-step timing tolerance recovers few events missed by our deterministic models. This structure also guides repair: a rule recorded before four repair outcomes were known predicts when a diffusion model repairs these failures. Event patches improve plan ranking, and the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events.

body_start:
Abstract

World models are increasingly used for planning, where a planner ranks candidate actions by returns imagined by the model. However, these models are judged mainly by how well they render frames, even though a visually faithful rollout can still assign the wrong return. To identify where this mismatch arises, we introduce a transition-level diagnostic that replaces imagined transitions with real ones and measures the reduction in return error against a budget-matched random control. Our analysis yields two findings. (1) Event transitions, the few steps where a reward is earned or an episode ends, are rendered as well as other steps (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error. In contrast, restoring transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error removes less than a random choice. Across the 44 Atari-100k model–collection pairs that pass our reliability checks, including three released families, event patches outperform random patches in 39 (sign test $p=1.4\times 10^{-7}{}$ ), with a median gain of +44 percentage points. (2) The remaining error is structured: a complementary patch separates errors at true events from those elsewhere, while an eight-step timing tolerance recovers few events missed by our deterministic models. This structure also guides repair: a rule recorded before four repair outcomes were known predicts when a diffusion model repairs these failures. Event patches improve plan ranking, and the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events.

## 1 Introduction

World models let an agent imagine the consequences of an action before taking
it [18]. A planner rolls candidate action sequences forward inside the model and
acts on the ordering of their imagined
returns [11, 20, 48, 23, 22, 2, 36]. Released pixel world models
support this pipeline in Atari, continuous control, and
manipulation [12, 60, 52], and their progress is mainly
measured by how faithfully they render the
future [59, 65, 53].

Rendering quality, however, is only loosely tied to what a planner needs. A return often hinges on
a few transitions that carry a reward or end an episode, so a model can render a rollout well yet
misprice it by missing a single paddle contact. Model-level studies expose this mismatch:
rankings by visual quality can disagree with rankings by task
success [33, 64], and whole-model oracle substitutions find that
average prediction accuracy does not consistently explain planning
performance [41, 49, 7]. Yet neither these
analyses nor compounding-error bounds [26] reveal where that error occurs: is it
spread across all sixty steps of a rollout, or concentrated in only a few? We therefore ask:

Where inside an imagined rollout does the error that changes a planner’s decision occur?

Figure 1: Return error concentrates at event transitions that pixel error does not single out.
A: A saved Seaquest MSE model predicts a 60-step future from 36 real context frames
and recorded actions. B: Each selected detector input substitutes both frames of a
transition, keeping its action fixed. C: Event and random masks each select three
of sixty steps here; complement and all-real inputs complete the controls.
D: Saved return-error reductions over 400 probes.
E: Five selected times show real frames, predictions, absolute RGB residuals on a shared
square-root colour scale, and the frames supplied by the two substitution arms. Coloured
borders mark real-pair substitutions.

To answer this question, we introduce a transition-level substitution diagnostic
(Fig. 1). Each imagined rollout is paired with a real rollout that starts from
the same context and follows the same recorded actions, so the two differ only in who drew the
frames. A frozen, memoryless detector, trained once per game, reads reward and termination from
each pair of consecutive frames; replacing one imagined pair with the real one therefore changes
the return only at that step. We patch the pairs at true events, the same number of random pairs,
all non-event pairs, or every pair. These four patches isolate the targeting effect, its
budget-matched control, the error away from events, and an all-real reference.

Our analysis yields two findings. First, return error concentrates at events that do not
look wrong. In Fig. 1D, restoring three transitions around a Seaquest reward
removes almost all return error; three random ones remove little. Across 44 reliable
Atari model–collection pairs, event patches beat random patches in 39 by a median of
+44 points, and the advantage appears within a few patches (Fig. 2).
Event frames are rendered as well as others (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet
restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error; the same pattern holds on
eighteen games added after our predictions were recorded. Second, the remaining error
is structured rather than merely mistimed. Complementary patches separate errors at true events
from errors elsewhere, and timing-tolerant recall shows that temporal offset explains little
of the events our deterministic models miss. This structure also predicts where a diffusion
model helps; event patches improve plan ranking and carry over to control tasks with rare reward events.

We summarise our contributions as follows:

• 

We introduce a per-transition substitution diagnostic with a budget-matched random control.
It treats the world model as a black box, and we apply it to three released model families on all 26 Atari-100k games.

• 

We show, for the first time on released pixel world models, that return error concentrates
at reward and termination transitions, also under each model’s own reward head and without the
score display, and that a complementary patch separates errors at true events from other errors.

• 

We show that a temporal offset explains little of the events missed by deterministic
models, predict all four repair outcomes with a rule recorded in advance, and show that event
patches improve plan ranking in every counted pair and carry over to control tasks with rare reward events.

## 2 Related Work

Figure 2: Targeting advantage across patch budgets. 9 sweeps, three games,
3 released families. Solid/dashed curves denote event/random patches; markers identify
families. Lower panels show their difference, $L$ , at matched coverage. Dotted guides mark
the second DIAMOND budget; annotations give its mean patched-step count and lift.
All-frame reference ranges are listed above each panel. Sweeps use one sampling seed; Table 1 reports three-seed means.

Pixel world models support prediction and control in
games [40, 10, 29, 21, 46, 66, 36, 37, 2, 12]
and interactive video
simulators [62, 6, 54, 60]. Yet visual fidelity can
diverge from physical correctness [38] and task
success [33, 64, 58]; the same disconnect appears for
training likelihood [31, 13, 16], synthetic
training data [1], and token pruning [57].
Concurrent work weights error by decision-relevant state dimensions [56], while
DIAMOND shows that visual details matter [2]. We instead locate where
decision-relevant error occurs inside a rollout.

Oracle substitution localises such failures. Cloning Deterministic Worlds [61]
substitutes true states for learned representations, while whole-model oracle interventions relate
accuracy to planning [41, 49, 7]; a concurrent
diagnostic uses a kinematic null [47]. Closest to ours, counterfactual
debugging [32] assigns Shapley credit over time steps to a policy’s
sim-to-real gap under injected faults, and agent explanations identify steps that decide a
return [17, 8, 3]. We instead operate directly on
released world-model rollouts, replacing individual transition pairs under a budget-matched
random control. This brings perturbation-based
attribution [63, 14, 44, 25],
used and tested on Atari agents [15, 4], from pixels
to time steps.

Other work improves prediction with multi-step
training [50, 55], goal-aware
objectives [39], keyframe
targets [27, 43], region- and event-aware
objectives [34, 42], causal rollout structure [67], and
architecture-level probing [28]. Conditional-mean effects are also
studied in video prediction [35] and perception and driving
models [45]. We test which explanation accounts for missed events using event
survival, a diffusion model, and the same network trained deterministically.

## 3 Diagnostic Setup

Figure 3: Task-event transitions beyond Atari. Six tasks, two real trajectory segments per
task, and three frames per segment. Blue borders mark reward onset, the first rewarded step after at least four reward-free steps. Cases are selected
from real events, separated by more than 96 steps within each task. Aggregate targeting and
detector results are in the supplement.

The diagnostic needs only rendered frames, so it applies to released checkpoints without access
to their internals.

## Return from a Predicted Trajectory.

A probe is a real context with fixed actions $a_{1:H}$ (Fig. 1A); from it, a model produces imagined observations
 $\hat{o}_{1:H}$ . A frozen detector, shared by all world models of a game, reads each transition pair and its action as a reward sign and
a termination flag, $(\hat{r}_{t},\hat{d}_{t})=D(\hat{o}_{t},\hat{o}_{t+1},a_{t})$ for $t<H$ ; the last frame
has no successor, so $\hat{r}_{H}=\hat{d}_{H}=0$ . The emulator, replaying the same actions, supplies $r_{1:H}$ and $d_{1:H}$ ,
and both returns stop at the first termination. Rewards enter through their sign, as in
Atari-100k training, so all games share one scale:

 $\hat{G}=\sum_{t=1}^{H}\gamma^{t-1}\operatorname{sgn}(\hat{r}_{t})\prod_{j<t}(1-\hat{d}_{j}),\quad E=\mathbb{E}\lvert\hat{G}-G\rvert,$ 

(1)

where $G$ is computed in the same way from $r$ and $d$ , and $\mathbb{E}$ averages over probes.
Atari uses $H=60$ and $\gamma=0.99$ .

## Substitutions and Their Controls.

For channel $c$ (observation $o$ , reward $r$ or termination $d$ ) and a binary mask $m$ , let $\hat{G}^{c,m}$ be the return after
substituting the selected real information (Fig. 1). Observation patches replace both frames of
the selected transition before detection, so no pair mixes real and generated frames; unselected pairs keep their predictions.
Reward and termination interventions replace $\hat{r}$ or $\hat{d}$ .
We report the fractional reduction in mean absolute return error:

 $R(c,m)=1-\frac{\mathbb{E}[|\hat{G}^{c,m}-G|]}{\mathbb{E}[|\hat{G}-G|]}.$ 

(2)

The all-frame value
 $R(o,\mathbf{1})$ measures performance when the detector sees only real transition pairs.

The event mask starts from nonzero real reward or termination and is dilated by one step, i.e., the
transitions just before and after are also selected, to cover delays in the visual markers. We report its realised coverage
 $q=\penalty\mathbb{E}[H^{-1}\sum_{t}m_{t}^{\rm ev}]$ , which includes dilation. The random mask selects the same number of steps in each
rollout.
The targeting advantage is

 $L=R(o,m^{\rm ev})-R(o,m^{\rm rnd}).$ 

(3)

The complementary mask $\bar{m}^{\rm ev}$ measures errors away from the selected events, and
its contrast with the event patch classifies the failure pattern of each model.

## 4 Localising the Return Error

We localise the return error with one frozen, memoryless detector per game, shared by every
world model of that game. A random patch also hits true events, and more of them as coverage
grows, so the lift of Eq. (3) credits the event patch only with what it adds beyond chance.

Figure 2 widens the event neighbourhood step by step and plots the lift against the
resulting coverage. In 8 of 9 sweeps over three games and three released
families, the event curve stays well above the random curve. For DIAMOND on Freeway, patching
2.8 of sixty steps removes 69% of the error, against
 $-4{}$ % for random patches and 86% when every frame is real; on Pong,
2.1 steps remove 43% against 5%. The sweep also exposes a
timing effect: without dilation the Freeway event patch is negative, consistent with the reward
digit appearing after the transition that earns it, so we treat the neighbourhood as part of the
measurement.

The sweep also shows why the random control is needed. For DIAMOND and Simulus on Seaquest, both
patches remove more error as coverage grows while the lift stays flat, so the event-patch
reduction alone would overstate the targeting effect. Table 1 reports every game at
a one-step neighbourhood, and Fig. 3 shows events beyond Atari.

title: MERP: A Latent-Bottleneck Framework for Robust Multi-Modal Multi-Label Emotion Recognition
abstract: Multimodal multi-label emotion recognition is important for affect-aware systems, but models trained with complete text, visual, and acoustic streams often degrade sharply when some streams are unavailable at deployment. We address this train-test gap by learning a compact representation that preserves emotion-specific evidence from any available subset of modalities. We propose the Multi-modal Emotion Recognition Perceiver (MERP), which maps the joint sequence into a fixed-size latent bank, thereby keeping repeated reasoning independent of raw input length; it extracts label-specific evidence before and after latent reasoning and aligns the two levels through reconstruction. MERP further uses positive and negative class prototypes, a noise-gated feature enhancer with frequency-shaped perturbations during training, and confidence-aware class-wise fusion to strengthen separability, reduce sensitivity to missing inputs, and combine complementary predictors. Under 20 percent test-time random modality drop, MERP achieves micro-F1 scores of 0.563 on CMU-MOSEI and 0.780 on M3ED, exceeding the strongest evaluated baselines by 0.004 and 0.005, respectively; in the severe CMU-MOSEI audio-only setting, it retains 0.473 micro-F1 versus 0.022 for LDDU. These results show that fixed latent reasoning provides a practical, testable route to robust multimodal emotion recognition without requiring missing-modality examples during training. Code is available at https://github.com/Creative-zcx/MERP.

body_start:
Abstract

Multimodal multi-label emotion recognition is important for affect-aware systems, but models trained with complete text, visual, and acoustic streams often degrade sharply when some streams are unavailable at deployment. We address this train–test gap by learning a compact representation that preserves emotion-specific evidence from any available subset of modalities. We propose the Multi-modal Emotion Recognition Perceiver (MERP), which maps the joint sequence into a fixed-size latent bank, thereby keeping repeated reasoning independent of raw input length; it extracts label-specific evidence before and after latent reasoning and aligns the two levels through reconstruction. MERP further uses positive and negative class prototypes, a noise-gated feature enhancer with frequency-shaped perturbations during training, and confidence-aware class-wise fusion to strengthen separability, reduce sensitivity to missing inputs, and combine complementary predictors. Under 20% test-time random modality drop, MERP achieves micro-F1 scores of 0.563 on CMU-MOSEI and 0.780 on M3ED, exceeding the strongest evaluated baselines by 0.004 and 0.005, respectively; in the severe CMU-MOSEI audio-only setting, it retains 0.473 micro-F1 versus 0.022 for LDDU. These results show that fixed latent reasoning provides a practical, testable route to robust multimodal emotion recognition without requiring missing-modality examples during training. Code is available at https://github.com/Creative-zcx/MERP.

Index Terms: 
Multi-modal emotion recognition, multi-label classification, missing modality, Perceiver-IO, latent bottleneck.

## I Introduction

Understanding human affect from language, voice, and facial behaviour is central to affect-aware interfaces, conversational systems, and large-scale media analysis [1]. These modalities provide complementary evidence, making their joint analysis more informative than isolated unimodal prediction [2]. Multi-modal multi-label emotion recognition (MMER) is especially valuable because an utterance can express several emotions simultaneously, but this setting must resolve both cross-modal ambiguity and correlations among co-occurring labels [3].

Fig. 1: Fixed latent reasoning preserves class-specific evidence under compound modality loss. With text and visual streams unavailable, the schematic input-bound path loses the Surprise label after late fusion (a). MERP maps the same zeroed input into a fixed latent workspace and uses class-specific readouts to retain both labels (b).

MMER has advanced substantially through increasingly structured dependency and representation learning. HHMPN propagates information over a hierarchy of modality features and emotion labels [4], while TAILOR separates common and private modality factors before label-guided decoding [5]. More recent systems improve label discrimination through contrastive reconstruction in CARAT [6] and probabilistic uncertainty modeling in LDDU [7]. In parallel, recent studies have strengthened categorical multi-modal emotion recognition through emotion-shift-aware cross-modal fusion [8], relational subgraph interaction [9], and interpretable hybrid fusion [10]. These advances demonstrate the value of structured fusion, but the categorical models assign one emotion to each instance, whereas MMER must distinguish several correlated labels. Moreover, their computation remains organized around modality-specific or joint input sequences. Directional cross-modal attention, for example, captures fine-grained interactions but retains token-level costs that grow with the input streams [11]; label-specific decoding and late probabilistic fusion improve prediction without removing this structural dependence.

Incomplete input exposes a second, closely coupled limitation. Existing approaches recover missing representations through cross-modal imagination [12], align complete and incomplete views in a shared space [13], construct a stable proxy modality [14], or adapt a pretrained model to missing inputs with a small parameter overhead [15]. Recent work further suppresses missing-input noise through heterogeneous graph denoising for conversational emotion recognition [16]. These strategies have broadened the scope of robust multi-modal learning, but they predominantly address single-label sentiment or emotion tasks and usually treat missingness through imputation, alignment, denoising, or missing-pattern adaptation [17]. They therefore do not resolve the central tension in deployable MMER: the model must preserve distinct evidence for multiple correlated emotions as modalities disappear, while its computational burden should not grow with repeated processing of the full input streams. Robustness, label-specific reasoning, and efficiency remain largely separate design objectives.

This work asks whether MMER can retain class-specific evidence under incomplete input within a compact representation whose deep computation is decoupled from the raw sequence length. We propose MERP (Multi-modal Emotion Recognition Perceiver), which follows the latent-query principle of Perceiver IO [18]: available multi-modal evidence is compressed into a fixed latent workspace before iterative reasoning, and emotion-specific evidence is extracted and reinforced across representation levels. This design supports a single predictor for complete and incomplete inputs while bounding the cost of the deeper computation. As illustrated in Figure 1, MERP replaces input-bound late fusion with fixed-latent, class-specific reasoning under compound text–visual loss.

The main contributions are:

• 

We show that robust MMER should not be framed as recovering an absent modality or assigning a single reliability score to each stream. Our depth-wise diagnostic reveals that repeated full-sequence fusion amplifies missingness and corrupts label evidence unevenly across classes and feature channels; the central design objective is therefore to aggregate available cues into a compact workspace and preserve class-specific evidence throughout deeper reasoning.

• 

We design MERP around a fixed latent bottleneck, cross-level class-specific readouts, prototype-guided noise-gated enhancement, and confidence-aware class-wise fusion. The same predictor handles complete and incomplete inputs while decoupling deeper reasoning from the raw sequence length.

• 

MERP achieves the best micro-F1 under 20% test-time modality drop on CMU-MOSEI (0.563) and M3ED (0.780), leads LDDU throughout $p_{\text{miss}}\!\in\![0,0.5]$ , and avoids its compound-failure collapse, with 5.28 M parameters and 5.28 ms latency on CMU-MOSEI.

## II Related Work

## II-A Multi-Modal Multi-Label Emotion Recognition

Multi-modal multi-label emotion recognition extends categorical emotion recognition by allowing several affective states to coexist in one utterance. Early work explicitly modeled modality-to-label and label-to-label dependencies to exploit this structure [3]. Transformer-based label-set generation subsequently captured label correlations through sequential decoding [19], while HHMPN represented modalities and emotions as a heterogeneous hierarchy and propagated information between them [4]. These approaches established the importance of structured label reasoning, although sequential generation imposes a decoding order and hierarchical message passing repeatedly operates on modality-specific features. TAILOR later separated modality-common and modality-private factors before label-guided decoding [5], and AMP used adversarial masking and perturbation to improve the stability of multi-modal representations [20].

Recent MMER methods place greater emphasis on discriminative label evidence. CARAT combines contrastive learning with feature reconstruction and aggregation [6]; UniVA transfers valence–arousal structure learned from individual modalities [21]; LDDU represents prediction uncertainty through decoupled latent distributions [7]; and HGE models heterogeneous interactions among modalities and labels [22]. Related advances in categorical conversational emotion recognition capture emotion shifts [8] and inter- and intra-speaker dependencies [9], but produce one emotion category per instance. Collectively, these methods improve cross-modal interaction and inter-label discrimination, yet their deep computation remains tied to modality streams, and most do not preserve class-specific evidence under single- and multiple-stream loss. MERP addresses both limitations by conducting repeated reasoning in a fixed latent bank and extracting emotion-specific evidence at successive latent depths.

## II-B Robust Learning with Incomplete Modalities

Robust multi-modal learning under missing inputs has developed along two complementary directions [17]. Recovery-based methods estimate the information carried by an absent stream. SMIL combines Bayesian meta-learning with feature reconstruction for severe missingness [23]; MMIN imagines missing modality representations from the observed streams [12]; and TFR-Net reconstructs missing temporal segments while learning task representations [24]. Recent main-conference approaches use duplex diffusion to reduce modality-dependent recovery bias [25] or structured knowledge extracted by large multi-modal models for training-free, out-of-distribution completion [26]. Such recovery can restore a complete input interface, but the estimated features may propagate cross-modal prediction error to the downstream classifier. It also introduces auxiliary generation and reconstruction paths whose cost and reliability depend on the missing pattern.

Representation-based methods instead encourage observed subsets to remain predictive. MissModal aligns complete and incomplete views through geometric and distributional constraints [13], whereas parameter-efficient adaptation modifies a pretrained multi-modal model with few additional parameters [15]. P-RMF constructs a stable proxy modality to reduce the discrepancy between complete and incomplete samples [14], and contrastive masked autoencoding learns modality-agnostic emotion representations [27]. SimMLM dynamically gates modality experts and regularizes predictions so that additional available modalities do not reduce task performance [28]. More recently, heterogeneous graph denoising has been used to suppress noisy propagation in incomplete multi-modal conversations [16]. These methods substantially improve missing-modality robustness, but they predominantly optimize a global representation for single-label sentiment and emotion prediction; they do not explicitly protect the distinct evidence required by multiple correlated labels. Across this family, training commonly involves simulated missing views, auxiliary completion, and missing-pattern adaptation. MERP uses one predictor for complete and incomplete inputs, avoids synthesizing an absent stream, and maintains class-specific evidence within a shared fixed-size latent space.

## II-C Latent-Space Multi-Modal Fusion

Multi-modal fusion architectures differ chiefly in where cross-modal interaction occurs. MulT applies directional cross-attention between unaligned modality sequences, enabling fine-grained temporal exchange at a cost that grows with pairwise token interactions [11]. Common–private factorization in MISA compresses each modality into invariant and modality-specific components before fusion [29], while VISTANet combines intermediate and late fusion with adaptive modality weighting for interpretable categorical prediction [10]. These designs retain useful modality structure, but their fusion computation remains coupled to the number and length of the input streams.

Latent-bottleneck architectures decouple repeated processing from raw input length. Perceiver IO first cross-attends from a fixed latent array to arbitrary inputs and then performs deep self-attention only among the latent tokens [18]. The Multimodal Bottleneck Transformer similarly restricts audio–visual exchange to a small collection of fusion tokens [30]. Recent robust-fusion methods further model unimodal aleatoric uncertainty [31] and learn an information-bottleneck latent space shared by complete and incomplete inputs [32]. Nevertheless, these architectures target general perception and single-label sentiment tasks and provide no mechanism ensuring that the compact space retains separable evidence for every co-occurring emotion. MERP connects fixed-size latent computation to label-attentive readouts, cross-level consistency, and class-wise fusion, thereby making the bottleneck directly support robust MMER rather than only global multi-modal compression.

## III Preliminary Study

Before introducing MERP, we examine why a multi-modal fusion model trained with complete observations becomes fragile under modality loss. We conduct a controlled diagnostic study with a conventional dense-fusion Transformer, isolating failure patterns of the fusion process from the components introduced in our framework.

## III-A Diagnostic Protocol

Probe model.
We train a six-layer Transformer fusion model on the CMU-MOSEI training split using only complete multi-modal inputs. Text, visual, and acoustic features are independently projected to a common hidden dimension and concatenated into one sequence, followed by six self-attention layers and a multi-label classification head. The probe excludes latent queries, cross-level reconstruction, class prototypes, feature-noise enhancement, and adaptive branch fusion.

All reported diagnostic metrics are computed on the CMU-MOSEI validation split with the probe parameters frozen; the training split is used only to fit the probe and estimate the clean class centroids. For each validation utterance $\mathbf{x}$ , we evaluate the intact input and six corrupted views,

## III-B Findings and Design Implications

Modality loss is amplified with fusion depth.
Figure 2 shows a progressive shift toward lower CKA across all six fusion layers and every corruption pattern. Averaged over the three single-modality drops, CKA decreases from 0.921 at layer 1 to 0.794 at layer 6. When only one modality remains, the decrease is larger, from 0.720 to 0.480. Meanwhile, the unavailable-token attention ratio increases from 1.049 to 1.240 for single-modality drops and from 1.171 to 1.595 for single-retained views. Repeated full-sequence fusion therefore amplifies a local input failure by continually mixing the surviving evidence with positions whose modality content has been removed.

The failure is class-structured and feature-concentrated.

conclusion: This work addresses robust multi-modal multi-label emotion recognition when parts of the multi-modal evidence are unavailable. MERP compresses the cues that remain into a fixed latent workspace and preserves emotion-specific evidence through cross-level readout and reconstruction, prototype-guided noise-gated enhancement, and confidence-aware class-wise fusion. Experiments across two benchmarks and complementary modality-drop settings show that this design achieves leading recognition performance while degrading gracefully under increasingly severe and compound modality loss. These results suggest a broader lesson for robust multi-modal learning: protecting task-relevant evidence after compact aggregation can be more effective than reconstructing missing streams or assigning a single reliability estimate to each modality. Building on this principle, future work can investigate adaptive latent workspaces that retain bounded deep reasoning while supporting evolving label spaces and longer multi-modal contexts.

title: Solving Go under Positional Superko: Sound Proof Transfer and New Board Values
abstract: Positional superko (PSK) forbids recreating any earlier whole-board position. It is part of the Chinese rules as written and of the rules used in computer Go. Yet almost all solved Go boards were computed under a simpler basic-ko rule set. PSK makes solving hard: legality depends on the whole game history, and this breaks the three tools that make solving tractable, namely transposition tables (the graph-history interaction problem), static life-and-death recognition, and safe move pruning. We present Sanko, a parallel depth-first proof-number solver that restores all three soundly. Its core is a cheap proof-transfer theorem: a stored proof stays valid on a new path unless a board that the proof's winner must create has already occurred. Sanko proves 5x5 Go in 16 minutes with six threads, where the previous state of the art needed 5.25 hours with six processes, and in about a minute and a half on one 192-thread machine. It also establishes the first PSK values of twenty-three further boards, eleven of which were unsolved under any rules. Superko changes game-theoretic values: 4x7, a full-board win under basic ko, is worth only 12 points under PSK, and we pinpoint the move at which the previously published optimal line fails. Unlike earlier solutions of empty Go boards, we release the solver source together with the command line and outcome of every run behind our values and measurements, so that all reported values can be reproduced.

body_start:
Abstract

Positional superko (PSK) forbids recreating any earlier whole-board position.
It is part of the Chinese rules as written and of the rules used in computer Go.
Yet almost all solved Go boards were computed under a simpler basic-ko rule set.
PSK makes solving hard: legality depends on the whole game history, and this breaks the three tools that make solving tractable, namely transposition tables (the graph-history interaction problem), static life-and-death recognition, and safe move pruning.
We present Sanko, a parallel depth-first proof-number solver that restores all three soundly.
Its core is a cheap proof-transfer theorem: a stored proof stays valid on a new path unless a board that the proof’s winner must create has already occurred.
Sanko proves $5{\times}5$ Go in 16 minutes with six threads, where the previous state of the art needed 5.25 hours with six processes, and in about a minute and a half on one 192-thread machine.
It also establishes the first PSK values of twenty-three further boards, eleven of which were unsolved under any rules.
Superko changes game-theoretic values: $4{\times}7$ , a full-board win under basic ko, is worth only 12 points under PSK, and we pinpoint the move at which the previously published optimal line fails.
Unlike earlier solutions of empty Go boards, we release the solver source together with the command line and outcome of every run behind our values and measurements, so that all reported values can be reproduced.

## 1 Introduction

Solving games exactly is a long-standing benchmark for search algorithms.
Checkers has been solved Schaeffer et al. (2007), and so have Hex on small boards Henderson et al. (2009) and many smaller games.
For Go, computer proofs exist for many boards up to 30 intersections van der Werf et al. (2003); van der Werf and Winands (2009).
However, these classic Go results were computed under a special-purpose rule set designed to make a position’s value independent of how it was reached.
Specifically, they use the basic ko rule, let a pass lift a ko ban, end a game at a repeated position and score the cycle by its passes van der Werf (2004); van der Werf and Winands (2009).

Superko, the rule that forbids recreating earlier whole-board positions, is part of everyday play.
The Chinese rules forbid recreating any earlier whole-board position Chinese Weiqi Association (1988), the American and New Zealand rules forbid it only with the same player to move (situational superko) AGA Rules Committee (1991); New Zealand Go Society (2017), and computer Go commonly uses the Chinese form, for example in the Tromp–Taylor rules Tromp (1995).
Solving under superko is hard, however, and it has received far less attention than basic ko.
We approach solving Go under said positional superko (PSK), which forbids recreating any earlier whole-board position.
Legality of a move therefore depends on the entire history of the game.
This rule breaks three pillars of game solving:

• 

Transposition tables.
Reusing the result of a position reached along another path becomes unsound.
This is the graph-history interaction (GHI) problem Campbell (1985); Kishimoto and Müller (2004).

• 

Static knowledge.
Benson-style life and territory recognition Benson (1976) assumes that the owner can always capture intruders.
Under PSK those captures may be illegal.

• 

Pruning.
Moves that never help under basic ko, such as filling one’s own eye, can become decisive tempo moves van der Werf (2004).

The cost of losing these advantages is very large.
Even with situational superko, the MIGOS solver needed 1.1 hours for $4{\times}4$ , against 3.3 seconds with basic ko van der Werf et al. (2003). Now, Sanko solves $4{\times}4$ so fast that it no longer suits for performance comparisons.
The first PSK solution of $5{\times}5$ , by Expected Work Search (EWS), took 5.25 hours with six processes Randall et al. (2024), a board we solve in minutes.
Beyond $5{\times}5$ , no board with at least two rows had been solved under PSK.
It was also open whether the basic-ko values carry over.

This paper shows that PSK solving can be both sound and fast.
Our contributions are:

• 

A proof-transfer theorem for PSK (Section 3).
Using the observation that only boards created by a proof’s winner can invalidate it, five small attributes per stored proof allow for soundness-preserving proof reuse under PSK.
Proof-transfer under this theorem cuts search effort by a factor of about 6,000 compared to reusing results only in the identical superko game.

• 

Static knowledge that is sound under PSK (Section 4).
We introduce pure-eye analysis, a variant of Benson’s algorithm that is sound under PSK play-out, prove the two conditions it needs beyond Benson’s classic analysis, and give acyclic local region games.

• 

Sanko, a parallel solver (Section 5).
It runs df-pn on shared lock-free tables, and checks proof identity on 128 bits. We show that the probability of a hash collision is magnitudes below that of hardware errors, even on our largest runs.
We also verify against an oracle with no static knowledge.

• 

New results (Section 6).
 $5{\times}5$ takes 16 minutes on six threads, 20 $\times$ faster than EWS.
We give the first PSK values of $4{\times}5$ , $3{\times}7$ , $3{\times}8$ , $3{\times}9$ , $4{\times}6$ , $4{\times}7$ , $5{\times}6$ , $3{\times}10$ , $2{\times}10$ – $2{\times}15$ and $1{\times}10$ – $1{\times}18$ .
Of these, $3{\times}10$ , $2{\times}12$ – $2{\times}15$ and $1{\times}13$ – $1{\times}18$ were unsolved under any rules. A quick overview shows Figure 1.

• 

A rule-dependent value (Section 7).
 $4{\times}7$ is a full-board win under basic ko (value 28), but is worth only 12 points under PSK.
We locate the move at which the published optimal line van der Werf and Winands (2009) fails.

• 

An open, reproducible artifact (Section 9).
Earlier solutions of empty Go boards were published without their solvers, so none of them can be reproduced independently.
We release the solver source and the exact command line and outcome of every solver run behind our values and measurements.11

The value is Black’s winning margin with optimal play.
Besides $2{\times}2$ , whose superko value was known van der Werf et al. (2003), $4{\times}7$ (framed) is the one board whose value differs from its basic-ko value.
The smaller boards agree with earlier results.
Linear boards from $1{\times}19$ to $1{\times}30$ remain open.

## 2 Background

We use the Chinese rules as written Chinese Weiqi Association (1988), whose repetition ban is the positional superko of EWS Randall et al. (2024).
Black moves first on an $R{\times}C$ board.
A move is a pass or the placement of a stone.
Opponent chains without liberties are captured, and suicide is illegal.
The ban on repeating a whole-board position is positional superko: a stone move may not recreate any board that occurred earlier in the game.
Passes are always legal.
Two consecutive passes end the game, which is scored by area: each player counts their stones plus the empty regions bordered only by their stones.
Where human players agree on dead stones, we play the game out, so stones that remain on the board count as alive.
Under area scoring, playing in ones own territory costs neither side anything, so this does not change any value.
The komi $k$ (a half-integer) is added to White’s score.
The value $v$ of a board is Black’s margin under optimal play.
We establish it with two proofs: a Black win at komi $v-\frac{1}{2}$ and a White win at $v+\frac{1}{2}$ .
A full-board win ( $v=R\cdot C$ ) needs only the first.

MIGOS van der Werf et al. (2003); van der Werf and Winands (2009); van der Werf (2004) formalizes the Chinese rules, but replaces their ban on repeated positions by a basic ko rule and special conventions for cycles, passes and dead stones.

A node is a position together with the history that leads to it.
Under PSK, two nodes with the same position but different histories may have different values.
Proof-number search Allis et al. (1994) treats the game as an AND/OR graph of nodes.
Each node carries a proof number $\phi$ and a disproof number $\delta$ , which estimate the effort to prove or disprove it.
Depth-first proof-number search (df-pn) Nagai (2002) explores the graph with thresholds, with the $1{+}\varepsilon$ refinement of Pawlewicz and Lew (2007).
A transposition table (TT) stores proven and unproven nodes, and its hit rate is what makes large proofs feasible.
An expansion is one call of df-pn’s recursive procedure on a node.
The call generates the legal moves and classifies each child as terminal, static leaf, stored proof, or unproven with initial proof numbers.
It stops early at a child that already proves the node, and then repeatedly descends into the most promising child until the node’s thresholds are exceeded.
Each call counts once, including later calls on a node that was already expanded.
We measure search effort in expansions.
The revisit factor of a search is the number of expansions divided by the number of distinct nodes expanded.
EWS reports the number of nodes in its best-first search tree, and MIGOS counts every node visit of its iterative-deepening search van der Werf and Winands (2009), so the three counts are related but not identical.

Superko has three effects.

• 

Transpositions are unsound.
Two paths to the same board can have different sets of earlier boards.
A ko recapture, or any capture that recreates an earlier board, is legal on one path and illegal on the other, so the two nodes can have different values.
Storing ‘won’ for one path and reusing it on the other is unsound: this is the GHI problem Campbell (1985); Breuker et al. (2001); Kishimoto and Müller (2004).
The safe alternative, keying the table on the position and the set of earlier boards, almost eliminates reuse (Section 6.3).
This is why superko slowed MIGOS down by more than 1,000 $\times$ on $4{\times}4$ van der Werf et al. (2003); Kishimoto and Müller (2004).

• 

Static knowledge from basic ko is unsound.
Benson’s unconditional life Benson (1976) certifies groups that the opponent can never capture.
Claiming their territory however, means the owner must actually capture intruders.
Section 4 shows that superko can forbid those captures.
In addition, a static verdict taken just after the owner’s own pass is wrong, because the opponent can pass and end the game immediately at the current position.

• 

Pruning becomes incomplete.
Under PSK, any board-changing move can make a later capture legal, even filling one’s own eye (a move that is never useful under basic ko).
Section 4 gives an example where this is the only winning move.

## 3 Sound Proof Transfer under Superko

Kishimoto and Müller Kishimoto and Müller (2004); Kishimoto and Müller (2005) solve GHI in general: they re-check, or simulate Kawano (1996), a stored proof on the new path, at a cost that grows with the proof.
We instead give a sufficient condition for reuse under PSK that can be checked in time linear in the path length, independent of the proof’s size.

A history $H$ is the sequence of positions from the empty board to the current node $N$ .
We also write $H$ for its set of boards.
A proof $T$ that player $w$ wins from $N$ is a finite tree.
At $w$ -nodes it picks one move, and at opponent nodes it contains every legal move.
Its leaves are terminal wins for $w$ or certified static wins (Section 4).
We say line for a sequence of consecutive moves from a given position, so a path in the game tree.

Definition 1.

For a proof $T$ of a win for $w$ :

• 

 $B_{w}(T)$ is the set of boards created by $w$ ’s stone moves in $T$ .

• 

 $X(T)$ is the set of boards $b\in H$ that made some opponent move in $T$ illegal (exclusion targets).

• 

 $\mathrm{terr}(T)$ is the union of the territories certified at $T$ ’s static leaves.

• 

 $\mathrm{cap}_{w}(H)$ is the set of points at which a $w$ stone was captured along $H$ .

Theorem 1 (Transfer).

Let $T$ prove that $w$ wins from $N$ under history $H$ .
Then $T$ also proves that $w$ wins from $N$ under any history $H^{\prime}$ that satisfies

(i) 

 $B_{w}(T)\cap H^{\prime}=\emptyset$ ,

(ii) 

 $X(T)\subseteq H^{\prime}$ ,

(iii) 

 $\mathrm{cap}_{w}(H^{\prime})\cap\mathrm{terr}(T)=\emptyset$ .

Proof sketch.

Induction over $T$ (full proof in Appendix A).
The line inside $T$ is the same under $H$ and $H^{\prime}$ .
Only the prefix differs.

• 

A stone move of $w$ creates a board $b\in B_{w}(T)$ .
That board was not in $H$ or on the line, because the move was legal.
By (i) it is not in $H^{\prime}$ either, so the move stays legal.

• 

An opponent move that is legal under $H^{\prime}$ but was illegal under $H$ must recreate a board of $H\setminus H^{\prime}$ .
Such a board would lie in $X(T)$ , which (ii) rules out.
So the opponent gains no new options.
Opponent moves that become illegal only remove options.

• 

Terminal scores do not depend on the history.
Static leaves need their own history condition (Lemma 1), and (iii) supplies it on the new prefix.

∎

The theorem is asymmetric, in that only the winner’s boards matter.
If the loser would recreate a board of $H^{\prime}$ , that merely removes a losing option, and the proof survives (Figure 2).
Proofs are stored in negamax form, each for its own winner, so the theorem covers wins of both players.

Both histories start at the empty board $\varnothing$ .
A board that occurs both on $H^{\prime}$ and in $T$ (dashed) makes $T$ invalid only if the winner creates it in $T$ , because that winner move becomes illegal.

The exact sets are too large to store.
Each proof entry instead carries conservative summaries that compose bottom-up.
A won node takes its winning child’s attributes plus the board its winning move creates, and a lost node takes the join of all children:

• 

a 64-bit Bloom filter Bloom (1970) of the canonical hashes of $B_{w}(T)$ ,

• 

the stones common to all boards of $B_{w}(T)$ , and their minimum stone count,

• 

the territory bitboard,
