a flag that marks proofs with an exclusion target.

A strict ancestor board $a\in H^{\prime}$ can lie in $B_{w}(T)$ only if it hits the Bloom filter, contains the common stones, and has at least the minimum number of stones.
If any of these fails, (i) holds for $a$ (Algorithm 1).
Condition (iii) is checked exactly against the capture bitboard of the current path.
Condition (ii) holds because every proof with an exclusion target is stored path-specifically and is never transferred, so a transferred proof has $X(T)=\emptyset$ .
Path-specific proofs live under a twin key, the position key combined with a non-linear hash of the set of earlier boards, and are reused only on the identical board with an identical set, which the solver recognizes by two independent such hashes.
Note that an XOR of Zobrist keys Zobrist (1990) is not a sound set identifier.
Base entries are written once, and a proof without an exclusion target that finds its base slot taken by another path’s proof goes to one of two alternate slots, where any path can reuse it through Algorithm 1.
Canonical hashing makes the test invariant under the board’s symmetries.
Sibling moves are merged only under symmetries that map every board on the path onto itself.

## 4 Static Knowledge under Superko

Leaves that end the search before the game ends are essential: on $5{\times}5$ , kill-all proofs would otherwise run through every mop-up capture.
Under PSK and play-out scoring they need two corrections.

Let $w$ be a player and $o$ the opponent.
A region is a maximal connected set of non- $w$ points.
A region $E$ is a pure eye of a $w$ -chain $K$ if every point of $E$ , empty or occupied by $o$ , is adjacent to $K$ .
Let $X^{*}$ be the largest set of $w$ -chains in which each chain has two pure eyes bordered only by chains of $X^{*}$ .
Let $T^{*}$ be the union of the regions bordered only by $X^{*}$ in which every point is adjacent to $X^{*}$ .
We call $X^{*}$ and $T^{*}$ the pure-eye analysis.
It follows Benson’s fixpoint Benson (1976) but replaces ‘vital’ by ‘pure’, and together with the conditions of Lemma 1 it is sound under PSK play-out.

Lemma 1 (Static leaves under PSK).

Suppose (C1) no $w$ stone was ever captured on a point of $T^{*}$ during the history, and (C2) the last move was not a pass by $w$ with $o$ to move.
Then $w$ can enforce a final area of at least $|X^{*}|+|T^{*}|$ .

Proof sketch.

The winner follows the strategy $\sigma$ : if an $o$ stone lies in $T^{*}$ , play on a liberty of an $o$ -chain there, and otherwise pass.

conclusion:
The factors in Table 3 multiply.
Proof transfer is by far the largest of them. It restores most of the reuse that superko takes away.
The learned prior and the region solver cut the remaining tree by factors of 4.7 and 2.3.
The region solver helps most in kill-all positions, where proofs would otherwise play out every capture.
Shared-table parallelism adds a factor of 42 on 192 threads, because proofs found by one thread are immediately visible to all others, at the cost of 2.4 times as many expansions.

On every board where both rule sets have a value, the values agree except on $2{\times}2$ , whose superko value MIGOS already reported, and on $4{\times}7$ .
The disagreement does not come from an error in either search.
It comes from rules that matter only at the very end of a game, namely what a pass does to a ko ban, and how many passes end the game.
Values computed under conventions that make repetition harmless should therefore not be quoted as values of superko Go without checking.
Superko also produces strategies with no basic-ko counterpart, such as the eye-filling sacrifice on $1{\times}12$ .

A claimed value rests on the following:

• 

the soundness arguments for transfer, static leaves and pruning (Theorems 1, 1 and A),

• 

differential testing against an oracle with no static knowledge, on the claimed boards themselves,

• 

independent re-solves.

Each claim uses only proofs that are trusted for the reported winner.
Because pruning is applied only to the side being proven, a failed proof is reported as unknown, never as a win for the opponent.

Larger boards split naturally: the $5{\times}6$ upper bound decomposes into ten independent subproblems, one per first move of Black, which can run on separate machines.
Extrapolating Figure 6, $6{\times}6$ would need about $10^{14}$ expansions or more, about 50 days on one of our machines, and boards above 30 points need position keys wider than 64 bits to stay exact.
Stronger knowledge would cut this further.
Our learned prior is a first step, and a stronger model, as in learned solvers Wu et al. (2023), may cut much more.

title: From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context?
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied across the scientific discovery pipeline, from synthesizing literature to generating hypotheses to informing experimental design. A unifying principle behind these tasks is the need to continuously update beliefs as evidence accumulates, for which Bayesian inference provides a natural framework. However, existing work assumes that LLMs cannot carry out principled Bayesian belief updating in context, instead relying on simplifications and heuristics. To challenge this assumption, we present a principled evaluation of Bayesian reasoning capabilities in LLMs, analyzing both the model's internal consistency as well as its ability to recover an externally determined posterior. Specifically, we build an evaluation framework spanning qualitative epistemological examples to probe probabilistic coherence, quantitative benchmarks of Bayesian inference capabilities, and analyses of the impact of non-Bayesian updates on downstream task performance. Across different scenarios, we find that LLMs generally violate Bayes' rule when updating their beliefs in context. However, when equipped with modern reasoning abilities and code execution capabilities, their performance drastically improves, enabling even the close approximation of analytically intractable posteriors. Our evaluation shows that current LLMs with access to appropriate tools could already be used to make complex belief updates in scientific discovery, enabling rapid acceleration of the efficiency and scale of AI-powered scientific discovery.

## From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context?

body_start:
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied across the scientific discovery pipeline, from synthesizing literature to generating hypotheses to informing experimental design. A unifying principle behind these tasks is the need to continuously update beliefs as evidence accumulates, for which Bayesian inference provides a natural framework. However, existing work assumes that LLMs cannot carry out principled Bayesian belief updating in context, instead relying on simplifications and heuristics. To challenge this assumption, we present a principled evaluation of Bayesian reasoning capabilities in LLMs, analyzing both the model’s internal consistency as well as its ability to recover an externally determined posterior. Specifically, we build an evaluation framework spanning qualitative epistemological examples to probe probabilistic coherence, quantitative benchmarks of Bayesian inference capabilities, and analyses of the impact of non-Bayesian updates on downstream task performance. Across different scenarios, we find that LLMs generally violate Bayes’ rule when updating their beliefs in context. However, when equipped with modern reasoning abilities and code execution capabilities, their performance drastically improves, enabling even the close approximation of analytically intractable posteriors. Our evaluation shows that current LLMs with access to appropriate tools could already be used to make complex belief updates in scientific discovery, enabling rapid acceleration of the efficiency and scale of AI-powered scientific discovery.

## 1 Introduction

LLMs are rapidly moving from passive tools for retrieving and summarizing scientific information toward active components of the scientific workflow. Recent systems use LLMs to generate hypotheses, synthesize literature, write and execute code, design experiments, interpret results, and even assemble full research papers (Lu et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025; Reddy and Shojaee, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). This trend has motivated the broader vision of “AI scientists”: autonomous or semi-autonomous agents that participate in the iterative production of scientific knowledge rather than merely assisting with isolated subtasks.

A central requirement for such agents is the ability to rationally revise beliefs in light of evidence, iteratively reallocating probability to hypotheses which best explain current experimental results (Howson and Urbach, 2006; Sprenger and Hartmann, 2019). However, current AI-scientist systems typically take a significant shortcut, which strongly limits their potential performance: They evaluate hypotheses through task-specific heuristics or experimental scores, rather than by maintaining and updating probabilistic beliefs over competing hypotheses (Song et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025).

Bayesian inference provides a natural framework to satisfy this requirement. It enables both explicit incorporation of the extensive prior knowledge LLMs possess and information-theoretically optimal belief updates when presented with new evidence (Robert, 1994). Using non-Bayesian belief updating rules risks introducing logical incoherence and biases into the AI scientist’s scientific reasoning (Howson and Urbach, 2006). This allows overreacting to noisy experimental anomalies or prematurely discarding valid hypotheses (Jaynes, 2003). An ideal AI scientist must therefore be capable of performing Bayesian inference to correctly update its beliefs when presented with complex evidence. This requirement exposes a critical research question for the development of LLM-driven research agents: To what extent can LLMs perform or approximate Bayesian inference in context?

Figure 1: Overview of our evaluation framework for In-Context Bayesian Inference We present our three axes of evaluation, using example task: ”Who will win the World Cup - Brazil, France, Germany, or Italy?”. Left: Probabilistic Coherence, evaluated using Dutch-Book scenarios in the same chat and across conversations to find violations of probability axioms. Middle: Posterior Fidelity, as KL divergence between LLM posterior and Bayesian oracle. Right: Downstream Task Performance, assessing how non-Bayesian updates affect success in Experimental Design.

To answer this question, we evaluate LLMs along three progressive axes: probabilistic coherence of their beliefs, tested via Dutch-Book constructions (Ramsey, 1926) that expose violations of probability axioms; posterior fidelity, measured as divergence of model-generated distributions from a Bayesian oracle; and downstream task performance in adaptive experimental design, to determine whether non-Bayesian drift has practical consequences. We use two complementary environments, 20 Questions for internal consistency and our new ProteinWorld framework for recovery of externally determined posteriors, and vary model release year, reasoning, and code execution to isolate which factors drive Bayesian capabilities.

Our main contributions can be summed up as follows:

• 

A principled evaluation of the extent to which LLMs can approximate Bayesian inference in context, covering internal consistency and recovery of externally determined posteriors.

• 

ProteinWorld, a highly configurable environment that mimics scientific discovery and explicitly benchmarks iterative Bayesian inference.

• 

Evidence that LLMs violate Bayes’ rule without reasoning, but that modern reasoning models compute externally determined posteriors exactly, remain consistent over 10+ data points, and, with tools, correctly approximate intractable posteriors, potentially rendering current belief-updating harnesses unnecessary and enabling more capable AI scientists.

## 2 Related Work

Bayesian inference in LLMs

There exist some previous approaches looking at in-context Bayesian inference of LLMs. Purpose-trained Transformers can indeed approximate Bayesian inference in context (Müller et al., 2022; Panwar et al., 2024; Reuter et al., 2025; Agarwal et al., 2025). For general-purpose LLMs, ICL has been cast as implicit Bayesian inference over latent task concepts (Xie et al., 2022). However, they have been found to violate exchangeability (Falck et al., 2024), weight evidence by its position in context (Kossen et al., 2024), and being Bayesian only in expectation over context orderings (Chlon et al., 2026). We continue in this line of work by evaluating explicitly stated belief distributions of general purpose LLMs and asking if capabilities like reasoning or tools can serve to close the non-Bayesian gap.

Probabilistic coherence and calibration

Before looking at the quality of LLM-based belief updates, it is important to clarify whether LLMs can work with probabilities. Goldstein (2024) argues that LLM-sampled linguistic probabilities preclude ideal rationality, and Zhu and Griffiths (2024) find incoherent judgments empirically, though only in two-event toy settings, with further coherence audits emerging recently (Matta et al., 2026; Yamin et al., 2026; Freedman and Toni, 2025; Li and Sreedhar, 2026). Calibration work instead scores stated confidences against outcomes (Lin et al., 2022; Kadavath et al., 2022; Tian et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2024; Halawi et al., 2024; Karger et al., 2025), an external and orthogonal criterion. We test coherence only so that violations reflect failures of internal logic rather than world knowledge, and contrast cross- with single-dialogue elicitation, a dimension largely absent from prior work.

Measuring belief updates against a Bayesian oracle

Some previous work looks at the quality of LLM-based belief updates. Existing evaluations differ in where the reference posterior originates. With a fully specified generative process, the reference is exact: biased-coin sequences (Gupta et al., 2025), verbal probabilistic reasoning problems (Jin et al., 2023; Nafar et al., 2025; Schrader et al., 2024), and, concurrent with our work, multi-turn environments with closed-form references (Samanta et al., 2026). Our work introduces ProteinWorld, which adds out-of-distribution procedural worlds, engineered analytical intractability over continuous latent attributes, and a downstream metric to analyze cost of deviations. Absent a ground-truth model, the reference must be built from the model’s own quantities: Patania et al. (2024) score 20Q updates via proxies such as falsely retained hypotheses, while Chen et al. (2026) measure KL divergence against products of self-elicited priors and likelihoods over four fixed hypotheses. We expand on this by analyzing the self-consistency paradigm with an open, dynamically evolving hypothesis and experiment space.

Improving belief updates

Due to the assumption of low-quality belief updates, previous work has either utilized strict harnesses (Arnould et al., 2026) or finetuning (Qiu et al., 2026) to force Bayesian updates in sequential tasks. The harnessed approach is exemplified by Choudhury et al. (2026), the work most closely related to ours, since we build directly on their 20Q protocol. We differ from this line of work by evaluating the premise itself, and treating access to reasoning and code execution as the intervention.

## 3 Background

Bayesian inference

A key capability of a Bayesian agent is Bayesian inference: the process of updating beliefs over a set of hypotheses $\Theta$ in light of new evidence. In scientific discovery, evidence arrives sequentially (Rainforth et al., 2024): starting from a prior $p_{0}$ , the agent performs experiments $\xi_{i}$ , observes outcomes $y_{i}$ , and accumulates a history $h_{1:k}$ with $h_{i}=(\xi_{i},y_{i})$ . Given a likelihood model $p(y\mid\theta,\xi)$ specifying how probable outcome $y$ is under hypothesis $\theta$ and experiment $\xi$ , Bayes’ rule (Bayes, 1763) yields the posterior after the $k$ -th experiment: The posterior after experiment $k-1$ serves as the prior for experiment $k$ , and assuming outcomes are conditionally independent given $\theta$ and the experiment, the update takes the form

 $p_{k}(\theta):=p(\theta\mid h_{1:k})\propto p(y_{k}\mid\theta,\xi_{k})\,p_{k-1}(\theta)\propto p_{0}(\theta)\prod_{i=1}^{k}p(y_{i}\mid\theta,\xi_{i}).\vskip-5.69046pt$ 

(1)

While this is a closed-form equation in principle, finding a solution is often analytically intractable in practical settings, due to the complex structure of $p(y\mid\theta,\xi)$ or $\Theta$ in the normalizing integral. It therefore remains a challenging problem, making an analysis of current LLM capabilities in solving it interesting since it goes beyond basic mathematical calculations.

We analyze the posterior distribution over $\Theta$ generated by the LLM either through verbalization (Tian et al., 2023) or by using token-logprobs when being passed prior and experimental data in context. We denote these LLM-elicited probabilities as $p_{\text{LLM}}^{k}:=p_{\text{LLM}}(\theta\mid h_{1:k})$ , and compare the distribution to the rational Bayesian posterior $p_{\text{oracle}}^{k}$ calculated following Eq. 1.

Dutch Books

If an agent’s beliefs over $\Theta$ are inconsistent with core probability axioms, they can be exploited via a Dutch Book. A Dutch Book is a collection of simultaneous bets formed from an agent’s stated subjective probabilities that yields a guaranteed loss, regardless of the realized outcome (Ramsey, 1926). This relies on the fair-price assumption: if the agent assigns probability $q_{j}=p(H_{j})$ to event $H_{j}$ , then they should be willing to buy a unit contract paying $1$ if $H_{j}$ occurs and $0$ otherwise for at most $q_{j}$ , or sell it for at least $q_{j}$ (de Finetti, 1937).

Beyond the formal definition in App. C.1, consider the simple example $\Theta=\{A,B\}$ with disjoint events $H_{1}=A$ and $H_{2}=B$ , and suppose the agent assigns $q_{1}=0.6$ and $q_{2}=0.5$ . Selling the agent a unit contract on both those events yields a guaranteed net loss, since it pays $1.1$ up front, while receiving exactly $1$ in the end. In this case, the probabilities sum to $1.1$ , violating Kolmogorov’s normalization axiom (Kolmogorov, 1933). More generally, the existence of Dutch Books in declared beliefs is directly equivalent to the violation of one of Kolmogorov’s core axioms (Vineberg, 2022; Lehman, 1955; Kemeny, 1955), making them an appropriate tool to check whether stated beliefs can even be interpreted as a probability distribution.

Experimental Design

Experimental design addresses the question of which experiment $\xi$ out of a set of available experiments $\Xi$ an agent should perform next to learn as much as possible about its hypotheses. The Bayesian approach frames the choice of experiment as a decision problem: given current beliefs $p(\theta)$ over $\Theta$ , the agent should select the experiment $\xi\in\Xi$ that maximizes the expected utility of its outcome (Lindley, 1956; Chaloner and Verdinelli, 1995). Following Lindley (1956), the canonical utility is the information gained about $\theta$ , leading to the Expected Information Gain (EIG), which can equivalently be written as the expected reduction in entropy over the hypotheses or over the experimental outcomes:

 $\operatorname{EIG}(\xi)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p(y\mid\xi)}\!\left[\mathrm{H}\!\left[p(\theta)\right]-\mathrm{H}\!\left[p(\theta\mid\xi,y)\right]\right]\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim p(\theta)}\!\left[\mathrm{H}\!\left[p(y\mid\xi)\right]-\mathrm{H}\!\left[p(y\mid\xi,\theta)\right]\right]$ 

(2)

In sequential or adaptive experimental design, this selection step is interleaved with belief updating: Given a hidden ground truth $\theta^{\star}$ , the agent chooses the maximally informative experiment $\xi_{k}$ based on its current beliefs $p_{k-1}(\theta)$ , observes the outcome $y_{k}\sim p(\cdot\mid\theta^{\star},\xi_{k})$ , updates its beliefs to $p_{k}(\theta\mid h_{1:k})$ , and repeats (Ryan et al., 2016; Rainforth et al., 2024). This iterative loop of design, observation, and inference formalizes the scientific discovery process, and its efficiency depends critically on the quality of belief updates made by the agent: since the EIG is computed under the agent’s current beliefs, belief updates propagate directly into future experiment choices, potentially degrading performance long-term. Since Bayesian updating is optimal here (Wald, 1947; Zellner, 1988), running this loop with an LLM agent against a Bayesian oracle lets us quantify belief divergence and resulting cost in discovery performance.

## 4 Methodology

The goal of our work is to answer the central research question posed in Sec. 1: To what extent can LLMs perform or approximate Bayesian inference in context? Answering this question requires more than a single accuracy metric, since in-context belief updates can fail in qualitatively different ways. We therefore evaluate in-context Bayesian inference along three progressive axes that span from foundational probability theory to practical application.

## 4.1 Probabilistic Coherence

A necessary prerequisite to interpreting the outputs of an LLM as posterior distributions is that they are coherent with the basic laws of probability theory. If a model assigns mutually inconsistent probabilities, or fails to define a valid distribution over hypotheses, any direct comparison to a Bayesian oracle becomes conceptually limited. As discussed in Sec. 3, the existence of Dutch Books is directly equivalent to beliefs being incoherent. We use binary judgmental forecast questions from ForecastBench (Karger et al., 2025) (June 21, 2026 version) about future political, economic, technological, and social events as basis to elicit probabilities. Each binary ForecastBench question is interpreted as an event $A\subseteq\Theta$ within a broader outcome space $\Theta$ . For example, the question “Will Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse get a $95$ % or higher on Rotten Tomatoes?” defines the event $A=\{\theta^{\star}\geq 95\}$ , where $\theta^{\star}$ denotes the eventual Rotten Tomatoes Rating. We elicit probabilities for collections of related events, checking for violations of extensionality, normalization, and monotonicity. The precise Dutch Book constructions for each violation type is in App. C.2.

We consider two elicitation settings. First, we query each event independently in a separate chat. This setting tests whether the model’s responses across independent interactions can be represented by a single coherent probability distribution. Second, we elicit the same set of probabilities jointly within a single chat, checking the weaker hypothesis of the model maintaining probabilistic coherence within one context. Fig. 1 (left) illustrates one example of this procedure.

## 4.2 Sequential belief updating

Following probabilistic coherence, we move to the scientific discovery loop from Sec. 3. Since the rational posterior is only well-defined relative to a prior $p_{0}$ , we fix that externally. In practice, $p_{0}$ could be derived from existing literature; for evaluating belief updates, it is only important that all agents share the same $p_{0}$ . We run three trajectories: We use the LLM to update beliefs ${p}^{\,k}_{\text{LLM}}$ and choose experiments. Then, we compute a passive oracle trajectory based on this run: $p^{\,k}_{\text{ora-pas}}$ is obtained by applying Eq. 1 with $p_{0}$ and the experimental results of the first runs. A rational agent ought to hold this belief state given the model’s evidence. Third, we let an active Bayesian agent update beliefs $p^{\,k}_{\text{ora-act}}$ using Eq. 1 and choose experiments based on those beliefs.

Posterior fidelity

Given the trajectories $p^{k}_{\text{LLM}}$ and $p^{\,k}_{\text{ora-pas}}$ , we analyze whether the LLM moves its beliefs as the evidence warrants, following the principles of Bayesian inference. We compare the two distributions directly, using the KL divergence (Kullback and Leibler, 1951):

Are LLM-elicited beliefs probabilistically coherent?

Figure 2: Share of elicited probability judgments that are Dutch Bookable under cross-conversation and within-dialogue elicitation. While beliefs elicited across different conversations frequently violate normalization (N), monotonicity (M), and extensionality (E), stronger LLMs are mostly coherent in the within-dialogue setting.

App. E.1 shows Dutch Books constructed from judgments elicited across separate conversations, demonstrating that such judgments need not be jointly representable by a single probability measure. Fig. 2 shows that this depends strongly on the elicitation setting. Across conversations, violation rates exceed 50% of the 30 scenarios for almost all model-constraint combinations. Access to the preceding judgments therefore appears sufficient to enforce consistency, suggesting that cross-conversation incoherence reflects the absence of a persistent common representation rather than an inability to apply elementary probability rules.

Result 1. 
When probabilities are elicited within a single dialogue, modern reasoning LLMs generally satisfy basic probability axioms, and their outputs can be treated as evaluations from a coherent probability distribution within the scope of these tests.

While these tests do not establish universal within-dialogue coherence, they suffice for what follows: In our scientific-discovery setting, the model receives hypotheses, priors, and evidence in one dialogue and returns a posterior in that same context. The strong within-dialogue performance observed therefore supports treating the outputs as valid probability assignments.

Abstract

How do LLM agents’ strategies differ, and how much can instructions to adopt a persona change their behavior over a game? We study these questions with AgentMonopoly, an environment where agents communicate, buy and trade properties, and make decisions that affect later turns. We compare models from four families, each at two sizes, in games with identical models, different sizes of the same family, or different families. We also assign one agent a persona, a description of how it should behave, intended to change a tendency observed in games without that persona. The tested models differ in how often they trade, waive rent, and manage cash and properties. Larger models do not consistently win more games. Persona instructions change the words agents use and some of their actions, but the changes do not always match the role across all decisions. These results show why persona following should be assessed through actions and outcomes as well as language. As our findings are conditional on the tested checkpoints, prompts, and five seeds per configuration, the open-source nature of AgentMonopoly provides the experimental infrastructure for further extending these comparisons. Our code is available at: AgentMonopoly

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as autonomous or semi-autonomous agents that can perceive an environment, make decisions, use tools, and communicate with humans or other artificial agents. As these systems move from isolated question answering toward multi-agent settings, their behavior may depend not only on their individual objectives, but also on assigned social roles, communication structures, group composition, and the strategies adopted by other agents. Such interactions can produce cooperation, negotiation, competition, persuasion, coalition formation, deception, and collusion. These behaviors are difficult to understand through conventional single-agent benchmarks, which typically evaluate an LLM independently and do not capture the social and strategic dynamics that emerge when multiple agents interact over time.

Figure 1: Examples of communication and actions in AgentMonopoly.

In this paper, our research centers on three questions about these interactions. First, how do models differ in trading, rent waiving, and cash and property management under the same rules? Second, how do game outcomes vary with model size, and encountered opponents? Third, when an agent receives a persona intended to change an observed tendency, how do its words and actions differ from those of opponents without that persona?

To study these questions, we develop AgentMonopoly, an environment in which LLM agents communicate and play Monopoly. Purchases, trades, and rent payments change the cash and properties available for later turns, so an agent’s decisions also affect its opponents’ choices. AgentMonopoly records messages, private explanations, executed actions, and game outcomes, allowing us to compare what agents say with what they do over a game (Fig. 1). Its open-source implementation supports reproducing and extending these comparisons.

Using this environment, we evaluate four model families at two sizes each in four-player games. Games with identical models establish behavior under a shared prompt. Games combining different sizes of the same family or different families compare outcomes against different opponents, and we examine win counts by position in the turn order. In persona games, one agent receives a persona selected to change a tendency observed in games without that persona. Its three opponents use the same model without the additional persona instruction.

These comparisons yield three main findings:

• 

The tested models differ in their patterns of behavior.
Under the shared prompt, models differ in how often they trade, waive rent, and manage cash and properties. Some trading patterns appear at both tested sizes, while rent-waiving behavior can differ substantially within a model family.

• 

Larger model scale does not necessarily translate into better strategic performance.
Increasing model size does not consistently improve game performance. Smaller models can outperform larger counterparts, and outcomes vary across opponent configurations.

• 

Persona assignment does not ensure agreement between words and actions.
Persona instructions change language and some actions, yet decisions can still conflict with stated priorities. As an example, Mistral’s “Conservative” agent considers buying a property to complete a color group but declines the $400 purchase to preserve cash. It then joins the auction and buys the same property for $420 while describing its approach as cautious. This illustrates why persona following should be assessed through actions and outcomes as well as language.

## 2 Related Work

## Social and strategic interaction.

Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023) and Concordia (Vezhnevets et al., 2023) offer ways to simulate agents in social settings. Game studies examine rationality (Fan et al., 2024), repeated interaction (Akata et al., 2025), and collaboration and competition in Avalon (Lan et al., 2024). SOTOPIA (Zhou et al., 2024) evaluates agents pursuing social goals, while NegotiationArena (Bianchi et al., 2024) studies bargaining and tactics in tasks involving resource sharing, trading, and price negotiation. Our interest is likewise in social interaction among agents. We examine communication, trading, and rent waiving in repeated multi-player games, where agreements change what players own and what they can afford later.

## Monopoly: social versus financial perspectives.

FinBoardBench (Hu et al., 2026) evaluates dynamic financial decision-making in Cashflow, Acquire, and also in Monopoly. It analyzes cash management, investment, negotiation, and auctions to assess whether decisions and interactions lead to financial success. AgentMonopoly focuses on social interaction, with three differences in emphasis: (1) we characterize communication, trade proposals and responses, and rent waiving; (2) we assign personas intended to change observed behavior, comparing persona agents with same-model opponents without personas; and (3) we examine whether stated priorities agree with actions under these personas. FinBoardBench assesses interactions primarily through their financial consequences and does not report this persona comparison. Our game-outcome comparisons across model sizes and opponents provide context for these interaction patterns.

## Personas and behavior.

Ou et al. (2025) study social preferences and behavior under personas in trust games. PERIL (Licato and Steinle, 2025) studies how persona descriptions can be converted into rules for choosing moves in a strategic board game, including a method that uses a personality questionnaire as an intermediate step. In AgentMonopoly, the LLM itself chooses an action and produces a message at each decision point. This lets us compare its words and actions throughout the game. Wang et al. (2026) keep the available decisions the same across different investigation-game stories. They find that personas guide behavior more consistently across stories when the descriptions refer to concrete actions. Their analysis focuses on actions across stories. We keep the game setting fixed and examine both language and actions while opponents respond to each other and earlier purchases and trades affect later options.

Table 1 summarizes these differences. We study how interactions vary across models and how personas are reflected in words and actions during repeated competition.

## 3 Research Questions

We organize the analysis around three questions:

• 

RQ1 (Behavioral patterns). Under the same prompt and game rules, how do the tested models differ in trading, rent waiving, and cash and property management? Which patterns appear at both tested model sizes?

• 

RQ2 (Behavior and performance). How do game outcomes vary with model size and the opponents in a game? Do win counts differ by player position in the turn order?

• 

RQ3 (Persona following). When an agent receives a persona intended to change its baseline behavior, how do its language and actions differ from those of its opponents without that persona?

A behavioral profile summarizes the actions measured under a particular game setup. Persona control refers to how well instructions guide an agent’s behavior. Using words associated with a persona does not, by itself, show that the agent follows it in its decisions. We do not treat these profiles as fixed personalities, or generated explanations as direct evidence of intent.

## 4 Experimental Setup

## Environment and outcomes.

AgentMonopoly supports up to six players. All experiments reported here use four agents on a fixed 40-square Monopoly board, with street names replaced by names from Oldenburg (see Fig.6 in Appendix A). Random dice rolls and card events affect play. Agents buy properties, bid at auctions, trade, build, and manage cash. Owners can waive rent, and a player is eliminated when its cash balance becomes negative. Games end when only one player remains or at the 150-step limit. At the limit, the player with the highest net worth wins. These rule changes affect which strategies succeed. Renaming the streets does not rule out familiarity with Monopoly from training.

## Agent interface.

The engine tracks the game and applies its rules. At each decision point, the acting agent receives the rules, its assigned role, current game information, the type of decision, and the allowed actions. It returns a private explanation, a public message, and a proposed action. The engine checks actions before carrying them out and separately records outputs that have the wrong format or break the rules. It also logs public messages and changes to the game. We use private reasoning to refer to the generated explanation hidden from opponents. This text does not directly reveal how the model computes its decision.

## Shared prompt.

All experiments use the same base prompt. It asks agents to outsmart opponents, encourages bluffing, and explicitly allows strategic rent waiving. It also prohibits public messages that contradict the action taken. Observed bluffing and rent waiving must therefore be interpreted in light of these instructions. Using the same prompt supports comparisons within the study, but does not show how the models would behave under a neutral prompt. Appendix A.2 gives the available excerpts.

## Models and repeated games.

We evaluate models with publicly available weights from Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025), DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025), Gemma (Team et al., 2026), and Mistral11
 1

 https://huggingface.co/mistralai. We test two size groups: approximately 24–32 billion and 8–12 billion parameters. These groups describe the tested model versions; similar parameter counts do not imply equal capabilities across families. Differences in training and model design also affect the comparison. Models run locally at temperature $0.0$ . Each configuration uses five random seeds, 42–46, which set the starting point for random-number generation. Appendix A.3 lists model names and the details needed to repeat the experiments.

## Game configurations.

We use four configurations, summarized in Table 3(Appendix A.3).

1. 

Same-model games (S1). All four players use the same model version. We run five games for each family and size to measure baseline behavior for RQ1.

2. 

Mixed-size games (S2). Two players use a larger model and two use a smaller model from the same family. The intended design swaps the sizes assigned to earlier and later positions in the turn order across two settings, giving ten games per family. These games compare outcomes by size for RQ2.

3. 

Cross-family games (S3). One agent from each family plays within the same size group. We rotate the player order through four arrangements so that each family plays first once, with five seeds per arrangement. These games measure performance against other model families.

4. 

Persona games (S4). One larger-model agent at the first position (P1) receives a persona intended to change its baseline behavior. The other three players use the same model and base prompt without that persona. We test each family–persona pair with five seeds.

The personas are Zen for Qwen, Independent for DeepSeek, Diplomatic for Gemma, and Conservative for Mistral. They ask agents to propose fewer trades, rely less on other players, interact more with others, and keep more cash, respectively (Table 2). We selected them after examining baseline behavior. Since each family receives a different persona, we cannot separate the effect of the persona from how a particular model responds to it.

## Measurements and comparisons.

For RQ1, we measure trade proposals per 100 dice rolls, the share of received offers accepted, how often agents waive rent, and how they manage cash and properties. For RQ2, we count wins by model size, family, and position in the turn order. For RQ3, we compare the persona agent with its three opponents in the same games. We measure persona-related words, message length, trading, properties and buildings held, and minimum cash balance. The opponents occupy different positions and may respond to the persona agent. The comparison therefore reflects the persona instructions, how the game unfolds, and how opponents respond. Actions within a game affect one another, so many recorded actions do not replace the need for more independent games. Appendix A.4 describes the measures and flags details that still need verification.

## 5 Results

## 5.1 RQ1: Behavioral patterns under shared rules

Fig. 2 compares the same-model games. Each behavioral profile summarizes a tested model’s actions in these games. It does not establish a fixed personality or show that the model would behave the same way in other settings.

Figure 2: Behavior in same-model games: (a) trade proposals per 100 dice rolls, (b) acceptance of received trade offers, and (c) rent-waiver rate. Each dot represents a game, with five games per model version. Size labels identify the tested models; similar sizes do not imply equal capabilities across families.

## Qwen: frequent trading at both sizes.

Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-8B make 110 and 94 trade proposals per 100 dice rolls, respectively, with acceptance rates of 58% and 76%. Multiple proposals can occur between rolls, so the proposal rate can exceed 100. Qwen proposes trades most often at both sizes and accepts a relatively high share of offers. Rent waiving, however, differs sharply: the 32B model waives rent in 25% of rent decisions, whereas the 8B model waives none in these games. Both models trade frequently, but they differ in how they collect rent.

## DeepSeek: frequent proposals with selective acceptance.

DeepSeek-R1-32B and DeepSeek-R1-8B make 90 and 74 proposals per 100 dice rolls. Their acceptance rates are 53% and 33%; the smaller model has the lowest acceptance rate among the smaller models. Their rent-waiver rates are 11% and 59%. The smaller model therefore accepts a lower share of offers while waiving rent more often. Its generated explanations sometimes describe keeping opponents in the game for future interaction. These explanations do not verify why the model waived rent.

## Mistral: high acceptance, but different proposal rates.

Mistral has the highest trade-acceptance rate in each size group: 67% for Mistral-Small-24B and 86% for Mistral-Nemo-12B. Their proposal rates differ substantially, at 65 and 18 per 100 rolls. Rent-waiver rates also differ, at 3% and 54%. The larger model often uses generous language but rarely waives rent. This shows why several actions need to be examined: generous words or frequent acceptance of trades do not show consistent generosity across decisions.

## Gemma: few proposals, but different rent decisions.

The models labeled Gemma4-26B and Gemma4-12B make 33 and 1.5 proposals per 100 dice rolls, the lowest rates in their size groups. Their acceptance rates are 17% and 55%, and their rent-waiver rates are 37% and 3%. Both propose relatively few trades, but they differ in acceptance and rent collection. The game summaries also describe little mortgage use by the smaller model and substantial building by the larger model after completing a color group.

## Patterns shared across sizes.

Qwen proposes trades most frequently, Mistral accepts the largest share of offers, and Gemma proposes trades least frequently at both sizes. Other behaviors, especially rent waiving, differ sharply within families. These results support describing models through several kinds of actions. They do not justify assigning one fixed strategy to an entire family or assuming that behavior against identical models
conclusion:
We presented AgentMonopoly and used it to study how LLM agents behave and respond to persona instructions in Monopoly. Under a shared prompt, the tested models differ in trading and rent waiving. Some patterns appear at both model sizes, while others differ substantially. Larger models do not consistently win more games. Personas intended to change baseline behavior affect the agents’ words and some actions, but the changes do not consistently extend to every behavior the role calls for. Assessing whether instructions guide an agent therefore requires examining communication, several types of actions, and outcomes together.

AgentMonopoly also provides a basis for further studies. Its game engine and recorded interactions support repeating these comparisons with other prompts, personas, model families, and player counts. Future experiments can assign each persona to each model and use more games to test which findings hold across these settings. The environment can also be extended with different rules to study how the choices available to agents affect their behavior.
